dataset: Matric Practice Question Bank — generated from the chapter study notes
source: Derived strictly from the 171 extracted study-note chapters (assets/notes/*.json) of the supplied archive
generation: Each chapter produced 5 exam-style questions (easy->hard) with worked step-by-step solutions, plus 2 similar practice questions per question

questions.question: In parts of Eritrea, families keep a permanent or semi-permanent village base where they live for several months of the year, often planting crops in riverbeds or under spate irrigation, and during the hot dry season they move with their livestock from the hot lowlands to the cool highlands in search of pasture and water. This seasonal movement, called transhumance, is the defining practice of which farming system described in the chapter?
options: A. Nomadic pastoralism
B. Semi-nomadic pastoralism
C. Sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming)
D. Intensive commercial poultry farming
questions.answer: B. Semi-nomadic pastoralism

solution_steps.title: Recall the meaning of transhumance
solution_steps.detail: Transhumance is the seasonal migration of people and their livestock from the hot lowlands to the cool highlands in search of pasture and water.

solution_steps.title: Match the practice to the correct system
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that semi-nomadic pastoralism is the system in which families establish a permanent or semi-permanent village base, plant crops in riverbeds or under spate irrigation (such as in the Sheeb area), and practise transhumance during the hot dry season. It accounts for approximately $$22\%$$ of the population.

solution_steps.title: Check every other option against the chapter
solution_steps.detail: Nomadic pastoralism moves the entire family constantly with no settled base; sedentary agro-pastoralism keeps permanent villages in the highlands without seasonal migration; intensive commercial poultry farms keep birds under confinement for egg production. Each of these contradicts the description, so none is also correct.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The only system that combines a semi-permanent village base, spate-irrigation cropping and seasonal lowland-to-highland migration is semi-nomadic pastoralism.

similar_questions.question: A community in the North Western lowlands of Eritrea owns its grazing land communally, and the entire family moves continuously with its herds of cattle, camels, sheep, goats and donkeys in search of pasture and water. Livestock are kept mainly for milk and social prestige rather than for meat. Which farming system described in the chapter does this community practise?
similar_questions.answer: Nomadic pastoralism, which represents approximately $$11\%$$ of the population

solution_steps.title: List the distinguishing features
solution_steps.detail: The description gives three key features: communal land ownership, constant movement of the whole family, and livestock kept mainly for milk and social prestige.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the chapter's systems
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes nomadic pastoralism as prevalent in the dry, semi-desert zones of the Red Sea coast and the North Western lowlands, with families that do not settle in one place, communal land ownership, and livestock kept primarily for milk and social prestige; it represents about $$11\%$$ of the population.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the other systems
solution_steps.detail: Semi-nomadic pastoralism has a permanent or semi-permanent village base, sedentary agro-pastoralism has permanent villages with cultivation and livestock on the same farm, and commercial systems are fixed and specialized, so none fits a community that is always on the move.

similar_questions.variant_note: The target system is changed from semi-nomadic to nomadic pastoralism, and the stem is rewritten around communal land ownership plus constant movement of the whole family instead of transhumance and spate irrigation.

similar_questions.question: Peri-urban dairy farms around Asmara keep specialized Holstein-Friesian cattle in fixed units and rely on purchased feeds such as alfalfa, wheat bran and sesame cake, while commercial poultry farms nearby produce eggs under confinement using the White Leghorn breed. Under which category of farming does the chapter place these enterprises?
similar_questions.answer: Intensive commercial systems (peri-urban dairy farms and commercial poultry farms)

solution_steps.title: Identify the features of the enterprises
solution_steps.detail: Fixed location near a city, specialized high-yielding breeds and purchased concentrate feeds or confinement are all features of production organized for the market rather than for subsistence.

solution_steps.title: Recall the chapter's category
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that in addition to the three traditional systems, intensive commercial systems are expanding, and it names peri-urban dairy farms (Holstein-Friesian, purchased alfalfa, wheat bran and sesame cake) and commercial poultry farms (White Leghorn, eggs under confinement) as examples.

solution_steps.title: Confirm the exclusion of traditional systems
solution_steps.detail: The three traditional systems are nomadic pastoralism ($$11\%$$), semi-nomadic pastoralism ($$22\%$$) and sedentary agro-pastoralism ($$67\%$$); all three are based on communal or village land and family labour, not on specialized purchased inputs, so the dairy and poultry units do not belong to them.

similar_questions.variant_note: The question moves from identifying a traditional system by its migration pattern to identifying the non-traditional intensive commercial category, using the Asmara dairy and confinement poultry examples instead of transhumance.

questions.question: Two $$3\text{-hectare}$$ plots are monitored in Eritrea. Plot A lies on the steep Eastern Escarpment, where the chapter estimates annual soil loss at $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$. Plot B lies in the dry lowlands, where annual soil loss is $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$. (a) Calculate the total annual soil loss in tons for each plot. (b) Determine how many times greater the soil loss on Plot A is than on Plot B, and state the difference in tons.
questions.answer: Plot A loses $$111\text{ tons per year}$$ and Plot B loses $$18\text{ tons per year}$$; Plot A loses about $$6.2$$ times as much soil, a difference of $$93\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working formula
solution_steps.detail: Total annual soil loss = soil-loss rate per hectare x area of the plot in hectares.

solution_steps.title: Compute the loss on Plot A
solution_steps.detail: Plot A: $$37\text{ tons per hectare} \times 3\text{ ha} = 111\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the loss on Plot B
solution_steps.detail: Plot B: $$6\text{ tons per hectare} \times 3\text{ ha} = 18\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find how many times greater Plot A's loss is
solution_steps.detail: Ratio = $$\dfrac{111}{18} = 6.17$$, which rounds to about $$6.2$$ times.

solution_steps.title: Find the difference and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Difference = $$111 - 18 = 93\text{ tons per year}$$. The Eastern Escarpment plot therefore loses about $$6.2$$ times as much soil as the dry lowland plot, that is, $$93\text{ tons}$$ more each year.

similar_questions.question: A farmer near Massawa farms two $$5\text{-hectare}$$ plots. The first plot lies in the moist lowlands, where the chapter estimates annual soil loss at $$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$; the second lies in the dry lowlands, where the estimate is $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$. Calculate the annual soil loss of each plot and state how many times greater the moist lowland loss is.
similar_questions.answer: The moist lowland plot loses $$235\text{ tons per year}$$ and the dry lowland plot loses $$30\text{ tons per year}$$; the moist lowland loss is about $$7.8$$ times greater.

solution_steps.title: Apply the soil-loss formula
solution_steps.detail: Total annual soil loss = rate per hectare x area, so each plot is treated separately with its own chapter rate.

solution_steps.title: Moist lowland plot
solution_steps.detail: $$47\text{ tons per hectare} \times 5\text{ ha} = 235\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Dry lowland plot
solution_steps.detail: $$6\text{ tons per hectare} \times 5\text{ ha} = 30\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two losses
solution_steps.detail: Ratio = $$\dfrac{235}{30} = 7.83$$, which rounds to about $$7.8$$ times greater.

similar_questions.variant_note: The zones compared are changed from steep Eastern Escarpment versus dry lowlands to moist lowlands ($$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$) versus dry lowlands, and the plot area is increased from $$3\text{ ha}$$ to $$5\text{ ha}$$.

similar_questions.question: An extension agent compares an $$8\text{-hectare}$$ block of steep highland fields with an $$8\text{-hectare}$$ block on the Eastern Escarpment. The chapter gives the minimum steep-highland loss as $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$ and the Eastern Escarpment loss as $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$. Find the annual soil loss of each block and express the steep-highland excess as a ratio and in tons.
similar_questions.answer: The steep highland block loses $$400\text{ tons per year}$$ and the Eastern Escarpment block loses $$296\text{ tons per year}$$; the steep highland block loses about $$1.35$$ times as much, an excess of $$104\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify the two chapter rates
solution_steps.detail: Steep highland minimum = $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$; Eastern Escarpment = $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$; both blocks are $$8\text{ ha}$$.

solution_steps.title: Steep highland block
solution_steps.detail: $$50\text{ tons per hectare} \times 8\text{ ha} = 400\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Eastern Escarpment block
solution_steps.detail: $$37\text{ tons per hectare} \times 8\text{ ha} = 296\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Ratio and excess
solution_steps.detail: Ratio = $$\dfrac{400}{296} = 1.35$$; excess = $$400 - 296 = 104\text{ tons per year}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: The plot area is raised from $$3\text{ ha}$$ to $$8\text{ ha}$$ and the comparison now pairs the steep highland zone (used at its $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$ minimum) with the Eastern Escarpment, and it asks for both a ratio and the absolute excess.

questions.question: A survey of $$2\,000$$ rural households in a district of Eritrea found that their farming systems follow the national pattern given in the chapter: $$11\%$$ nomadic pastoralism, $$22\%$$ semi-nomadic pastoralism and $$67\%$$ sedentary agro-pastoralism. Calculate the number of households in the survey that belong to each of the three farming systems, and verify that the three numbers add up to the surveyed total.
questions.answer: $$220$$ nomadic pastoralist, $$440$$ semi-nomadic pastoralist and $$1\,340$$ sedentary agro-pastoralist households; the three figures add up to $$2\,000$$ households.

solution_steps.title: State the method
solution_steps.detail: Number of households in a category = percentage of that category x total number of households surveyed, with the percentage written as a decimal fraction.

solution_steps.title: Nomadic pastoralist households
solution_steps.detail: $$0.11 \times 2\,000 = 220$$ households.

solution_steps.title: Semi-nomadic pastoralist households
solution_steps.detail: $$0.22 \times 2\,000 = 440$$ households.

solution_steps.title: Check the total
solution_steps.detail: $$220 + 440 + 1\,340 = 2\,000$$ households, which equals the number surveyed, so the allocation is consistent.

similar_questions.question: In the Anseba region, $$4\,500$$ farming households are classified according to the chapter's national pattern of $$11\%$$ nomadic pastoralism, $$22\%$$ semi-nomadic pastoralism and $$67\%$$ sedentary agro-pastoralism. How many households fall into each of the three systems, and how many are not nomadic pastoralists?
similar_questions.answer: $$495$$ nomadic pastoralist, $$990$$ semi-nomadic pastoralist and $$3\,015$$ sedentary agro-pastoralist households; $$4\,005$$ households are not nomadic pastoralists.

solution_steps.title: Set out the percentages as decimals
Nomadic pastoralists
solution_steps.detail: $$0.11 \times 4\,500 = 495$$ households.

solution_steps.title: Semi-nomadic pastoralists
solution_steps.detail: $$0.22 \times 4\,500 = 990$$ households.

solution_steps.title: Non-nomadic households and check
solution_steps.detail: $$4\,500 - 495 = 4\,005$$ households are not nomadic pastoralists; also $$495 + 990 + 3\,015 = 4\,500$$, confirming the allocation.

similar_questions.variant_note: The sample size is changed from $$2\,000$$ to $$4\,500$$ households, the setting is named as the Anseba region, and an extra sub-question asks for the number of households that are not nomadic pastoralists.

similar_questions.question: In a district survey, $$670$$ households were classified as sedentary agro-pastoralists and this group made up $$67\%$$ of all the households surveyed. Using the chapter's percentages, find the total number of households surveyed and then the number of nomadic and semi-nomadic pastoralist households.
similar_questions.answer: $$1\,000$$ households were surveyed in total: $$110$$ nomadic pastoralist and $$220$$ semi-nomadic pastoralist households.

solution_steps.title: Work backwards from the known group
solution_steps.detail: If $$670$$ households are $$67\%$$ of the sample, the total sample $$T$$ satisfies $$0.67 \times T = 670$$.

solution_steps.title: Solve for the total
solution_steps.detail: $$T = \dfrac{670}{0.67} = 1\,000$$ households surveyed.

solution_steps.title: Nomadic pastoralist households
solution_steps.detail: $$0.11 \times 1\,000 = 110$$ households.

solution_steps.title: Semi-nomadic pastoralist households
solution_steps.detail: $$0.22 \times 1\,000 = 220$$ households, and the check $$110 + 220 + 670 = 1\,000$$ confirms the answer.

similar_questions.variant_note: The calculation is reversed: instead of being given the sample total, the solver is given the $$67\%$$ sedentary group of $$670$$ households and must find the total and the other two categories.

questions.question: A catchment near Keren contains $$200\text{ ha}$$ of steep highland fields, $$300\text{ ha}$$ of moist lowland fields and $$500\text{ ha}$$ of dry lowland fields. Using the chapter's annual soil-loss estimates of $$50\text{ to }100\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for steep highlands, $$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for moist lowlands and $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for dry lowlands, calculate (a) the minimum and (b) the maximum total annual soil loss of the catchment, and (c) the percentage of the minimum total loss that comes from the dry lowland fields.
questions.answer: Minimum total loss = $$27\,100\text{ tons per year}$$; maximum total loss = $$37\,100\text{ tons per year}$$; the dry lowland fields contribute about $$11.1\%$$ of the minimum total loss.

solution_steps.title: Set up the calculation
solution_steps.detail: For each zone, soil loss = rate per hectare x area in hectares. Because the steep highland rate is given as a range, the minimum total uses $$50\text{ tons per hectare}$$ and the maximum total uses $$100\text{ tons per hectare}$$.

solution_steps.title: Steep highland contribution
solution_steps.detail: Minimum: $$200 \times 50 = 10\,000\text{ tons}$$; maximum: $$200 \times 100 = 20\,000\text{ tons}$$.

solution_steps.title: Moist lowland contribution
solution_steps.detail: $$300 \times 47 = 14\,100\text{ tons}$$, a single value because only one rate is given.

solution_steps.title: Dry lowland contribution
solution_steps.detail: $$500 \times 6 = 3\,000\text{ tons}$$, also a single value.

solution_steps.title: Total the catchment loss
solution_steps.detail: Minimum total = $$10\,000 + 14\,100 + 3\,000 = 27\,100\text{ tons per year}$$; maximum total = $$20\,000 + 14\,100 + 3\,000 = 37\,100\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the dry lowland share of the minimum
Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The catchment loses between $$27\,100$$ and $$37\,100\text{ tons}$$ of soil each year, and the dry lowland fields - the largest area but the gentlest zone - account for only about $$11.1\%$$ of the minimum total loss.

similar_questions.question: A catchment in the Asmara highlands has $$400\text{ ha}$$ of steep highland fields, $$250\text{ ha}$$ of moist lowland fields and $$750\text{ ha}$$ of dry lowland fields. Using the chapter's rates of $$50\text{ to }100\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for steep highlands, $$47\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for moist lowlands and $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$ for dry lowlands, find the minimum and maximum total annual soil loss and the percentage of the minimum total that comes from the dry lowland fields.
similar_questions.answer: Minimum total loss = $$36\,250\text{ tons per year}$$; maximum total loss = $$56\,250\text{ tons per year}$$; the dry lowland fields contribute about $$12.4\%$$ of the minimum total loss.

solution_steps.title: Steep highland contribution
solution_steps.detail: $$400 \times 50 = 20\,000\text{ tons}$$ at minimum and $$400 \times 100 = 40\,000\text{ tons}$$ at maximum.

solution_steps.title: Moist lowland contribution
solution_steps.detail: $$250 \times 47 = 11\,750\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Dry lowland contribution
solution_steps.detail: $$750 \times 6 = 4\,500\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Dry lowland share of the minimum

similar_questions.variant_note: The zone areas are changed ($$400$$, $$250$$ and $$750\text{ ha}$$ instead of $$200$$, $$300$$ and $$500\text{ ha}$$), the setting moves from Keren to the Asmara highlands, and the dry lowland block is proportionally larger so its share rises from about $$11.1\%$$ to about $$12.4\%$$.

similar_questions.question: An extension agent works in a catchment on the Eastern Escarpment that has $$250\text{ ha}$$ of escarpment fields and $$900\text{ ha}$$ of dry lowland fields. The chapter's estimates are $$37\text{ tons per hectare}$$ per year on the Eastern Escarpment and $$6\text{ tons per hectare}$$ per year in the dry lowlands. Calculate the total annual soil loss of the whole catchment and the percentage by which the escarpment fields lose more soil than the dry lowland fields.
similar_questions.answer: Total catchment loss = $$14\,650\text{ tons per year}$$; the escarpment fields lose about $$71.3\%$$ more soil than the dry lowland fields.

solution_steps.title: Escarpment loss
solution_steps.detail: $$250\text{ ha} \times 37\text{ tons per hectare} = 9\,250\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Dry lowland loss
solution_steps.detail: $$900\text{ ha} \times 6\text{ tons per hectare} = 5\,400\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Percentage excess of the escarpment fields
Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Although the dry lowland block is more than three times larger in area, its gentler slope means the smaller escarpment block still loses about $$71.3\%$$ more soil than it does.

similar_questions.variant_note: The range-based steep highland zone is replaced by the single-valued Eastern Escarpment rate, the areas are changed, and the final sub-question asks for a percentage excess over the dry lowlands instead of a share of the catchment total.

concepts: agriculture as raw material for industry
questions.question: The chapter shows that agriculture supplies industry with raw materials and also earns Eritrea foreign currency. Choose two products from the chapter's agricultural-product table and, for each, trace the chain from farm product to industrial raw material to derived industrial good to non-food by-product. Then explain how the foreign-currency role and the raw-material role reinforce one another in a developing economy such as Eritrea's.
questions.answer: Cotton supplies fiber for clothes, textiles and canvas while its cottonseed cake feeds animals, and malting barley supplies grain starch for beer and malt beverages while brewers' spent grain feeds livestock; exports of farm products such as live animals, skins, hides, meat, oil seeds, cotton and processed fruits and vegetables earn the foreign exchange used to import petroleum, machinery, medicine and fertilizers, and those imports in turn raise the raw-material output that keeps agro-industries and exports growing.

solution_steps.title: State the chain principle
solution_steps.detail: Agriculture is the foundation of agro-based industries: each farm product supplies a raw material that industry converts into a main derived good, and the conversion leaves a non-food by-product that is usually returned to agriculture.

solution_steps.title: Trace the cotton chain
solution_steps.detail: Cotton crop -> fiber -> clothes, textiles and canvas, with cottonseed cake left over as an animal feed by-product.

solution_steps.title: Trace the malting barley chain
solution_steps.detail: Malting barley -> grain starch -> beer and malt beverages, with brewers' spent grain left over as a livestock feed by-product.

solution_steps.title: Explain the foreign-currency role
solution_steps.detail: Exporting products such as live animals, skins, hides, meat, oil seeds, cotton and processed fruits and vegetables earns foreign exchange, and that currency is used to import petroleum, machinery, medicine and fertilizers.

solution_steps.title: Show how the two roles reinforce each other
solution_steps.detail: Export earnings pay for the machinery and fertilizer that raise farm output, so more raw material reaches agro-industries and more finished goods and by-products become available; the by-products then lower livestock feed costs, and livestock itself is an export item (live animals, skins, hides), so industrial demand and export earnings continually feed back into farm production.

similar_questions.question: Sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming) is described in the chapter as a highly integrated system. Explain the two-way linkage between crops and livestock in this system and state the approximate share of the Eritrean population that practises it.
similar_questions.answer: Crop residues such as straw are saved to feed the animals during the dry season, and animal manure is returned to the fields to maintain soil fertility; this system represents approximately $$67\%$$ of the population.

solution_steps.title: Identify the system and its setting
solution_steps.detail: Sedentary agro-pastoralism is the most dominant farming system in Eritrea, practised in permanent villages of the moist and arid Highlands, where crops and livestock are kept on the same farm.

solution_steps.title: Link from crops to livestock
solution_steps.detail: Crop residues, especially straw, are saved and used as feed for the animals during the dry season, when grazing is scarce.

solution_steps.title: Link from livestock back to crops
solution_steps.detail: Animal manure is returned to the fields to maintain soil fertility, so the livestock enterprise supports the next crop cycle.

solution_steps.title: State the population share
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives this system as approximately $$67\%$$ of the population, compared with $$22\%$$ semi-nomadic and $$11\%$$ nomadic pastoralism.

similar_questions.variant_note: The focus shifts from the industrial raw-material and foreign-currency chains of specific export products to the internal crop-livestock linkage of sedentary agro-pastoralism, and the answer must also supply the chapter's $$67\%$$ population share.

similar_questions.question: The chapter states that agriculture has both negative and positive environmental impacts. Using the examples given in the chapter, name two negative impacts arising from agricultural chemicals, overgrazing and deforestation, and two positive practices that can be achieved through sustainable management; then explain the chapter's pro-tip about balancing economic gains with environmental impacts.
similar_questions.answer: Negative impacts include pollution and damage from the misuse of pesticides, herbicides and synthetic fertilizers, overgrazing, and deforestation; positive impacts come from afforestation, land reclamation, soil conservation and organic manuring, and the pro-tip advises balancing tangible economic gains such as crop yields against intangible environmental effects such as soil erosion or loss of biodiversity so that production remains sustainable.

solution_steps.title: Recall the negative impacts
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists the misuse of agricultural chemicals (pesticides, herbicides and synthetic fertilizers), overgrazing, and deforestation as the sources of negative environmental impact.

solution_steps.title: Recall the positive practices
solution_steps.detail: Sustainable practices named in the chapter are afforestation, land reclamation, soil conservation and organic manuring.

solution_steps.title: Explain the balancing principle
solution_steps.detail: The pro-tip states that when planning agricultural development you must balance the tangible economic gains, such as crop yields, with the intangible environmental impacts, such as soil erosion or loss of biodiversity.

solution_steps.title: State why this matters
solution_steps.detail: Balancing the two ensures long-term sustainability, because practices that raise yields today but destroy soil and biodiversity reduce the land's productive potential for future seasons.

similar_questions.variant_note: The question moves from industrial and foreign-exchange linkages to environmental-impact analysis, requiring the negative impacts, the positive sustainable practices, and the reasoning behind the chapter's pro-tip on long-term sustainability.

questions.question: A meteorological station at Keren must find out how much water is lost from an open water surface so that the irrigation requirement of a nearby vegetable field can be estimated. Which instrument should the technician read?
options: A. Sunshine Recorder
B. Barograph
C. Evaporation Pan
D. Self-recording Anemometer
questions.answer: C. Evaporation Pan

solution_steps.title: Identify the climate element needed
solution_steps.detail: The task is to measure the rate at which water evaporates from an open surface, which is the water loss the crop field must replace through irrigation.

solution_steps.title: Match the element to the instrument
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists the Evaporation Pan as the instrument that measures the rate of water evaporation from an open surface, and states its practical value as calculating irrigation water requirements.

solution_steps.title: Check every distractor
solution_steps.detail: The Sunshine Recorder records the daily duration of bright sunlight hours; the Barograph continuously records atmospheric pressure changes; the Self-recording Anemometer measures wind speed and direction. None of these three measures evaporation, so none is also correct.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only option C measures the evaporation rate of an open water surface, so C is the single defensible answer.

similar_questions.question: A station near Massawa is required to record the daily duration of bright sunlight hours for a crop-weather summary. Which instrument should be installed?
similar_questions.answer: B. Sunshine Recorder

solution_steps.title: State the element required
solution_steps.detail: The station needs the daily duration of bright sunlight hours, not rainfall, temperature or humidity.

solution_steps.title: Match element to instrument
solution_steps.detail: The chapter assigns the recording of daily bright sunshine duration to the Sunshine Recorder.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the distractors
solution_steps.detail: The Standard Rain Gauge measures the quantity and rate of precipitation; the Thermo-hygrograph records temperature and relative humidity together; the Digital Thermometer measures maximum and minimum daily ambient temperatures. None records sunshine duration.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The correct and only fitting instrument is the Sunshine Recorder, so the answer is B.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the MC format and the instrument-to-element matching skill but changes the location from Keren to Massawa, the climate element from evaporation to sunshine duration, the correct answer from an Evaporation Pan to a Sunshine Recorder, and supplies a completely new distractor set.

similar_questions.question: At a station in the Arid Highland, an officer must keep a continuous record of atmospheric pressure changes. Which instrument is designed for this?
similar_questions.answer: A. Barograph

solution_steps.title: Identify the element
solution_steps.detail: The requirement is a continuous record of atmospheric pressure changes.

solution_steps.title: Recall the instrument list
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the Barograph continuously records atmospheric pressure changes.

solution_steps.title: Test the distractors
solution_steps.detail: The Evaporation Pan measures the evaporation rate from an open surface, the Standard Rain Gauge measures precipitation quantity and rate, and the Digital Thermometer measures maximum and minimum daily ambient temperatures. All three measure different elements.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only the Barograph records pressure, so the answer is A.

similar_questions.variant_note: Same instrument-identification skill, but the target element becomes atmospheric pressure and the answer becomes the Barograph; the setting moves to the Arid Highland and the distractors are redrawn so that no option overlaps with the main question.

questions.question: Complete the following statement with the correct term: __________ is the general state of the atmosphere over a long period of time, resulting from energy and mass exchange within the atmosphere and between the atmosphere and the Earth's surface.
questions.answer: Climate

solution_steps.title: Read the definition for its key phrases
solution_steps.detail: The decisive phrases are 'general state of the atmosphere' and 'over a long period of time'.

solution_steps.title: Rule out the short-term concept
solution_steps.detail: Weather describes short-term atmospheric changes, so weather does not fit a definition built on a long period of time.

solution_steps.title: Match the chapter definition
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines climate as the general state of the atmosphere over a long period of time, resulting from energy and mass exchange within the atmosphere and between the atmosphere and the Earth's surface.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The missing term is Climate, which is the long-term condition that determines an area's suitability for crop and livestock production.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statement with the correct term: the soil moisture level at which plants can no longer extract water and therefore wilt permanently is called the __________.
similar_questions.answer: Wilting Point

solution_steps.title: Recall the three soil water states
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives saturation, field capacity and wilting point as the key water states of soil.

solution_steps.title: Distinguish them
solution_steps.detail: At saturation all pores are completely filled with water; at field capacity the excess water has already drained away under gravity.

solution_steps.title: Match the description given
solution_steps.detail: The level at which plants can no longer extract water and wilt permanently is by definition the wilting point.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The missing term is wilting point.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the fill-in-the-blank format but moves the concept from a climate definition to a soil-water state; the required term, the supporting facts and the reasoning chain are all different from the main question.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statement with the correct term: the upper portion of the regolith, consisting of the O, A and B horizons, is called the __________.
similar_questions.answer: Solum

solution_steps.title: Recall the soil profile horizons
solution_steps.detail: A vertical cross-section of soil shows the O, A, B and C horizons, which together make up the soil profile.

solution_steps.title: Note what the C-horizon is
solution_steps.detail: The C-horizon is unconsolidated parent material, little affected by soil-forming processes, so it lies outside the biochemically active upper section.

solution_steps.title: Recall the chapter term
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the upper portion of the regolith, comprising the O, A and B horizons, is called the solum and represents the true biochemically active soil layer.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The missing term is solum.

similar_questions.variant_note: Still a one-term completion item, but it draws on soil-profile terminology instead of the climate definition, and it tests a different named concept (the solum) from the wilting-point variant.

questions.question: A soil scientist collected a core sample from a barley field near Asmara. The core has a total volume of $$200\text{ cm}^3$$. Its moist mass is $$300\text{ g}$$, and its mass after oven drying is $$260\text{ g}$$. Calculate the bulk density of this soil and state its standard unit.

solution_steps.title: Name the formula
solution_steps.detail: Bulk density is the mass of oven-dry soil per unit of total volume: $$BD = \frac{W_d}{V_t}$$, where $$W_d$$ is the mass of dry soil and $$V_t$$ is the total volume including both solids and pore spaces.

solution_steps.title: Select the correct mass and volume
solution_steps.detail: The formula requires the oven-dry mass, so $$W_d = 260\text{ g}$$ and $$V_t = 200\text{ cm}^3$$. The moist mass of $$300\text{ g}$$ includes water held in the pores and must not be used.

solution_steps.title: Substitute into the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$BD = \frac{260\text{ g}}{200\text{ cm}^3}$$

solution_steps.title: State the result with its unit
solution_steps.detail: Bulk density is reported in grams per cubic centimeter, so $$BD = 1.3\text{ g/cm}^3$$. This is a moderately dense soil, since the pore spaces occupy the remaining volume fraction.

similar_questions.question: A core sample taken from a sorghum plot in the Mereb-Gash area has a total volume of $$250\text{ cm}^3$$. Its moist mass is $$400\text{ g}$$ and its oven-dry mass is $$350\text{ g}$$. Calculate the bulk density of this soil.

solution_steps.title: Name the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$BD = \frac{W_d}{V_t}$$, the mass of oven-dry soil divided by the total volume of soil.

solution_steps.title: Pick the oven-dry mass
solution_steps.detail: Use $$W_d = 350\text{ g}$$; the moist mass of $$400\text{ g}$$ contains water and would overstate the density.

solution_steps.title: Substitute
solution_steps.detail: $$BD = \frac{350\text{ g}}{250\text{ cm}^3}$$

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: $$BD = 1.4\text{ g/cm}^3$$, a slightly denser soil than the Asmara barley-field sample.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the location and crop and replaces all three data values (200 cm3, 300 g, 260 g become 250 cm3, 400 g, 350 g), so the result changes from 1.3 to 1.4 g/cm3 while the same formula and the same moist-mass trap are tested.

similar_questions.question: A cylindrical core of total volume $$400\text{ cm}^3$$ is taken from a pasture in the Central Highlands; its oven-dry mass is $$500\text{ g}$$. Calculate the bulk density, and state what a much higher bulk density value would indicate about the pore spaces of a soil.
similar_questions.answer: $$BD = 1.25\text{ g/cm}^3$$; a much higher bulk density indicates a compacted soil whose pore spaces have been compressed.

solution_steps.title: Name the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$BD = \frac{W_d}{V_t}$$, with volume taken as the total volume of solids plus pores.

solution_steps.title: Interpret a higher value
solution_steps.detail: Because the total volume includes the pore spaces, a higher bulk density means more solid mass packed into the same volume, that is, compressed pore spaces; the chapter notes that compacted soils have high bulk density due to compressed pore spaces.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The pasture soil has $$BD = 1.25\text{ g/cm}^3$$, and a much higher figure would signal compaction.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses a different setting (Central Highlands pasture) with new numbers (400 cm3 and 500 g giving 1.25 g/cm3), gives no moist mass so the learner cannot be misled by it, and adds an interpretive part asking what a higher bulk density implies about pore spaces.

questions.question: Two adjacent fields at Keren have developed from the same parent material and both have a particle density of $$2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$$. Field A has received organic matter additions and has a bulk density of $$1.325\text{ g/cm}^3$$. Field B was repeatedly worked with heavy machinery while wet and has a bulk density of $$1.855\text{ g/cm}^3$$. (a) Calculate the total porosity of each field. (b) State which field has the greater water-holding capacity and explain why in terms of pore spaces.
questions.answer: (a) Field A = $$50\%$$ porosity, Field B = $$30\%$$ porosity. (b) Field A has the greater water-holding capacity because its higher porosity leaves more pore space to hold water, while compaction in Field B has compressed the macropores that store and transmit water.

solution_steps.title: Name the porosity formula
solution_steps.detail: Porosity can be derived from the two densities as $$f = \left(1 - \frac{BD}{PD}\right) \times 100$$, where $$BD$$ is bulk density and $$PD$$ is particle density.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the values for Field A
solution_steps.detail: $$f_A = \left(1 - \frac{1.325}{2.65}\right) \times 100$$

solution_steps.title: Compute the porosity of Field A
Substitute and compute for Field B
Interpret the pore-space difference
solution_steps.detail: Field A has 50% of its volume as pore space while Field B has only 30%. The chapter states that compacted soils have a lower water-holding capacity because compressing the soil reduces the larger pores (macropores), which are critical for soil aeration and rapid water movement.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Field A has the greater water-holding capacity. Its higher porosity means more pore volume available to store water, whereas the machinery traffic on wet Field B compressed the pore spaces and lowered its porosity to 30%.

similar_questions.question: Two plots at Massawa are formed from the same material and both have a particle density of $$2.65\text{ g/cm}^3$$. Plot X has a bulk density of $$1.06\text{ g/cm}^3$$ and Plot Y has a bulk density of $$1.59\text{ g/cm}^3$$. Calculate the total porosity of each plot and say which plot is the more compacted.
similar_questions.answer: Plot X = $$60\%$$ porosity, Plot Y = $$40\%$$ porosity; Plot Y is the more compacted soil.

solution_steps.title: Name the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$f = \left(1 - \frac{BD}{PD}\right) \times 100$$

solution_steps.title: Compare and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Plot Y has the higher bulk density and therefore the lower porosity, so its pore spaces are more compressed and Plot Y is the more compacted soil.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the location to Massawa and the two bulk densities to 1.06 and 1.59 g/cm3, giving porosities of 60% and 40% instead of 50% and 30%; the comparison is now phrased as identifying the more compacted plot rather than the one with greater water-holding capacity.

similar_questions.question: A $$300\text{ cm}^3$$ soil sample from the Arid Lowland contains $$135\text{ cm}^3$$ of pore space. (a) Calculate its porosity using the pore-volume form of the formula. (b) Compare it with an ideal loam surface soil of 50% porosity and state whether this sample can be described as compacted.
similar_questions.answer: $$f = 45\%$$; since 45% is below the 50% porosity of an ideal loam surface soil, the sample has less pore space than ideal and can be described as somewhat compacted.

solution_steps.title: Name the pore-volume formula
solution_steps.detail: Porosity is the percentage of total soil volume occupied by pore spaces: $$f = \left(\frac{V_p}{V_t}\right) \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the values
solution_steps.detail: $$V_p = 135\text{ cm}^3$$ and $$V_t = 300\text{ cm}^3$$, so $$f = \left(\frac{135}{300}\right) \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the ideal loam
solution_steps.detail: An ideal loam surface soil has about 50% pore space, split between air and water. At 45% the sample has fewer pores, which is consistent with compression of pore spaces in a compacted soil.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The sample has a porosity of 45% and, being below the 50% ideal, can be described as somewhat compacted.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the porosity concept but switches to the pore-volume formula and supplies volumes rather than densities (300 cm3 total, 135 cm3 of pores giving 45%), so the learner must choose the correct formula and add a comparison with the ideal loam figure rather than comparing two fields directly.

questions.question: A development agency plans to expand an irrigated cotton and sesame scheme on the south-western plains and the Upper Mereb valley. (a) Name the agro-ecological zone that covers this area. (b) State the percentage of the national land area it occupies and its average annual rainfall range. (c) Name two other crops listed for this zone.
questions.answer: (a) The Moist Lowland zone. (b) It occupies $$16\%$$ of the total land area and receives an average annual rainfall of $$500 - 800\text{ mm}$$. (c) Sorghum and maize (the zone also supports cattle, goats and camels).

solution_steps.title: Use the geographical clue
solution_steps.detail: The chapter locates the Moist Lowland in the south-western plains and the Upper Mereb valley, which matches the area described by the agency.

solution_steps.title: Confirm with the vegetation and crop description
solution_steps.detail: The zone is dominated by savannah woodlands and the chapter states it has high potential for sorghum, sesame, cotton and maize, which is consistent with a cotton and sesame scheme.

solution_steps.title: Read the share of land area and rainfall
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table gives the Moist Lowland as $$16\%$$ of the total land area with an average annual rainfall of $$500 - 800\text{ mm}$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify two other crops
solution_steps.detail: Besides cotton and sesame, the zone is listed for sorghum and maize; its livestock types are cattle, goats and camels.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: (a) Moist Lowland; (b) $$16\%$$ of the total land area and $$500 - 800\text{ mm}$$ average annual rainfall; (c) sorghum and maize.

similar_questions.question: A farmers' cooperative on the Eastern Escarpment wants to grow coffee and maize under rain-fed conditions. Name the agro-ecological zone of this area, state the percentage of the national land area it occupies and its average annual rainfall range, and name the two tree genera that dominate its forests.
similar_questions.answer: The Sub-humid Escarpment, occupying $$1\%$$ of the total land area with an average annual rainfall of $$700 - 1\,100\text{ mm}$$; its forests are dominated by *Juniperus* and *Olea*.

solution_steps.title: Match the location to the zone
solution_steps.detail: The chapter places the Sub-humid Escarpment on the Eastern Escarpment, with steep terrain and high rainfall.

solution_steps.title: Check the crop clue
solution_steps.detail: The crops listed for this zone are coffee and maize, which matches the cooperative's plan.

solution_steps.title: Read the area share and rainfall
solution_steps.detail: The table gives the Sub-humid zone as $$1\%$$ of the total land area with $$700 - 1\,100\text{ mm}$$ average annual rainfall.

solution_steps.title: Identify the dominant tree genera
solution_steps.detail: The high rainfall supports *Juniperus* and *Olea* forests.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The zone is the Sub-humid Escarpment ($$1\%$$ of land area; $$700 - 1\,100\text{ mm}$$ rainfall), forested mainly with *Juniperus* and *Olea*.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the identify-the-zone, quote-area-and-rainfall, name-the-associated-plants structure but moves the setting from the south-western plains to the Eastern Escarpment, changes the zone to the Sub-humid Escarpment, the land share to 1%, the rainfall to 700-1100 mm, and asks for tree genera instead of crops.

similar_questions.question: Eritrea's water resources are unevenly distributed. (a) Name the only perennial river basin listed among the country's five major basins. (b) State the approximate percentage range of precipitation that is lost through evaporation and transpiration before it reaches streams or aquifers. (c) Name the type of underground water-bearing formation that stores groundwater, and give one example of an alluvial aquifer named in the chapter.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The Setit basin. (b) Approximately $$80\%\text{ to }87\%$$ of precipitation is lost through evaporation and transpiration. (c) Groundwater is stored in aquifers; examples given are the alluvial aquifers along seasonal riverbeds such as the Gash, Barka and Anseba.

solution_steps.title: Recall the river basins
solution_steps.detail: The five major basins are the Setit, Mereb-Gash, Barka-Anseba, Red Sea and the arid Danakil Depression.

solution_steps.title: Identify the perennial one
solution_steps.detail: The chapter identifies the Setit as the only perennial river among these basins.

solution_steps.title: Recall the loss fraction
solution_steps.detail: Approximately $$80\%\text{ to }87\%$$ of the precipitation is lost through evaporation and transpiration before reaching streams or aquifers.

solution_steps.title: Name the storage formation
solution_steps.detail: Groundwater is stored in underground layers of water-bearing rock or sediment called aquifers; major alluvial aquifers lie along seasonal riverbeds such as the Gash, Barka and Anseba.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The Setit is the only perennial basin, $$80\%\text{ to }87\%$$ of precipitation is lost to evaporation and transpiration, and groundwater is held in aquifers such as those along the Gash, Barka and Anseba riverbeds.

similar_questions.variant_note: Departs from agro-ecological zoning and instead tests the chapter's water-resource facts: the Setit as the only perennial basin, the 80-87% evaporation and transpiration loss, and the definition and examples of aquifers, so the required facts and reasoning differ entirely from the main question and from the other variant.

questions.question: Complete the photosynthesis equation that your chapter uses to explain how a cereal crop such as sorghum builds its food: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{______} \xrightarrow{\text{______}} \text{Sugar} + \text{______}$$ Fill in the three blanks in order, and name the pigment written above the arrow.
questions.answer: Blank 1 = Light Energy; Blank 2 = Chlorophyll; Blank 3 = O2, i.e. $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$. The pigment above the arrow is chlorophyll.

solution_steps.title: Recall the chapter equation
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines photosynthesis as the biological process in which light energy is transformed into chemical energy, and writes it as $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.

solution_steps.title: Fill the first blank (energy input)
solution_steps.detail: The only input still missing from the left-hand side is the energy source, so the first blank is Light Energy (sunlight).

solution_steps.title: Fill the second blank (the substance above the arrow)
solution_steps.detail: The chapter places Chlorophyll above the reaction arrow. Chlorophyll is the green pigment of the leaf (the leaf is the site of photosynthesis) that captures the light energy needed to drive the reaction.

solution_steps.title: Fill the third blank (by-product)
solution_steps.detail: The right-hand side already shows Sugar; the second product released by the plant is oxygen gas, so the third blank is O2.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Blank 1 = Light Energy, Blank 2 = Chlorophyll, Blank 3 = O2, giving the complete equation $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.

similar_questions.question: A farmer in Akordat wants to explain to a neighbour why a maize field must be exposed to sunlight. Complete the statement using the chapter equation: in photosynthesis, $$\text{CO}_2$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ are joined using ______ energy in the presence of the pigment ______ to produce ______ and oxygen.
similar_questions.answer: Light (solar) energy; chlorophyll; sugar. Full statement: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.

solution_steps.title: Write the chapter equation
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.

solution_steps.title: Match each blank to a term in the equation
solution_steps.detail: The energy term on the left is Light Energy; the term written above the arrow is Chlorophyll; the carbon-containing product on the right (besides O2) is Sugar.

solution_steps.title: State the completed statement
solution_steps.detail: Carbon dioxide and water are joined using light energy in the presence of chlorophyll to produce sugar and oxygen, so shaded maize cannot carry out this process normally.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed from a three-blank equation completion to a sentence-completion task, with the blanks moved from the reaction itself to a farmer-to-neighbour explanation set in Akordat; the same equation, terms and order of ideas are used.

similar_questions.question: Identify the three raw materials/inputs of photosynthesis listed in the chapter equation and name the two products formed. Then state in one sentence why the chapter calls photosynthesis the process that 'transforms light energy into chemical energy'.
similar_questions.answer: Inputs: carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$), water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) and light energy. Products: sugar and oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$). It is called a transformation of energy because light energy is captured by chlorophyll and stored in the chemical bonds of the sugar produced.

solution_steps.title: List the inputs
solution_steps.detail: Left of the arrow the chapter gives three inputs: carbon dioxide, water and light energy.

solution_steps.title: List the products
solution_steps.detail: Right of the arrow the products are sugar and oxygen gas.

solution_steps.title: Explain the energy wording
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that light energy is transformed into chemical energy; chlorophyll traps the light and the energy ends up stored in the sugar, which is why the sugar is the plant's food.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the task type from filling blanks to identifying inputs and products and justifying the chapter's definition of photosynthesis; no numbers are involved, so the whole question is conceptual rather than equation-completion.

questions.question: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands sows two plots on the same day: Plot A with field peas and Plot B with common beans. Several days later the farmer notices that in Plot B the cotyledons have been pushed above the soil surface, while in Plot A the cotyledons are still below the soil. (a) Name the type of germination shown in Plot A and in Plot B. (b) Explain which elongating structure is responsible in each case. (c) In which plot, if any, do the cotyledons act as the first photosynthetic leaves?
questions.answer: (a) Plot A (peas) = hypogeal germination; Plot B (common beans) = epigeal germination. (b) Hypogeal: the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons stay below the soil. Epigeal: the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the soil. (c) Only in Plot B (epigeal), where the cotyledons act as the first photosynthetic leaves.

solution_steps.title: Recall the two germination types
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines two types based on cotyledon movement: hypogeal germination, in which the cotyledons remain below the soil surface while the epicotyl elongates (peas, broad beans), and epigeal germination, in which the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the soil surface (common beans, castor oil).

solution_steps.title: Classify Plot A (field peas)
solution_steps.detail: In Plot A the cotyledons stay below the soil; peas are named in the chapter as an example of hypogeal germination.

solution_steps.title: Classify Plot B (common beans)
solution_steps.detail: In Plot B the cotyledons are carried above the surface; common beans are the chapter's example of epigeal germination.

solution_steps.title: Name the elongating structures
solution_steps.detail: Plot A (hypogeal): the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain underground. Plot B (epigeal): the hypocotyl elongates, lifting the cotyledons out of the soil.

solution_steps.title: Decide where cotyledons photosynthesise
solution_steps.detail: Only in Plot B, because the chapter states that in epigeal germination the cotyledons are pulled above the soil surface where they act as the first photosynthetic leaves.

similar_questions.question: A school garden in Asmara plants broad beans in one bed and castor oil in another. For each crop, state the type of germination, say whether the cotyledons finish above or below the soil surface, and name the structure whose elongation decides the position of the cotyledons.
similar_questions.answer: Broad beans: hypogeal germination, cotyledons remain below the soil, epicotyl elongates. Castor oil: epigeal germination, cotyledons are pulled above the soil, hypocotyl elongates.

solution_steps.title: Apply the chapter definitions
solution_steps.detail: Hypogeal = cotyledons remain below the surface while the epicotyl elongates; epigeal = the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the surface.

solution_steps.title: Match broad beans
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists broad beans under hypogeal germination, so their cotyledons stay below the soil and the epicotyl is the elongating structure.

solution_steps.title: Match castor oil
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists castor oil under epigeal germination, so the hypocotyl elongates and the cotyledons are carried above the soil.

similar_questions.variant_note: Replaced peas/common beans with broad beans/castor oil (the chapter's other named examples) and changed the required output from naming a type to a full comparison of cotyledon position plus the elongating structure.

similar_questions.question: Explain why the seed of a crop such as maize can germinate to a strong seedling only when three environmental conditions are present. Name the three conditions given in the chapter and state the specific role of each one.
similar_questions.answer: The three conditions are adequate water (softens the seed coat and activates the enzymes), oxygen (needed for aerobic respiration) and optimum temperature (generally $$10^\circ\text{C}$$ to $$35^\circ\text{C}$$, with about $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ optimum for most crops). Without all three, the embryo cannot resume growth and germination fails or is weak.

solution_steps.title: State what germination is
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines germination as the process by which a seed embryo wakes from dormancy and begins to grow into a seedling.

solution_steps.title: Name the three environmental conditions
solution_steps.detail: Successful germination requires adequate water, oxygen and an optimum temperature.

solution_steps.title: Give the role of each condition
solution_steps.detail: Water softens the seed coat and activates enzymes; oxygen supports aerobic respiration; temperature must be in the range of about $$10^\circ\text{C}$$ to $$35^\circ\text{C}$$ with $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ being optimum for most crops.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: All three conditions must be met together, which is why waterlogged or very cold soil gives poor emergence even when good seed is sown.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifted the concept from cotyledon movement (germination type) to the three environmental requirements for germination, using maize instead of legumes and requiring the role of each condition rather than a classification.

questions.question: A wheat crop near Keren shows a pale yellowish-green colour. An extension agent observes that the symptom is visible on the old, lower leaves while the young upper leaves are still green, and explains that this happens because nitrogen is highly mobile in the plant. According to the chapter, why does a nitrogen shortage affect the old, lower leaves before the young leaves?
options: A. Because nitrogen is immobile in the plant, so it stays fixed inside the leaves that first received it
B. Because the plant moves nitrogen out of the old leaves to support new growth, and those old leaves are the first to run short
C. Because old leaves have the smallest leaf area, so they lose nutrients to the soil before the young leaves do
D. Because old leaves receive the least sunlight, so their chlorophyll breaks down before that of the upper leaves
questions.answer: B. Because the plant moves nitrogen out of the old leaves to support new growth, and those old leaves are the first to run short.

solution_steps.title: Recall the chapter's Pro-Tip
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's Pro-Tip states that nitrogen is highly mobile in plants and that when a deficiency occurs the plant moves nitrogen from old leaves to support new growth.

solution_steps.title: Link mobility to the visible pattern
solution_steps.detail: Because nitrogen can be withdrawn from the old, lower leaves and redirected to the growing points, the older leaves are the first to fall short of nitrogen and therefore the first to show the pale yellowish-green deficiency colour.

solution_steps.title: Check option A
solution_steps.detail: A contradicts the chapter: nitrogen is described as highly mobile, not immobile, so A is false.

solution_steps.title: Check option C
solution_steps.detail: Nutrient shortage is caused by internal redistribution to new growth, not by old leaves having a smaller area or by loss of nutrients to the soil; no such process is given in the chapter, so C is false.

solution_steps.title: Check option D
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives no role for sunlight differences among leaves in nitrogen deficiency; the symptom is explained by nutrient mobility, not by a light gradient, so D is false.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only option B states the chapter's reason: nitrogen is moved out of the old leaves to support new growth, so the old leaves yellow first.

similar_questions.question: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands tells an extension agent: 'My barley leaves are small and dull bluish-green with purplish tints, and the roots look weak.' Which nutrient deficiency in the chapter table best explains this description?
similar_questions.answer: A. Phosphorus (P)

solution_steps.title: Read the described symptoms
solution_steps.detail: Small, dull bluish-green leaves with purplish tints plus poor root growth are the field signs reported.

solution_steps.title: Match against the chapter table
solution_steps.detail: The table gives phosphorus deficiency as 'small, dull bluish-green leaves with purplish tints', and phosphorus is described as aiding seed germination, root growth and flowering.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the other options
solution_steps.detail: Nitrogen gives pale yellowish-green older leaves; potassium gives scorched brown tips and margins; calcium gives poorly developed hooked leaf tips and weak root tips. None matches bluish-green purplish leaves.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the target nutrient from nitrogen to phosphorus, changed the crop from wheat to barley and the location from Keren to an unnamed highland site, and removed the 'why older leaves first' reasoning in favour of a pure symptom-identification MC.

similar_questions.question: Which statement about the nutrient requirements of crop plants is correct according to the chapter?
similar_questions.answer: C. Plants require $$16$$ essential elements, and micronutrients such as Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo and Cl are needed in tiny amounts although they are equally essential

solution_steps.title: State the chapter's total requirement
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that for healthy growth plants require $$16$$ essential elements, divided into macronutrients and micronutrients.

solution_steps.title: Check option A
solution_steps.detail: A reverses the definition: micronutrients (trace elements) are required in tiny amounts, not in large quantities, so A is false.

solution_steps.title: Check option B
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from air and water, so they are not applied as fertilizer; B is false.

solution_steps.title: Check option D
solution_steps.detail: The chapter classifies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as primary nutrients and calcium, magnesium and sulphur as secondary nutrients, which is the reverse of D, so D is false.

solution_steps.title: Confirm option C
solution_steps.detail: C correctly combines the figure of $$16$$ essential elements with the chapter's list of micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl) and their tiny but equally essential requirement, so C is the only correct statement.

similar_questions.variant_note: Moved from identifying a deficiency symptom to evaluating statements about the chapter's nutrient classification (number of essential elements, micronutrient quantities, sources of C, H and O, and primary versus secondary macronutrients); it uses multi-statement elimination instead of a field-symptom match.

questions.question: A sorghum field of $$1$$ hectare near Keren has a plant population of $$30{,}000$$ plants. On average, each plant carries $$3$$ heads (panicles), and each head contains $$168$$ grains. Calculate the total number of grains produced in the hectare and express your answer in scientific notation. Then state, in one sentence, what this figure represents for the farmer.
questions.answer: Total grains = $$30{,}000 \times 3 \times 168 = 15{,}120{,}000$$ grains per hectare = $$1.512 \times 10^{7}$$ grains. This is the hectare's total grain (potential seed) harvest from the sorghum crop.

solution_steps.title: Name the quantities given
solution_steps.detail: Plant population = $$30{,}000$$ plants/ha; heads per plant = $$3$$; grains per head = $$168$$; area = $$1$$ ha. The chapter classifies sorghum as a cereal grown for its edible starchy seeds, so the harvestable unit is the grain.

solution_steps.title: Choose the working formula
solution_steps.detail: Total grains = plant population x heads per plant x grains per head, i.e. the seed output is built up from the number of seed-bearing plants and the seeds carried by each head.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the grains per plant
solution_steps.detail: $$3 \times 168 = 504$$ grains per plant.

solution_steps.title: Convert to scientific notation
solution_steps.detail: Place one digit before the decimal point: $$15{,}120{,}000 = 1.512 \times 10^{7}$$ grains.

solution_steps.title: Interpret the result
solution_steps.detail: The figure is the total number of grains (potential seeds) the hectare can yield; because it is a cereal, these grains are the starchy food harvest the farmer sells or stores, and the same figure is the largest possible number of seeds available for sowing the next season.

similar_questions.question: A sesame field of $$1$$ hectare in the lowlands of Eritrea carries $$40{,}000$$ plants. Each plant bears on average $$3$$ capsules, and each capsule contains $$50$$ seeds. Find the total number of seeds produced per hectare and write it in scientific notation.
similar_questions.answer: Total seeds = $$40{,}000 \times 3 \times 50 = 6{,}000{,}000 = 6 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds per hectare.

solution_steps.title: List the data
solution_steps.detail: Plants per hectare = $$40{,}000$$; capsules per plant = $$3$$; seeds per capsule = $$50$$. The chapter lists sesame as an oil crop, so its harvested propagules are the seeds.

solution_steps.title: State the formula
solution_steps.detail: Total seeds = plant population x capsules per plant x seeds per capsule.

solution_steps.title: Substitute and multiply step by step
solution_steps.detail: $$3 \times 50 = 150$$ seeds per plant; $$40{,}000 \times 150 = 6{,}000{,}000$$ seeds per hectare.

solution_steps.title: Convert to scientific notation
solution_steps.detail: $$6{,}000{,}000 = 6 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds per hectare.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the crop from sorghum (cereal, 3 heads of 168 grains, 30,000 plants) to sesame (oil crop, 3 capsules of 50 seeds, 40,000 plants) and replaced the interpretation part with a pure scientific-notation exercise.

similar_questions.question: A field pea plot of $$1$$ hectare on a farm near Mendefera has $$250{,}000$$ plants. Each plant forms $$4$$ pods, and each pod contains $$5$$ seeds. (a) Calculate the total number of seeds per hectare. (b) If the farmer must keep $$20\%$$ of these seeds for sowing next season, how many seeds are kept for sowing?

solution_steps.title: List the data
solution_steps.detail: Plants per hectare = $$250{,}000$$; pods per plant = $$4$$; seeds per pod = $$5$$; sowing reserve = $$20\%$$. Field peas are listed in the chapter as a pulse grown for protein-rich seeds.

solution_steps.title: Formula for total seed number
solution_steps.detail: Total seeds = plant population x pods per plant x seeds per pod.

solution_steps.title: Compute part (a)
solution_steps.detail: $$4 \times 5 = 20$$ seeds per plant; $$250{,}000 \times 20 = 5{,}000{,}000$$ seeds per hectare.

solution_steps.title: Compute part (b)
solution_steps.detail: Sowing reserve = $$\frac{20}{100} \times 5{,}000{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000$$ seeds, which can also be written $$1 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds.

solution_steps.title: Interpret
solution_steps.detail: The farmer harvests 5 million seeds and must set aside 1 million of them as the seed stock for the next planting, leaving 4 million seeds as the food/grain share.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the crop to field peas, used a much denser population (250,000 plants) with smaller seed numbers per plant ($$4 \times 5$$), and added a second calculation step requiring a $$20\%$$ sowing reserve, so the arithmetic chain is longer than in the main question.

questions.question: An agricultural extension officer working with farmers in the Eritrean highlands and western lowlands is preparing a planting plan based on the agronomic classification of field crops given in the chapter. The crops under consideration are: teff, niger seed (nihug), faba bean, cotton, sorghum, sesame and sugarcane. (a) Sort all seven crops into their correct agronomic groups (cereals, pulses, industrial crops, forage crops). (b) Name the sub-groups of the industrial crops into which niger seed, cotton and sugarcane fall. (c) The officer advises a farmer who grew sorghum this season to rotate it next season with faba bean rather than with another cereal. Using the chapter's description of pulses, justify this advice with one biological reason. (d) Which of the seven crops is a native of the Abyssinian center of diversity, and what does teff's origin there tell us about the crop?
questions.answer: (a) Cereals: teff and sorghum. Pulses: faba bean. Industrial crops: niger seed (oil), sesame (oil), cotton (fiber) and sugarcane (sugar). Forage crops: none of the seven crops listed. (b) Niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop. (c) Pulses such as faba bean are leguminous plants able to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, so a faba bean crop restores the nitrogen that the sorghum cereal removed, improving soil fertility for the next crop. (d) Teff is native to the Abyssinian center of diversity (Eritrean Highlands); because its wild progenitor Eragrostis pilosa is native there, teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.

solution_steps.title: Recall the four agronomic groups
solution_steps.detail: The chapter classifies field crops as cereals (grown for edible starchy seeds, rich in carbohydrates), pulses (leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen), industrial crops (raw materials for industries), and forage crops (grown as livestock feed, preserved as hay or silage or grazed).

solution_steps.title: Assign the cereals
solution_steps.detail: Teff (Eragrostis tef) and sorghum are stated in the chapter to be cereals because they are grown for their edible starchy seeds; the chapter's cereal examples include both.

solution_steps.title: Assign the pulse
solution_steps.detail: Faba bean (Vicia faba) is listed in the chapter's crop table as a pulse (legume), so it forms the single pulse entry among the seven crops.

solution_steps.title: Assign the industrial crops and their sub-groups
solution_steps.detail: Niger seed (nihug) and sesame are oil crops, cotton is a fiber crop and sugarcane is a sugar crop, so all four are industrial crops. The chapter's sub-groups are oil crops (sesame, linseed), sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).

solution_steps.title: Check for forage crops
solution_steps.detail: None of the seven crops is described in the chapter as a forage crop: forage crops are grown specifically as livestock feed and conserved as hay or silage. The forage group therefore has no member in this list, which is an important negative finding for the officer's plan.

solution_steps.title: Justify the rotation advice (part c)
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that pulses are leguminous plants valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. Sorghum, as a cereal, takes nutrients out of the soil during the season, whereas a faba bean crop adds nitrogen to the soil. Rotating sorghum with faba bean therefore restores soil nitrogen and improves the fertility of the field for the following cereal crop.

solution_steps.title: Identify the Abyssinian native and interpret it (part d)
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's table gives teff's native center of diversity as the Abyssinian Center (Eritrean Highlands); niger seed, barley, emmer wheat, linseed, safflower, chickpea, lentil and sesame are also named as crops domesticated there. The chapter's Did You Know note adds that the wild progenitor of cultivated teff, Eragrostis pilosa, is native to this center, which confirms that teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.

solution_steps.title: Conclude the classification
solution_steps.detail: Cereals: teff, sorghum. Pulse: faba bean. Industrial crops (oil): niger seed, sesame; (fiber): cotton; (sugar): sugarcane. Forage: none of the seven. Rotation with faba bean is justified because pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen, and teff belongs to the Abyssinian center of diversity, confirming local domestication.

similar_questions.question: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands plans a four-field rotation and can choose from barley, linseed, chickpea and sisal. (a) Classify each crop into its agronomic group and, for any industrial crop, name its sub-group. (b) Which two of these crops would you recommend the farmer grow in order to add nitrogen to the soil, and why? (c) State one reason from the chapter why a crop such as sisal is described as a fiber crop rather than a cereal.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Barley = cereal; linseed = industrial crop, oil crop; chickpea = pulse; sisal = industrial crop, fiber crop. (b) Chickpea would be recommended, because it is a leguminous pulse valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil; linseed is an oil crop and does not add nitrogen. (c) Sisal is grown as a raw material for industry (its fiber), whereas cereals are grown for their edible starchy seeds, so the two crops belong to different agronomic groups.

solution_steps.title: Recall the classification criteria
solution_steps.detail: Cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds rich in carbohydrates; pulses are legumes grown for protein-rich seeds and for nitrogen fixation; industrial crops are raw materials for industries, including oil crops (sesame, linseed) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).

solution_steps.title: Classify each of the four crops
solution_steps.detail: Barley is named in the chapter as a cereal; linseed appears in the chapter's oil crop examples; chickpea is named among pulses; sisal is listed as a fiber crop.

solution_steps.title: Answer part (b)
solution_steps.detail: Only chickpea is a leguminous pulse able to fix atmospheric nitrogen, so it is the crop that adds nitrogen to the soil; linseed, barley and sisal do not have this property in the chapter.

solution_steps.title: Answer part (c)
solution_steps.detail: Sisal is a fiber crop because it is grown as an industrial raw material, while a cereal is grown for its edible starchy seed; the harvested product and the purpose of growing it are therefore completely different.

similar_questions.variant_note: Replaced teff/niger seed/faba bean/cotton/sorghum/sesame/sugarcane with barley/linseed/chickpea/sisal, removed the sowing-plan prompt, and changed the reasoning demands to nitrogen-fixing crop selection and a cereal-versus-fiber-crop justification.

similar_questions.question: Three Eritrean buyers place orders with a farming cooperative: an oil press needs raw material, a flour mill needs starchy grain, and a textile factory needs natural fiber. From the crops teff, niger seed, sesame, chickpea, cotton and sugarcane, (a) select one crop for each buyer and name the agronomic group it belongs to; (b) state which of the six crops are pulses and explain the soil benefit they provide; (c) name the industrial sub-group of any remaining crop that is an industrial crop but was not chosen in (a).
similar_questions.answer: (a) Oil press: niger seed or sesame (oil crops within the industrial crops group). Flour mill: teff (cereal). Textile factory: cotton (fiber crop within the industrial crops group). (b) Chickpea is the only pulse among the six; as a leguminous plant it fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the soil and so improves soil fertility. (c) The remaining industrial crop is sugarcane, which is a sugar crop.

solution_steps.title: Match each buyer to a crop group
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's industrial crops include oil crops (sesame, linseed), fiber crops (cotton, sisal) and sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet); cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds. An oil press needs an oil crop, a flour mill needs a cereal, and a textile factory needs a fiber crop.

solution_steps.title: Answer part (a)
solution_steps.detail: Oil press: niger seed or sesame. Flour mill: teff, because teff is a cereal with starchy grain. Textile factory: cotton, because cotton is a fiber crop.

solution_steps.title: Answer part (b)
solution_steps.detail: Chickpea is the only pulse listed; the chapter states that pulses are leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, which raises soil fertility for the next crop.

solution_steps.title: Answer part (c)
solution_steps.detail: Sugarcane was not selected by any of the three buyers and is an industrial crop of the sugar crop sub-group.

solution_steps.title: Check that no crop is left unclassified
solution_steps.detail: Teff = cereal; niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop; chickpea = pulse. All six crops are accounted for.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reframed the classification task as a market-demand matching exercise (three buyers with different raw-material needs) built on the chapter's point that sowing is influenced by market demand, and changed the crop list to include chickpea and sugarcane while dropping faba bean and sorghum.

questions.question: A group of students in Keren is asked to classify the farm animals of Eritrea by the structure of their feet. Into which of the following Orders is a goat correctly placed?
options: A. Artiodactyla
B. Perissodactyla
C. Aves
D. Equidae
questions.answer: A. Artiodactyla

solution_steps.title: Recall the basis of the order-level division
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that mammals are divided into orders according to the structure of their feet.

solution_steps.title: Identify the foot structure of a goat
solution_steps.detail: A goat has an even number of functional toes or hooves.

solution_steps.title: Match the foot structure to the correct Order
solution_steps.detail: Animals with an even number of functional toes or hooves, such as cattle, sheep, goats, camels and pigs, belong to the Order Artiodactyla.

solution_steps.title: Test each distractor
solution_steps.detail: Perissodactyla (odd number of toes: horses and donkeys) is wrong for a goat; Aves is the Class of birds, not a mammalian order; Equidae is the Family of the horse, not the order of a goat. Only Artiodactyla is correct.

similar_questions.question: Using the same foot-structure rule, a donkey kept for transport in Massawa must be placed in which Order?
similar_questions.answer: B. Perissodactyla

solution_steps.title: Recall the classifying criterion
solution_steps.detail: Orders of mammals in this chapter are separated by the structure of the feet.

solution_steps.title: Count the functional toes
solution_steps.detail: A donkey has an odd number of toes, so it is an odd-toed animal.

solution_steps.title: Select the order
solution_steps.detail: Animals with an odd number of toes, such as horses and donkeys, belong to the Order Perissodactyla.

solution_steps.title: Justify the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Artiodactyla covers even-toed animals (cattle, sheep, goats, camels, pigs); Equidae and Mammalia are the family of the horse and the class of all these mammals, not the order. The answer is B.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the animal from a goat (even-toed) to a donkey (odd-toed), which reverses the correct Order from Artiodactyla to Perissodactyla, and reset the distractor set.

similar_questions.question: A farmer in Asmara records the full taxonomy of a goat. Which of the following is the correct Family and Genus of a goat?
similar_questions.answer: C. Bovidae and Capra

solution_steps.title: Locate the goat row of the classification table
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's taxonomy table lists the goat as Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Artiodactyla, Bovidae, Capra, hircus.

solution_steps.title: Read off Family and Genus
solution_steps.detail: Family = Bovidae; Genus = Capra; the species epithet is hircus.

solution_steps.title: Check the distractors
