solution_steps.detail: Ovis aries is the sheep, Equus caballus is the horse and Gallus domestica is the chicken, so none of those pairs belongs to the goat. The correct pair is Bovidae and Capra.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifted the taxonomic level tested from Order (based on feet) to Family and Genus, and placed the question inside a farm record-keeping context instead of a classroom exercise.

questions.question:
Complete the blank in the statement below.

Of the four compartments of a ruminant stomach, the ______________ is called the true stomach because it secretes digestive juices and acids just like a human stomach.
questions.answer: Abomasum

solution_steps.title: List the four compartments in order
solution_steps.detail: The four compartments of the ruminant stomach are the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum (remembered as R-R-O-A).

solution_steps.title: Separate fore-stomachs from the glandular stomach
solution_steps.detail: The chapter explains that the first three compartments are the fore-stomachs and serve as fermentation chambers.

solution_steps.title: Identify the compartment that secretes acid
solution_steps.detail: The abomasum is the only compartment that secretes digestive juices and acids, so it is the true stomach.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The blank must be filled with 'abomasum'.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the blank in the statement below.

A newborn calf behaves like a monogastric animal because milk bypasses the rumen and passes directly to the ______________ for digestion.
similar_questions.answer: Abomasum

solution_steps.title: State the newborn calf's condition
solution_steps.detail: A newborn calf has a very small, undeveloped rumen, so for the first weeks of life it behaves like a monogastric animal.

solution_steps.title: Trace the path of milk
solution_steps.detail: Milk bypasses the undeveloped rumen and passes directly to the single glandular compartment of the stomach.

solution_steps.title: Name the compartment
solution_steps.detail: That compartment is the abomasum, the true stomach where acid digestion occurs.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the tested context from the definition of the true stomach to the route taken by milk in a newborn calf, while keeping the same answer (abomasum) and using the chapter's 'Did You Know?' fact.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the blank in the statement below.

In the ruminant stomach, the ______________ absorbs water and minerals and squeezes food particles; it forms about $$7-8\%$$ of the stomach in a mature animal.
similar_questions.answer: Omasum

solution_steps.title: Read the function given in the statement
solution_steps.detail: The statement describes a compartment whose job is water and mineral absorption and the squeezing of food particles.

solution_steps.title: Check the proportion given
solution_steps.detail: In the chapter's table, the omasum forms $$10\%$$ of the stomach in a newborn and $$7-8\%$$ in a mature animal.

solution_steps.title: Confirm the identity of the compartment
solution_steps.detail: The rumen ($$80\%$$ in the mature animal) ferments fibre and the abomasum ($$7-8\%$$) secretes acid, so the compartment described is the omasum.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The blank is filled with 'omasum'.

similar_questions.variant_note: Kept the fill-in format but re-targeted it at a different stomach compartment, the omasum, so the student must use the function-and-percentage row of the table instead of the definition of the true stomach.

questions.question: During a practical lesson at an agricultural school near Asmara, students dissect the stomach of a mature cow and find that the abomasum (the true stomach) has a mass of $$154\text{ g}$$. The chapter table gives the composition of the mature ruminant stomach as: rumen $$80\%$$, reticulum $$5\%$$, omasum $$7-8\%$$ and abomasum $$7-8\%$$. Taking the abomasum as $$7\%$$ of the total stomach, calculate the mass of the rumen.
questions.answer: $$1760\text{ g}$$ ($$1.76\text{ kg}$$) of rumen

solution_steps.title: Identify the known and the unknown
solution_steps.detail: Known: mass of abomasum $$= 154\text{ g}$$, which is $$7\%$$ of the total stomach. Unknown: mass of the rumen, which is $$80\%$$ of the total stomach.

solution_steps.title: State the percentage principle
solution_steps.detail: Part $$= \dfrac{\text{percentage}}{100} \times \text{whole}$$, so the mass of any compartment is its percentage share of the total stomach mass.

solution_steps.title: Find the mass of the whole stomach
solution_steps.detail: Since $$7\%$$ of the total $$= 154\text{ g}$$, the total stomach mass $$= \dfrac{154 \times 100}{7} = 2200\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of the rumen
solution_steps.detail: Mass of rumen $$= \dfrac{80}{100} \times 2200\text{ g} = 1760\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check the answer for reasonableness
solution_steps.detail: The rumen ($$1760\text{ g}$$) is much larger than the abomasum ($$154\text{ g}$$), which agrees with $$80\%$$ being far greater than $$7\%$$. The rumen mass is $$1760\text{ g}$$ ($$1.76\text{ kg}$$).

similar_questions.question: A student at a livestock training centre in Keren works out that the abomasum of a mature goat makes up $$8\%$$ of the total stomach and has a mass of $$120\text{ g}$$. Using the chapter's mature-animal figures (rumen $$80\%$$, reticulum $$5\%$$), find the mass of the rumen.
similar_questions.answer: $$1200\text{ g}$$ ($$1.2\text{ kg}$$) of rumen

solution_steps.title: Set out the percentages
solution_steps.detail: Abomasum $$= 8\%$$ of the total stomach and has a mass of $$120\text{ g}$$; rumen $$= 80\%$$ of the total stomach.

solution_steps.title: Apply the percentage principle
solution_steps.detail: Part $$= \dfrac{\text{percentage}}{100} \times \text{whole}$$, therefore whole $$= \dfrac{\text{part} \times 100}{\text{percentage}}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the total stomach mass
solution_steps.detail: Total $$= \dfrac{120 \times 100}{8} = 1500\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the rumen mass
solution_steps.detail: Mass of rumen $$= \dfrac{80}{100} \times 1500\text{ g} = 1200\text{ g} = 1.2\text{ kg}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the result
solution_steps.detail: The rumen of the goat has a mass of $$1200\text{ g}$$ ($$1.2\text{ kg}$$), which is ten times the abomasum as expected from $$80\%$$ against $$8\%$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the animal from a cow to a goat, the abomasum percentage from $$7\%$$ to $$8\%$$ and its mass from $$154\text{ g}$$ to $$120\text{ g}$$, and moved the setting from Asmara to a training centre in Keren.

similar_questions.question: A dairy farm assistant at a milk collection centre in Asmara records the reticulum of a mature cow as $$75\text{ g}$$. In the mature animal the reticulum forms $$5\%$$ and the abomasum $$7\%$$ of the total stomach. Calculate the mass of the abomasum of the same cow.
similar_questions.answer: $$105\text{ g}$$ of abomasum

solution_steps.title: Identify the known and the unknown
solution_steps.detail: Known: reticulum $$= 75\text{ g} = 5\%$$ of the total stomach. Unknown: abomasum, which is $$7\%$$ of the total stomach.

solution_steps.title: State the percentage principle
solution_steps.detail: Because each compartment's mass comes from the same total stomach, the masses are in the same ratio as the percentages.

solution_steps.title: Find the total stomach mass
solution_steps.detail: Total $$= \dfrac{75 \times 100}{5} = 1500\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the abomasum mass
solution_steps.detail: Mass of abomasum $$= \dfrac{7}{100} \times 1500\text{ g} = 105\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Since $$7\% > 5\%$$, the abomasum ($$105\text{ g}$$) is heavier than the reticulum ($$75\text{ g}$$), which is consistent. The abomasum has a mass of $$105\text{ g}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reversed the logic: the given compartment is now the reticulum instead of the abomasum, and the required compartment is the abomasum instead of the rumen, with new numerical data ($$75\text{ g}$$, $$5\%$$).

questions.question: An agricultural officer in Eritrea is preparing a national livestock report. The chapter gives the national livestock population as approximately: $$2.2\text{ million}$$ cattle, $$5\text{ million}$$ goats, $$2.4\text{ million}$$ sheep, $$575\,000$$ donkeys, $$9\,000$$ mules, $$5\,000$$ horses, $$368\,000$$ camels and $$2.5\text{ million}$$ poultry. Calculate the total national livestock population, and state how many times larger the total is than the number of horses.
questions.answer: About $$13\,057\,000$$ animals (approximately $$13.06\text{ million}$$), which is roughly $$2611$$ times the number of horses ($$5\,000$$)

solution_steps.title: Convert the units to whole animals
solution_steps.detail: Write every figure in the same unit (single animals) so that the values can be added directly: $$2.2\text{ million} = 2\,200\,000$$ and $$2.5\text{ million} = 2\,500\,000$$.

solution_steps.title: Add the figures step by step
Compare the total with the number of horses
solution_steps.detail: Ratio $$= \dfrac{13\,057\,000}{5\,000} = 2611.4$$, so the total livestock population is about $$2611$$ times the number of horses.

solution_steps.title: State the final result
solution_steps.detail: The total national livestock population is approximately $$13\,057\,000$$ animals, that is about $$13.06\text{ million}$$ head, which is roughly $$2611$$ times the horse population.

similar_questions.question: A zoba livestock census in Eritrea records $$575\,000$$ donkeys, $$9\,000$$ mules, $$5\,000$$ horses and $$2\,500\,000$$ poultry. Work out the total number of these four groups of animals, and state how many times larger this total is than the number of mules.
similar_questions.answer: $$3\,089\,000$$ animals, about $$343$$ times the number of mules

solution_steps.title: Write the four census figures in whole animals
Divide the total by the number of mules
State the result
solution_steps.detail: The four groups together number $$3\,089\,000$$ animals, which is about $$343$$ times the number of mules.

similar_questions.variant_note: Restricted the sum to the equines and poultry of the census instead of all eight livestock groups, and changed the comparison animal from horses to mules.

similar_questions.question: In a highland district of Eritrea a development agent counts $$2\,200$$ cattle, $$5\,000$$ goats, $$2\,400$$ sheep and $$575$$ donkeys. Find the total number of animals counted, and state how many times larger the total is than the number of donkeys.
similar_questions.answer: $$10\,175$$ animals, $$17.7$$ times the number of donkeys

solution_steps.title: Divide the total by the number of donkeys
State the result
solution_steps.detail: The district count is $$10\,175$$ animals, about $$17.7$$ times the number of donkeys.

similar_questions.variant_note: Scaled the national census figures down to a single highland district (dividing by about $$1000$$), dropped the camel and poultry groups and compared with donkeys instead of horses.

concepts: Adaptation to heat and tropical disease
questions.question: A development agent in the hot, arid lowlands of the Northern Red Sea zone advises a livestock owner to keep humped Zebu cattle rather than imported temperate cattle, while expressing a preference for exotic dairy breeds only in the cool highlands near Asmara. Using the chapter's account of the two cattle species and of indigenous versus exotic breeds, explain the biological and management reasons behind this advice.
questions.answer: Zebu cattle (Bos indicus) are humped, heat-tolerant and highly resistant to tropical diseases, so they suit the hot, arid lowlands, where they match the indigenous breeds already kept in Eritrea; temperate Bos taurus and exotic dairy breeds such as Holstein-Friesian have been introduced only to raise production in specific areas such as the cool Asmara highlands, because feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to each animal's biological needs.

solution_steps.title: State the two cattle species and their characteristics
solution_steps.detail: The chapter explains that cattle are divided into two main species: Bos taurus, which is humpless and adapted to cool, temperate climates, and Bos indicus, the humped Zebu cattle, which are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases.

solution_steps.title: Link the species characters to the lowland environment
solution_steps.detail: The hot, arid lowlands impose high temperatures and a heavy burden of tropical disease, so the Zebu's heat tolerance and disease resistance make it the better biological match than the heat-sensitive, disease-susceptible Bos taurus.

solution_steps.title: Bring in the indigenous breeds of Eritrea
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that most of Eritrea's livestock are indigenous (local) breeds, which means they are already established and suited to the local feed, climate and disease conditions of the country.

solution_steps.title: Explain the role of exotic breeds
solution_steps.detail: Exotic breeds such as Holstein-Friesian dairy cattle have been introduced in specific areas to increase production, so they are useful where management and climate allow higher output rather than survival alone.

solution_steps.title: Justify the highland recommendation
solution_steps.detail: The cool highlands around Asmara resemble the temperate conditions to which Bos taurus and Holstein-Friesian cattle are adapted, so the exotic dairy breed can express its production potential there with less heat and disease stress.

solution_steps.title: Conclude with a management principle
solution_steps.detail: The chapter notes that animal feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to the biological needs of each class and order, so breed choice must follow the environment and the intended purpose: hardy Zebu for survival and work in the lowlands, and exotic dairy stock for high production where conditions are favourable.

similar_questions.question: A farmer in the lowlands of Eritrea can keep only animals that tolerate heat and resist tropical disease, while a neighbour in the cool highlands wants the highest possible milk yield. Using the chapter's distinction between indigenous and exotic breeds, explain what each farmer should keep and why.
similar_questions.answer: The lowland farmer should keep indigenous cattle such as the humped Zebu (Bos indicus), which are resistant to heat and tropical diseases and already adapted to local conditions, while the highland farmer may keep an exotic dairy breed such as the Holstein-Friesian, which has been introduced specifically to increase production and performs best where the climate is cool.

solution_steps.title: Recall the indigenous-breed advantage
solution_steps.detail: Most livestock in Eritrea are indigenous (local) breeds, adapted to the country's climate, feed and disease challenge.

solution_steps.title: Identify the lowland animal
solution_steps.detail: For heat and tropical disease, the chapter points to Bos indicus (Zebu), the humped cattle that are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases.

solution_steps.title: Recall the exotic-breed purpose
solution_steps.detail: Exotic breeds such as the Holstein-Friesian dairy cow have been introduced in specific areas of Eritrea to increase production.

solution_steps.title: Match breed to environment and purpose
solution_steps.detail: The lowland farmer needs survival and adaptability, so indigenous Zebu is appropriate; the highland farmer has temperate-like conditions and a production objective, so the exotic dairy breed is appropriate.

solution_steps.title: Conclude with the general rule
solution_steps.detail: Feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to the biological needs of the animal, so breed choice must match both the environment and the production goal.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed from a pure explanation of Zebu against temperate cattle into a two-farmer comparison that forces a decision for each environment, and shifted the emphasis from disease resistance alone to the indigenous-versus-exotic trade-off.

similar_questions.question: A cooperative near Massawa wants to introduce Holstein-Friesian cows alongside its local Zebu herd, and also plans to keep poultry. Explain, using the chapter's ideas of adaptation and of exotic breeds, the risks of the plan and the single management measure the chapter recommends for newly purchased animals.
similar_questions.answer: The Holstein-Friesian is an exotic dairy breed adapted to cooler conditions, so in the hot lowlands near Massawa it is exposed to heat and tropical disease stress that the local Zebu resists; the chapter's recommended safeguard for newly purchased animals is quarantine, the temporary isolation of the new animals for usually $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ to ensure they are not carrying hidden infections before they join the herd.

solution_steps.title: Recall the nature of the exotic breed
solution_steps.detail: The Holstein-Friesian is described as an exotic dairy breed introduced in specific areas to increase production, not as a heat- and disease-resistant local breed.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the local Zebu
solution_steps.detail: Bos indicus (Zebu) cattle are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases, whereas Bos taurus cattle are adapted to cool, temperate climates.

solution_steps.title: Deduce the risk near Massawa
solution_steps.detail: In the hot lowlands the imported Holstein-Friesian would face heat and tropical disease stress that the resident Zebu tolerates, so production and survival may be poor.

solution_steps.title: Recall the safeguard for new stock
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that quarantine is the temporary isolation of newly purchased animals for usually $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ to detect hidden infections.

solution_steps.title: State the recommendation
solution_steps.detail: The cooperative should quarantine the newly purchased cattle for $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ before mixing them with the local herd, and should expect that the exotic breed needs housing, feed and healthcare customized to its biological needs.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifted the scenario to a cooperative near Massawa and added the practical introduction of purchased stock, so the answer must combine breed adaptation with the chapter's quarantine rule ($$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$) instead of only comparing the two cattle species.

questions.question: In a highland forest near Segeneyti, tall canopy trees intercept most of the incoming sunlight, so that small herb species growing on the forest floor receive too little light to grow well. The canopy trees themselves are not affected by the herbs in any way. Which type of species interaction does this describe?
options: A. Commensalism, because one species benefits and the other is unaffected.
B. Amensalism, because one species is harmed while the other is unaffected.
C. Mutualism, because both species benefit from the interaction.
D. Competition, because both species are negatively affected.
questions.answer: B. Amensalism, because one species is harmed while the other is unaffected.

solution_steps.title: Identify the effect on each species
solution_steps.detail: Record the sign of the effect on both partners. The small forest herbs are harmed (they receive too little light, so they grow poorly), while the tall canopy trees are unaffected by the herbs' presence.

solution_steps.title: Write the interaction as signs
solution_steps.detail: Harmed species = negative ($$ - $$); unaffected species = neutral ($$ 0 $$). The interaction is therefore ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) when read from the canopy tree to the herb.

solution_steps.title: Match the sign pattern to the interaction type
solution_steps.detail: From the chapter's interaction table, ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) is amensalism, exactly matching the chapter example of large trees blocking light from reaching small forest herbs. Commensalism is ($$ + $$, $$ 0 $$), mutualism is ($$ + $$, $$ + $$) and competition is ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), so none of the other options fits the observed signs.

solution_steps.title: Reject the strongest distractor
solution_steps.detail: Option A is the classic misconception: it corrects the sign pattern of commensalism. In commensalism one species benefits (for example orchids gaining light by growing on high forest tree branches); here the herbs gain nothing at all, so commensalism cannot be correct.

similar_questions.question: Along a riverbank in the Gash-Barka lowlands, orchids grow on the high branches of a large tree, where they receive the light they need; the tree is neither helped nor harmed by the orchids. Which type of species interaction is this?
similar_questions.answer: Commensalism (+/0): one species (the orchid) benefits and the other (the tree) is unaffected.

solution_steps.title: State the effect on each species
solution_steps.detail: The orchids benefit because they gain a raised, well-lit growing position on the tree's branches; the tree is unaffected because the orchids neither help nor harm it.

solution_steps.title: Assign signs and match the chapter pattern
solution_steps.detail: Effect signs are ($$ + $$, $$ 0 $$), which the chapter's table lists as commensalism, using the very example of orchids growing on high forest tree branches for light.

solution_steps.title: Distinguish from mutualism and antagonism
solution_steps.detail: If the tree also benefited, the interaction would be mutualism ($$ + $$, $$ + $$); if the tree were harmed, it would be antagonism ($$ + $$, $$ - $$). Since the tree is unaffected, only commensalism fits.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the sign pattern from (0, -) amensalism to (+, 0) commensalism and replaced the canopy-tree/herb example with the chapter's orchid-on-branch example in a Gash-Barka riverbank setting.

similar_questions.question: A woodland herb is heavily shaded by a large overstorey tree and therefore grows poorly, while the tree's growth is unaffected. A student writes that this is competition between the tree and the herb. Is the student correct? Justify your answer using the chapter's interaction types.
similar_questions.answer: No. Competition requires both species to be negatively affected ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), but here the tree is unaffected, so the interaction is amensalism ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$).

solution_steps.title: State the definition of competition
solution_steps.detail: In competition both species are negatively affected because they compete for the same limited resource, such as light, water or soil nutrients.

solution_steps.title: Test the observed situation against that definition
solution_steps.detail: The herb is harmed (negative), but the large tree is unaffected (neutral), because the herb takes no resource the tree needs in limiting supply.

solution_steps.title: Conclude and correct the classification
solution_steps.detail: Since the effect pair is ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) and not ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), competition is ruled out; the correct label is amensalism (one species harmed, the other unaffected).

similar_questions.variant_note: Re-cast the item as a true/false-with-justification question that tests the same amensalism sign pattern against the definition of competition, instead of asking only for the interaction name.

questions.question: A reforestation project in the Central Highlands near Asmara will plant tree seedlings on a degraded site measuring $$15\text{ hectares}$$ at the standard recommended spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$. Calculate the number of tree seedlings required.
questions.answer: $$37\,500\text{ tree seedlings}$$ are required.

solution_steps.title: Identify the given data and what is asked
solution_steps.detail: Given: total planting area = $$15\text{ hectares}$$; spacing = $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$. Required: the total number of seedlings. The chapter gives the standard density that accompanies this spacing.

solution_steps.title: State the density principle
solution_steps.detail: The standard recommended spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ corresponds to a planting density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, because each seedling occupies a $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ square.

solution_steps.title: Set up the multiplication
solution_steps.detail: Total seedlings = density $$\times$$ area = $$2\,500\text{ seedlings/ha} \times 15\text{ ha}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the result with units
solution_steps.detail: The project requires $$37\,500\text{ tree seedlings}$$ at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing. A sensible follow-up for the project manager is to add a few percent extra seedlings to replace any that die after planting.

similar_questions.question: An enclosure protection and planting programme in the Buri Peninsula will establish trees on a flat area of $$8\text{ hectares}$$ at a spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, which gives a density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$. How many seedlings must the nursery raise?
similar_questions.answer: $$2\,500 \times 8 = 20\,000\text{ tree seedlings}$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify the data
solution_steps.detail: Area = $$8\text{ hectares}$$; spacing = $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, which the chapter equates to $$2\,500\text{ seedlings/ha}$$.

solution_steps.title: Apply the density relation
solution_steps.detail: Total seedlings = density $$\times$$ area = $$2\,500 \times 8$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute and label
solution_steps.detail: $$2\,500 \times 8 = 20\,000$$, so $$20\,000\text{ seedlings}$$ are needed for $$8\text{ hectares}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the planted area from $$15\text{ hectares}$$ to $$8\text{ hectares}$$ and relocated the site to the Buri Peninsula; the spacing and density are unchanged.

similar_questions.question: A nursery in Keren is asked how many seedlings are needed to fill a $$25\text{ hectare}$$ block of farmland shelterbelt at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing, at a density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$. Calculate the requirement.
similar_questions.answer: $$2\,500 \times 25 = 62\,500\text{ tree seedlings}$$.

solution_steps.title: Note the given density and area
solution_steps.detail: Density = $$2\,500\text{ seedlings/ha}$$; area = $$25\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Multiply density by area
solution_steps.detail: Total seedlings = $$2\,500 \times 25$$.

solution_steps.title: Complete the arithmetic and conclude
solution_steps.detail: $$2\,500 \times 25 = 62\,500$$, so $$62\,500\text{ seedlings}$$ are required.

similar_questions.variant_note: Kept the $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing but changed the area to $$25\text{ hectares}$$ and set the problem in a Keren farmland shelterbelt context.

questions.question: Historical records show that forest cover in Eritrea was approximately $$30\%$$ of the total land area in 1912, and that this had fallen to $$11\%$$ by 1952. Calculate the average annual decrease in forest cover over that period, in percentage points per year. Then convert this annual loss into square kilometres per year, taking Eritrea's total land area as $$125\,000\text{ km}^2$$.
questions.answer: The average annual decrease was $$0.475\text{ percentage points per year}$$, equivalent to approximately $$593.75\text{ km}^2\text{ (about }594\text{ km}^2\text{) of forest lost per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Extract the data from the record
solution_steps.detail: Forest cover in 1912 = $$30\%$$; forest cover in 1952 = $$11\%$$. Time elapsed = $$1952 - 1912 = 40\text{ years}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the total decline in percentage points
solution_steps.detail: Decline = $$30\% - 11\% = 19\text{ percentage points}$$.

solution_steps.title: Divide by the number of years
solution_steps.detail: Average annual decrease = $$\dfrac{19\text{ percentage points}}{40\text{ years}} = 0.475\text{ percentage points per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert one percentage point into an area
Convert the annual rate into square kilometres
solution_steps.detail: Area lost per year = $$0.475 \times 1\,250\text{ km}^2 = 593.75\text{ km}^2\text{ per year}$$ (approximately $$594\text{ km}^2\text{ per year}$$).

solution_steps.title: Interpret the result
solution_steps.detail: Forest was being lost at an average rate of about $$0.475$$ percentage points per year, roughly $$594\text{ km}^2$$ of forest per year, between 1912 and 1952. The chapter attributes such decline to land clearing for agriculture, overgrazing, timber extraction, firewood collection, recurrent droughts and the destructive effects of war.

similar_questions.question: Between 1912 and 1952, Eritrea's forest cover fell from $$30\%$$ to $$11\%$$ of the total land area. Using a total land area of $$125\,000\text{ km}^2$$, calculate how much forest area (in $$\text{km}^2$$) remained in 1952.
similar_questions.answer: Approximately $$13\,750\text{ km}^2$$ of forest remained in 1952.

solution_steps.title: Identify the required percentage
solution_steps.detail: The 1952 forest cover is given as $$11\%$$ of the total land area, which is $$125\,000\text{ km}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: Write the percentage as a fraction
Multiply by the total land area
solution_steps.detail: Remaining forest = $$0.11 \times 125\,000\text{ km}^2 = 13\,750\text{ km}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only $$13\,750\text{ km}^2$$ was still under forest in 1952, which shows how far the $$30\%$$ cover of 1912 had already been eroded.

similar_questions.variant_note: Instead of computing a rate of decline in percentage points per year, this variant asks for the absolute forest area remaining in 1952 by applying the 1952 percentage to the total land area.

similar_questions.question: In the same record, Eritrea's forest cover fell from $$30\%$$ in 1912 to $$5\%$$ in 1960. Calculate the average annual decrease in forest cover over 1912 to 1960, in percentage points per year.
similar_questions.answer: The average annual decrease was approximately $$0.52\text{ percentage points per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: List the values and the time span
Compute the total decline
solution_steps.detail: Decline = $$30\% - 5\% = 25\text{ percentage points}$$.

solution_steps.title: Divide by the number of years
solution_steps.detail: Average annual decrease = $$\dfrac{25}{48} = 0.5208\ldots \approx 0.52\text{ percentage points per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Interpret
solution_steps.detail: Over the longer 48-year span the loss averaged about $$0.52$$ percentage points each year, a slightly faster rate than the 1912 to 1952 average, because the 1950s saw rapid clearing and the country's cover fell to $$5\%$$ by 1960.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the end point of the record from 1952 ($$11\%$$) to 1960 ($$5\%$$), which lengthens the period to 48 years and changes the computed rate of decline.

questions.question: A forest block of $$10\text{ hectares}$$ in the Semenawi-Bahri highlands is surveyed and found to have a tree canopy covering $$15\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Using the chapter's classification by canopy density, how should this forest be classified?
options: A. As an open forest, because its canopy coverage is at least $$10\%$$ with a discontinuous canopy.
B. As a closed forest, because its canopy coverage exceeds $$20\%$$.
C. As a primary forest, because the canopy is undisturbed by human activity.
D. As an uneven-aged forest, because canopy cover varies from place to place.
questions.answer: A. As an open forest, because its canopy coverage is at least $$10\%$$ with a discontinuous canopy.

solution_steps.title: Convert the forest area to square metres
solution_steps.detail: $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, so the block covers $$10 \times 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ m}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the percentage canopy coverage
solution_steps.detail: Canopy coverage $$= \dfrac{15\,000\text{ m}^2}{100\,000\text{ m}^2} \times 100\% = 15\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Apply the canopy-density definitions
solution_steps.detail: A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$; an open forest has discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath. Since $$15\%$$ is below $$20\%$$ but above $$10\%$$, the block is an open forest.

solution_steps.title: Check the distractors one by one
solution_steps.detail: B is wrong because $$15\%$$ does not exceed $$20\%$$. C is wrong because primary forest is a classification by level of human interference, not by canopy density. D is wrong because even-aged or uneven-aged is a classification by age, and canopy variation is not the stated criterion. Only A states a criterion and conclusion consistent with the chapter, so it is the unique correct option.

similar_questions.question: A 40-hectare dry montane forest near Nakfa has a tree canopy covering $$96\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Classify this forest by canopy density using the chapter's definitions.
similar_questions.answer: It is a closed forest, because $$96\,000\text{ m}^2$$ out of $$400\,000\text{ m}^2$$ is $$24\%$$ canopy coverage, which is greater than $$20\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the threshold
solution_steps.detail: A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$. Since $$24\% > 20\%$$, the forest is closed.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the block size to $$40\text{ hectares}$$ and the canopy figure to $$96\,000\text{ m}^2$$ so the percentage rises above the $$20\%$$ threshold, giving the opposite classification (closed rather than open forest).

similar_questions.question: According to the chapter, a forest whose canopy coverage is greater than $$20\%$$ is classified as a ______ forest, while a forest with discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ and a continuous grass layer underneath is classified as an ______ forest.
similar_questions.answer: A closed forest (greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage) and an open forest (discontinuous canopy of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath).

solution_steps.title: Recall the canopy-density classes
solution_steps.detail: The chapter classifies forests by canopy density into closed forest and open forest, using canopy coverage as the distinguishing measure.

solution_steps.title: Match each definition to its term
solution_steps.detail: Greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage defines a closed forest; discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath defines an open forest.

solution_steps.title: State the completed sentence
solution_steps.detail: The sentence reads: greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage gives a closed forest, while $$10\%$$ or more with a discontinuous canopy and a continuous grass layer gives an open forest.

similar_questions.variant_note: Converted the calculation item into a completion item that recalls the two canopy-density definitions directly, instead of computing a percentage from given areas.

questions.question: A restoration team is given a fixed supply of $$5\,000$$ tree seedlings for a dry site on the Buri Peninsula. The chapter states that the standard spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ gives a density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, and that in drier areas the spacing is increased to $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ to reduce competition for water. (a) Calculate the number of seedlings per hectare at the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) Determine how many hectares the $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant at this dry-site spacing, and state how much more area this covers than the same $$5\,000$$ seedlings would cover at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
questions.answer: (a) $$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$ (exactly $$\frac{10\,000}{9}$$) at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) The $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$ at the dry-site spacing, which is $$2.5\text{ hectares}$$ more than the $$2\text{ hectares}$$ they would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.

solution_steps.title: Establish the area occupied by one seedling
solution_steps.detail: At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing each seedling occupies a square of side $$3\text{ m}$$, so each seedling occupies $$3 \times 3 = 9\text{ m}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert one hectare to square metres
solution_steps.detail: $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, the unit conversion needed to express the density per hectare.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the density at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$
solution_steps.detail: (a) Density $$= \dfrac{10\,000\text{ m}^2\text{ per hectare}}{9\text{ m}^2\text{ per seedling}} = 1\,111.1\ldots \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.

solution_steps.title: Cross-check the density with the standard spacing
solution_steps.detail: For comparison, the chapter's standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing gives $$\dfrac{10\,000}{4} = 2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, which matches the chapter value and confirms the method. Widening the spacing from $$2\text{ m}$$ to $$3\text{ m}$$ therefore more than halves the number of seedlings needed per hectare.

solution_steps.title: Find the area plantable at the dry-site spacing
solution_steps.detail: (b) Area $$= \dfrac{\text{number of seedlings}}{\text{density}} = \dfrac{5\,000\text{ seedlings}}{1\,111.1\text{ seedlings per hectare}} = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$. Equivalently, $$5\,000 \times 9\text{ m}^2 = 45\,000\text{ m}^2 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the area the same supply would cover at standard spacing
solution_steps.detail: At $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, area $$= \dfrac{5\,000}{2\,500} = 2\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two areas and conclude
solution_steps.detail: The extra area covered $$= 4.5 - 2 = 2.5\text{ hectares}$$. So $$5\,000$$ seedlings plant $$4.5$$ hectares at the dry-site spacing of $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$, which is $$2.5$$ hectares more than the same supply would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing. This is why the chapter recommends wider spacing in drier areas: each seedling has more soil water available and competition for water is reduced.

similar_questions.question: A nursery allocates $$9\,000$$ seedlings to a dry lowland enclosure site along the Anseba where foresters decide to use the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing ($$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$) instead of the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ ($$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$). (a) How many hectares can be planted at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$? (b) How many hectares would the same $$9\,000$$ seedlings have covered at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, and what is the difference?
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$8.1\text{ hectares}$$ at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$. (b) $$3.6\text{ hectares}$$ at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, a difference of $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Use the dry-site density
solution_steps.detail: At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ each seedling occupies $$9\text{ m}^2$$, giving $$\dfrac{10\,000}{9} \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the area at the wider spacing
solution_steps.detail: (a) Area $$= \dfrac{9\,000}{1\,111.1} = 8.1\text{ hectares}$$; equivalently $$9\,000 \times 9 = 81\,000\text{ m}^2 = 8.1\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the area at the standard spacing
solution_steps.detail: (b) Area $$= \dfrac{9\,000}{2\,500} = 3.6\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Difference $$= 8.1 - 3.6 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$, so the wider spacing allows the same nursery supply to cover $$4.5$$ hectares more land.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the seedling supply from $$5\,000$$ to $$9\,000$$ and the site from the Buri Peninsula to an Anseba lowland enclosure, which changes both hectare figures and the difference while keeping the same density reasoning.

similar_questions.question: In a Parkland Agroforestry system, multipurpose trees such as Balanites aegyptiaca and Faidherbia albida are kept at widely spaced intervals of $$10\text{ to }20\text{ trees per hectare}$$ among annual crops. (a) What average area, in square metres, is available to each tree if $$10\text{ trees}$$ are kept per hectare? (b) State one reason given in the chapter for keeping the trees so widely spaced.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$1\,000\text{ m}^2$$ of land per tree at $$10\text{ trees per hectare}$$. (b) Wide spacing lets the trees provide livestock feed, fuel wood and shade without blocking too much sunlight from the crops growing below.

solution_steps.title: Convert the hectare to square metres
solution_steps.detail: $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: Divide the area by the number of trees
solution_steps.detail: (a) Area per tree $$= \dfrac{10\,000\text{ m}^2}{10\text{ trees}} = 1\,000\text{ m}^2\text{ per tree}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the agronomic reason
solution_steps.detail: (b) The chapter explains that trees in parkland agroforestry are widely spaced so that they supply livestock feed, fuel wood and shade while not blocking too much sunlight from the sorghum, pearl millet or teff growing beneath them. Faidherbia albida helps further through reverse phenology: it sheds leaves in the wet season and keeps them in the dry season.

similar_questions.variant_note: Switched from tree-seedling spacing for reforestation to tree density in a parkland agroforestry system ($$10\text{ to }20\text{ trees per hectare}$$), so the calculation begins from a given tree count rather than from a spacing distance.

questions.question: While inspecting a gently sloping cropland near Keren, a farmer finds many small, shallow, parallel channels running down the field, each only about 20 cm deep. Which type of water erosion is this, and why can the farmer still correct it with ordinary tillage?
options: A. Splash erosion, because raindrop impact has formed a hard surface crust
B. Sheet erosion, because the channels are broad, thin sheets of flowing water
C. Rill erosion, because these are small, shallow, concentrated flow channels that ordinary farm tillage can smooth out
D. Gully erosion, because the channels are narrow and deep and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage
questions.answer: C. Rill erosion, because these are small, shallow, concentrated flow channels that ordinary farm tillage can smooth out

solution_steps.title: Recall the classification of water erosion
solution_steps.detail: The chapter divides water erosion into four types: splash (raindrop) erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion and gully erosion.

solution_steps.title: Match the field evidence to a type
solution_steps.detail: The field shows small, shallow, concentrated flow paths (channels) rather than craters from raindrop impact or a uniform thin sheet of moving water. Small, shallow, concentrated flow paths are the defining feature of rill erosion.

solution_steps.title: Check the depth against the chapter data
solution_steps.detail: The chapter records rill channels as up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, so the measured 20 cm depth falls inside the rill range, while gullies are $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$ deep.

solution_steps.title: Decide on correctability
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that rills are temporary and can easily be smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage operations, unlike gullies, which cannot be destroyed by normal tillage.

solution_steps.title: Evaluate the distractors
solution_steps.detail: A is wrong because splash erosion creates small craters and a hard crust, not channels. B is wrong because sheet erosion removes soil uniformly in broad, thin sheets, not in defined small channels. D is wrong because the channels are shallow and the chapter reserves the non-tillable, deep category for gullies.

similar_questions.question: On a bare, sloping plot at Tsorona, raindrops strike the unprotected soil and small crater-like marks appear, with loose soil particles splashed onto the leaves of young maize. The soil surface later dries into a hard crust. Which type of water erosion is responsible?
similar_questions.answer: Splash (raindrop) erosion

solution_steps.title: Recall the four types of water erosion
solution_steps.detail: Water erosion occurs as splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion, distinguished by how the soil is detached and moved.

solution_steps.title: Identify the detachment mechanism
solution_steps.detail: Here the soil is detached by the direct impact of raindrops on bare soil, which is the definition of splash (raindrop) erosion.

solution_steps.title: Confirm with the chapter description
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes splash erosion as producing small craters on bare soil, splashing soil onto plant leaves, destroying soil structure and forming a hard crust on dry soil - all features observed on the plot.

solution_steps.title: Rule out the other types
solution_steps.detail: There is no uniform removal of soil down the slope in thin sheets (sheet), no concentrated channels (rill) and no deep, incised channel (gully).

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the erosion type being asked about from rill to splash erosion, replaced the Keren cropland with a bare plot at Tsorona, and replaced channels with raindrop craters, splashed leaves and surface crusting.

similar_questions.question: A deep, wide ravine with steep, unstable walls has opened across a farm basin in the moist lowlands, splitting the field into fragments so that machinery can no longer move across it. Which type of water erosion is this, and why can normal plowing not remove it?
similar_questions.answer: Gully erosion; it is an advanced stage in which runoff cuts deep channels that cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations and that divide land into fragments, stopping machinery movement

solution_steps.title: Match the description to the erosion types
solution_steps.detail: The feature is a narrow, deep channel formed by surface runoff during or immediately after heavy rains, which is the definition of gully erosion.

solution_steps.title: Check the scale against the chapter data
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives gully depth from $$1\text{ to }2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ (and lists $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$ in the table), far beyond the $$30\text{ cm}$$ limit of rills.

solution_steps.title: Apply the correctability criterion
solution_steps.detail: Rills can be smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage, but the chapter states plainly that gullies cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations.

solution_steps.title: State the cultivation effect
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table notes that gullies divide land into fragments and stop machinery movement, which is exactly what has happened in the field.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifted the question from identifying rill erosion to identifying gully erosion, moved the setting to a moist lowland farm basin, and asked for both the type and the tillage consequence rather than the correctability of rills.

questions.question:
Complete the following statements using the correct water-erosion terms.
(1) ................ erosion detaches soil particles by the direct impact of raindrops on bare soil, destroying soil structure and forming a hard crust on dry soil.
(2) ................ erosion develops small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that are temporary and can be easily smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage.
(3) ................ erosion is the advanced stage in which runoff flows in narrow, deep channels that divide land into fragments and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage.
questions.answer: (1) Splash (raindrop) erosion; (2) Rill erosion; (3) Gully erosion

solution_steps.title: Use the detachment agent to name blank (1)
solution_steps.detail: Blank (1) describes detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by direct raindrop impact on bare soil. The chapter calls this splash (raindrop) erosion, and it notes the resulting hard crust on dry soil.

solution_steps.title: Use channel size to name blank (2)
solution_steps.detail: Blank (2) describes small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that are temporary and removable by ordinary tillage. This matches rill erosion, with channels up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep.

solution_steps.title: Use depth and permanence to name blank (3)
solution_steps.detail: Blank (3) describes narrow, deep channels formed during or immediately after heavy rains that divide land into fragments and resist normal tillage. This is gully erosion, ranging from $$1 - 2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ deep.

solution_steps.title: Check the sequence
solution_steps.detail: The three blanks follow the chapter's progressive order of water erosion: splash then rill then gully, each stage leaving features that are harder to repair than the one before.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the following statements.
(1) ................ is the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region by wind in arid and semi-arid climates.
(2) ................ is the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds.
similar_questions.answer: (1) Deflation; (2) Abrasion

solution_steps.title: Recall the two effects of wind erosion
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that wind erosion has two main effects: deflation and abrasion.

solution_steps.title: Match the removal process to blank (1)
solution_steps.detail: Lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles from one place to another is the definition of deflation, the process responsible for topsoil blowing in the dry lowlands.

solution_steps.title: Match the wearing process to blank (2)
solution_steps.detail: The wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended particles in high-velocity winds is abrasion, which also causes sand abrasion on seedlings.

similar_questions.variant_note: Replaced the three water-erosion types with the two wind-erosion effects (deflation and abrasion), so the answer terms and the physical processes change completely.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the following statements.
(1) ................ erosion removes soil particles uniformly down a slope in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels.
(2) ................ is the imaginary line joining points of the same elevation on the ground surface.
similar_questions.answer: (1) Sheet erosion; (2) A contour

solution_steps.title: Identify the uniform-removal process
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines sheet erosion as detachment of soil particles by raindrop impact and their uniform removal down a slope by overland flow in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels.

solution_steps.title: Identify the surveying term
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines a contour as an imaginary line joining points of the same elevation on the ground surface, the line along which conservation structures such as contour bunds are laid out.

solution_steps.title: Distinguish the two concepts
solution_steps.detail: Blank (1) names an erosion process that strips the most fertile topsoil and organic matter, while blank (2) names a surveying reference line used to place conservation measures, not an erosion type.

similar_questions.variant_note: Kept the completion format but changed the source content from the three water-erosion types to one erosion process (sheet erosion) plus a surveying definition (contour).

questions.question: A forester uses a line level to check the slope of a gently sloping cropland near Keren before laying out contour bunds. The two identical sticks are set $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart, and the reading on the stick at the lower ground position is $$0.9\text{ meters}$$ greater than the reading on the stick at the higher ground position. Calculate the percentage slope of the plot and state, with justification, whether the site is suitable for contour bunds.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$9\%$$; this is slightly steeper than the $$2\% - 8\%$$ ideal range for contour bunds, so bund spacing must be tightened or a stronger physical measure such as hillside terracing used.

solution_steps.title: Identify what the line level measures
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes the line level as two identical $$1.5\text{-meter}$$ sticks connected by a $$10\text{-meter}$$ cotton string with a small spirit level suspended in the middle. Because the string is exactly $$10\text{ meters}$$ long, the horizontal interval (HI) is the fixed stick spacing of $$10\text{ meters}$$.

solution_steps.title: Obtain the vertical interval
solution_steps.detail: The vertical interval (VI) is the difference in elevation between the two points. Since both sticks stand vertically, the difference in reading on the sticks equals the difference in ground elevation: $$\text{VI} = 0.9\text{ meters}$$.

solution_steps.title: Name the percentage slope formula
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the measured values
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.9}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.09 \times 100 = 9\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the slope with the ideal site for contour bunds
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table states that contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands of $$2\% - 8\%$$ slope. The computed slope of $$9\%$$ is slightly steeper than that ideal range.

solution_steps.title: Conclude with a justified recommendation
solution_steps.detail: The plot is at $$9\%$$ slope, just above the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band for which contour bunds are the recommended physical measure. Contour bunds would need closer spacing and careful design, and on such a slope a stronger structural measure such as hillside terraces, which break slope length and trap water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, should be considered.

similar_questions.question: While surveying a field at Mendefera with a line level whose two sticks are $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart, the assistant records the difference in stick readings as $$0.4\text{ meters}$$. Compute the percentage slope of the field and decide whether it falls within the slope range for which the chapter recommends contour bunds.
similar_questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$4\%$$; this lies within the $$2\% - 8\%$$ range, so contour bunds are suitable

solution_steps.title: Fix the horizontal interval
solution_steps.detail: The line level uses a $$10\text{-meter}$$ string, so the sticks are $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart and $$\text{HI} = 10\text{ meters}$$.

solution_steps.title: Read off the vertical interval
solution_steps.detail: The difference in stick readings equals the difference in ground elevation, so $$\text{VI} = 0.4\text{ meters}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute and compute
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.4}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.04 \times 100 = 4\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Judge suitability
solution_steps.detail: $$4\%$$ falls inside the $$2\% - 8\%$$ gently sloping cropland range given for contour bunds, so the site is suitable for this physical measure.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the vertical interval from $$0.9\text{ m}$$ to $$0.4\text{ m}$$ and the location from Keren to Mendefera, so the slope becomes $$4\%$$, which falls inside (rather than above) the recommended contour bund range.

similar_questions.question: On a hillside above Asmara, two points on the ground lie $$50\text{ meters}$$ apart horizontally, and a telescopic level shows that the upper point is $$7.5\text{ meters}$$ higher than the lower point. Compute the percentage slope of this hillside and explain what such a slope means for the choice between contour bunds and hillside terraces.
similar_questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$15\%$$; this far exceeds the $$2\% - 8\%$$ range for contour bunds, so hillside terraces (which break slope length and trap water and sediment) are the appropriate physical measure

solution_steps.title: Identify the given intervals
solution_steps.detail: The horizontal distance between the two points is $$\text{HI} = 50\text{ meters}$$ and the elevation difference is $$\text{VI} = 7.5\text{ meters}$$.

solution_steps.title: Apply the percentage slope formula
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute and compute
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{7.5}{50}\right) \times 100 = 0.15 \times 100 = 15\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Interpret the result on the landscape
solution_steps.detail: A $$15\%$$ slope is nearly twice the upper limit of the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band listed for contour bunds, so bunds alone would not safely handle the runoff on this hillside.

solution_steps.title: Select the matching measure
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists hillside terraces as the physical measure for sloping, cultivated or uncultivated hills because they break slope length, trap water and sediment, and create flat planting steps - the correct choice for a $$15\%$$ hillside.

similar_questions.variant_note: Replaced the $$10\text{-meter}$$ line level setup with a telescopic level survey over a $$50\text{-meter}$$ horizontal distance and a $$7.5\text{ m}$$ rise, producing a steep $$15\%$$ slope and requiring a choice between two physical conservation measures.

questions.question: Describe the transition of water erosion from splash erosion to the formation of a highly advanced gully system on a bare, sloping farm plot in the highlands. In your answer, name each stage in order, state the characteristic feature and approximate depth or scale of each, and explain how the farmer could detect the earliest stage of uniform soil removal before channels appear.
questions.answer: The sequence is splash (raindrop) erosion (micro-scale craters, hard crust, particles splashed up to $$1.5\text{ m}$$) then sheet erosion (uniform removal in broad, thin sheets, detectable early by soil pedestals) then rill erosion (small, shallow concentrated channels up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, removable by ordinary tillage) then gully erosion (narrow, deep channels of $$1 - 150\text{ m}$$ that fragment the land and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage).

solution_steps.title: Start with detachment by raindrop impact
solution_steps.detail: The process begins with splash (raindrop) erosion, the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by direct raindrop impact on bare soil. On a micro-scale it produces small craters, destroys soil structure and forms a hard crust on dry soil; the chapter notes raindrops can strike bare soil at speeds up to $$30\text{ kilometers per hour}$$ and splash particles up to $$1.5\text{ meters}$$ horizontally.

solution_steps.title: Move to uniform removal as sheet erosion
solution_steps.detail: Once detached, particles are removed uniformly down the slope by water flowing overland in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels. Sheet erosion strips very thin layers, removing the most fertile topsoil and organic matter and exposing stone bases.

solution_steps.title: Explain how to detect the sheet stage early
solution_steps.detail: The chapter pro-tip advises looking for soil pedestals - tiny columns of soil capped by small stones or wood chips that have protected the soil directly underneath from raindrop impact. Their appearance signals that the surrounding soil is being stripped away in thin sheets before any channels form.

solution_steps.title: Describe the appearance of concentrated flow paths
solution_steps.detail: As overland flow concentrates, rill erosion develops small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that appear as many small, parallel channels across the field, up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep. Rills are temporary and can be easily smoothed out by ordinary tillage, so the chapter pro-tip warns that if left untreated for even one rainy season they merge and deepen.

solution_steps.title: Explain the final, advanced stage
solution_steps.detail: In the advanced stage the runoff flows in narrow, deep channels during or immediately after heavy rains, producing gullies. Gullies range from $$1\text{ to }2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ deep (the chapter table gives $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$), with wide, steep, unstable walls that cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations.

solution_steps.title: State the consequence and the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The gully divides the land into fragments and stops machinery movement, making reclamation extremely difficult and expensive. The correct conclusion is that the stages form a continuous, accelerating chain - splash to sheet to rill to gully - so intervention at the rill stage (or earlier, by spotting soil pedestals and applying biological or physical conservation measures) is far cheaper than reclaiming a mature gully.

similar_questions.question: Explain how wind erosion acts on a dry, bare lowland plain such as the eastern dry lowlands, naming its two main effects and describing the damage each does to soil and crops.
similar_questions.answer: Wind erosion acts through deflation, the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region, and abrasion, the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds; together they strip topsoil and damage seedlings.

solution_steps.title: State where wind erosion occurs
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that wind erosion occurs primarily in arid and semi-arid climates where the soil is dry and unprotected by vegetation, which describes the dry lowlands receiving only about $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ of soil loss by wind.

solution_steps.title: Define the first effect
solution_steps.detail: Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region. It is the primary cause of topsoil blowing away from dry lowland fields.

solution_steps.title: Define the second effect
solution_steps.detail: Abrasion is the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds, and the chapter table records it as sand abrasion on seedlings.

solution_steps.title: Conclude on the agricultural impact
solution_steps.detail: Because the dry lowlands have only wind - not rainfall runoff - as the primary causative agent, the conservation response must protect the surface, for example by maintaining vegetative cover and mulch rather than by constructing water-intercepting structures.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the erosion agent from water to wind, replaced the highland sloping plot with the dry lowlands, and required the two wind-erosion effects (deflation and abrasion) instead of the four-stage water-erosion sequence.

similar_questions.question: Explain how rainfall and topography combine to make the Eritrean highlands the most erosion-prone area in the chapter's comparison of regions, and state the specific consequences this has for crop production there.
similar_questions.answer: In the highlands, high and intense rainfall produces large volumes of runoff that steep topography accelerates downslope, giving an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, the highest of the four regions; the consequences are exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil.

solution_steps.title: Recall the two controlling factors
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the speed and extent of soil degradation depend on factors such as soil types, topography, climate and the intensity of land use - here climate (rainfall) and topography (slope) are decisive.

solution_steps.title: Explain the role of the rainfall factor
solution_steps.detail: Rainfall in these highland areas supplies the water that detaches particles by raindrop impact and then carries them downslope as runoff, so water is listed as the primary causative agent for the highlands.

solution_steps.title: Explain the role of the topographic factor
solution_steps.detail: Slope steepness increases the velocity of runoff, so the water has more energy to detach and transport soil. The chapter records measured soil loss on steep slopes of $$3.4\text{ to }84.5\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$, with a mean of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ - about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil annually and roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the soil replacement rate.

solution_steps.title: Apply the regional comparison
solution_steps.detail: In the chapter's table the highlands have the highest estimated loss at $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, well above the moist lowlands ($$47$$), the eastern escarpment ($$37$$) and the dry lowlands ($$6$$), confirming the highlands as the most erosion-prone region.

solution_steps.title: State the agricultural consequences
solution_steps.detail: The table lists exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil for the highlands. The chapter adds that erosion depletes nitrogen and phosphorus, lowers water retention capacity, reduces soil depth and exposes roots, making crops highly vulnerable to drought.

similar_questions.variant_note: Switched from describing the temporal sequence of water-erosion forms to analysing the regional pattern of highland erosion ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$) and its crop-production consequences, using the chapter's regional table rather than the erosion-type table.

questions.question:
A soil conservation team compares two Eritrean sites using the chapter's regional soil-loss figures. Site A is highland farmland whose measured loss falls at the lower end of the highland range given in the chapter ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Site B is dry lowland farmland losing $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate how many times greater the soil loss at Site A is than at Site B.
(b) The chapter also notes that under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of fertile topsoil takes $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$ to form, and that a loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year represents approximately $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. Using the mid-point of the formation range ($$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), calculate the average annual topsoil formation in millimetres per year, and hence explain in one sentence how Site A's loss compares with it.
questions.answer: (a) Site A ($$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$) loses about $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B ($$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). (b) Using the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, natural topsoil formation averages $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$, so Site A's loss of roughly $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$100\text{ times}$$ faster than the soil can be replaced.

solution_steps.title: Extract the soil-loss figures for the two sites
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table gives the highlands an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ and the dry lowlands $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$. Site A lies at the lower end of the highland range, so its loss is $$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; Site B loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the ratio to be computed
solution_steps.detail: The required comparison is a ratio: $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Loss at Site A}}{\text{Loss at Site B}}$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute and carry out the division
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{50}{6} = 8.33$$, i.e. approximately $$8.3\text{ times}$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert the natural formation range into an annual rate
solution_steps.detail: Under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ ($$= 10\text{ mm}$$) of topsoil needs $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$. Taking the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, the average annual formation is $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{250\text{ years}} = 0.04\text{ mm per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Relate the computed loss rate to the formation rate
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that a loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. This is consistent with the computed formation rate: $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm}}{0.04\text{ mm per year}} = 100$$ - that is, at the lower-end highland loss of $$50\text{ t/ha/year}$$ the soil is still being removed many times faster than the $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$ at which fertile topsoil forms naturally.

solution_steps.title: State the agronomic consequence
solution_steps.detail: Because accumulation cannot keep pace with removal, the topsoil layer thins progressively. This matches the chapter's description of land degradation as a continuous process marked by progressive weakening of the physical, chemical and biological potential of land, and of erosion causing nutrient depletion (especially nitrogen and phosphorus), lower water retention, reduced soil depth and exposed plant roots.

solution_steps.title: Draw the conservation conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The comparison shows that Site A loses roughly $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B, and still loses topsoil dozens of times faster than nature rebuilds it, so a physical or biological soil and water conservation measure - for example hillside terraces on the sloping highland plot - is required rather than relying on natural soil formation.

similar_questions.question:
Two farms are compared using the chapter's regional figures. Farm X lies in the highlands, where the measured soil loss is at the upper end of the chapter's highland range ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Farm Y lies in the dry lowlands, where the primary causative agent is wind and the estimated loss is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate the ratio of Farm X's soil loss to Farm Y's.
(b) Using the chapter figure of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil lost per year at the mean steep-slope loss rate, and a natural formation time of $$100\text{ years}$$ for $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of topsoil, calculate the annual natural formation rate and state how many times larger the loss rate is.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$\dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ (roughly $$17\text{ times}$$). (b) $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{100\text{ years}} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$, so the $$4\text{ mm per year}$$ loss is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate

solution_steps.title: Read the required values from the chapter
solution_steps.detail: The upper end of the highland range is $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm X loses $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; the dry lowland figure is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm Y loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the ratio
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so Farm X loses about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Farm Y.

solution_steps.title: Convert formation time to an annual rate
solution_steps.detail: $$1\text{ centimeter} = 10\text{ mm}$$ forms in $$100\text{ years}$$, so the natural formation rate is $$\dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare loss with formation
solution_steps.detail: $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm per year}}{0.1\text{ mm per year}} = 40$$, so the loss rate is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate at the fastest possible natural formation.

solution_steps.title: Interpret the result
solution_steps.detail: Even under the most favourable natural soil-building conditions in the chapter ($$100\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), erosion on steep highland farmland removes topsoil far faster than it forms, which is why the chapter calls topsoil a precious, slow-forming resource and why conservation measures are indispensable.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed Site A from the lower end ($$50$$) to the upper end ($$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$) of the highland range and changed the formation time from the $$250\text{-year}$$ mid-point to the fastest rate of $$100\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, so the ratio becomes about $$16.7$$ and the loss-to-formation factor becomes $$40$$.

similar_questions.question:
A highland catchment of $$200\text{ hectares}$$ is losing topsoil by water erosion at the chapter's mean rate for steep slopes of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$.
(a) Calculate the total annual soil loss from the catchment in tons.
(b) Given that this mean rate corresponds to an annual loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, calculate the total volume of topsoil lost each year in cubic metres (take $$1\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil $$= 1.3\text{ tons}$$), and express your answer to the nearest whole cubic metre.
(c) State one conservation measure from the chapter that would directly reduce this loss on the sloping cultivated land, and one that would trap the sediment already being carried away.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$200 \times 42 = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$. (b) $$\dfrac{8\,400}{1.3} = 6\,461.5$$, so approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil per year. (c) Hillside terraces (or contour bunds) on the sloping cultivated land reduce detachment and runoff, while check dams built across active gullies trap the sediment and slow the water.

solution_steps.title: Identify the mean loss rate and area
solution_steps.detail: The chapter reports a mean soil loss of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ on steep slopes, and the catchment area is $$200\text{ hectares}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the total annual soil loss
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Total loss} = 42\text{ tons/ha/year} \times 200\text{ ha} = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert tons of soil to volume
solution_steps.detail: Using $$1\text{ m}^3 = 1.3\text{ tons}$$, the volume is $$\dfrac{8\,400\text{ tons}}{1.3\text{ tons/m}^3} = 6\,461.5\text{ m}^3$$, which rounds to approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ per year.

solution_steps.title: Link the loss to the thinning topsoil layer
solution_steps.detail: The chapter notes that the mean steep-slope loss represents an annual loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate, so this volume represents a layer of fertile topsoil that natural formation cannot replace within a human lifetime.

solution_steps.title: Select measures that reduce and trap the loss
solution_steps.detail: Hillside terraces are a physical measure that breaks slope length and traps water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, and contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands. Check dams are built across gullies to slow water velocity and trap sediment, preventing the gullies from widening.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reframed the calculation from a simple ratio between two sites to a catchment-scale loss estimate ($$200\text{ ha}$$ at $$42\text{ tons/ha/year}$$), added a tons-to-cubic-metres volume conversion, and required selection of a reducing measure plus a sediment-trapping measure from the chapter.

questions.question: A vegetable farm near Asmara owns a tractor, an irrigation system and a farm store building. Which one of the following items would be classified as working capital and NOT as fixed capital on this farm?
options: A. Fertilizer purchased for the coming tomato season
B. Tractor used for land preparation
C. Irrigation system fitted with a diesel pump
D. Farm store building for harvested vegetables
questions.answer: A. Fertilizer purchased for the coming tomato season

solution_steps.title: Recall the definition of capital
solution_steps.detail: Capital is the human-made factor of production. The chapter divides it into fixed capital (assets used over many years) and working capital (cash or inputs used up in a single production cycle).

solution_steps.title: Apply the test of a single production cycle
solution_steps.detail: Fixed capital such as tractors, buildings and irrigation systems gives service over many years and depreciates over time. Working capital such as seeds, fertilizers and pesticides is consumed within one season.

solution_steps.title: Screen each option
solution_steps.detail: B (tractor) and C (irrigation system) are listed in the chapter as fixed capital, and D (farm store building) is also a building used over many years. None of them is used up in one season.

solution_steps.title: Select and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only A, fertilizer for the coming tomato season, is an input used up inside a single production cycle, so it is working capital and not fixed capital.

similar_questions.question: On a dairy farm in the Eritrean highlands, which one of the following is working capital rather than fixed capital?
similar_questions.answer: A. Animal feed bought for the current milking cycle

solution_steps.title: State the classification rule
solution_steps.detail: Working capital is cash or inputs that are used up in a single production cycle; fixed capital is used over many years.

solution_steps.title: Check each item
solution_steps.detail: The milking shed and the milking machine are used over many years, so both are fixed capital.

solution_steps.title: Test the remaining option
solution_steps.detail: Animal feed is consumed by the cows within the current cycle and must be replaced continuously, so it is used up in one cycle.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Animal feed for the current cycle is working capital, therefore the answer is A.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the enterprise from a vegetable farm near Asmara to a highland dairy farm, and replaces fertilizer with animal feed while keeping the fixed-capital distractors (building and machinery).

similar_questions.question: A crop farm keeps the following on its records: family labour, a harrow, maize seed and a pickup truck. Which of these belongs to the working capital category?
similar_questions.answer: C. Maize seed

solution_steps.title: Separate the factors of production
solution_steps.detail: Family labour is the labour factor, while the harrow, the pickup truck and the maize seed are all capital (human-made assets).

solution_steps.title: Apply the single-cycle test
solution_steps.detail: The harrow and the pickup truck are used over many years, so they are fixed capital, not working capital.

solution_steps.title: Identify the single-cycle input
solution_steps.detail: Maize seed is planted and used up within one production cycle, exactly like the seeds and fertilizers named in the chapter.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Maize seed is working capital, so the answer is C.

similar_questions.variant_note: Adds a labour item (family labour) as an extra distractor so the student must first separate the labour factor from the capital factor before classifying capital.

questions.question: A farmer at Keren is considering replacing the local wheat variety on one hectare with a new high-yielding variety. The change would raise seed cost by $$30\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and fertilizer cost by $$9\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, and it would reduce the cost of hired labour for weeding by $$2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$.
