Yield would rise by $$12\text{ quintals}$$, each selling at $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$, but the crop would no longer be sold as local seed, which used to bring an extra $$3\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Using a partial budget, decide whether the farmer should adopt the new variety, and state the net change in returns.
questions.answer: The farmer should NOT adopt the new variety, because Added Returns + Reduced Costs ($$16\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$) are less than Added Costs + Reduced Returns ($$42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$); the change would make returns worse by $$25\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Name the tool and its decision rule
solution_steps.detail: This is a minor single-enterprise change on one hectare, so a partial budget is the correct tool. The rule from the chapter is: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute total added returns
solution_steps.detail: The extra yield is $$12\text{ quintals} \times 1\,200\text{ Nakfa} = 14\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, so Added Returns $$= 14\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute total reduced costs
solution_steps.detail: Hired weeding labour falls by $$2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, so Reduced Costs $$= 2\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. The left-hand side is $$14\,400 + 2\,500 = 16\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the added costs and reduced returns
solution_steps.detail: Added Costs are extra seed plus extra fertilizer: $$30\,000 + 9\,800 = 39\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$. Reduced Returns are the lost local-seed premium of $$3\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. The right-hand side is $$39\,800 + 3\,000 = 42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare and conclude
solution_steps.detail: $$16\,900\text{ Nakfa} < 42\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, so the right-hand side is larger. The change fails the partial-budget test by $$42\,800 - 16\,900 = 25\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, and the farmer should not adopt the new variety.

similar_questions.question: A farmer at Massawa plans to buy a small diesel pump to irrigate one hectare of vegetables. The pump costs $$18\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and annual fuel and maintenance add $$4\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, while it would save $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year in hired watering labour. Extra vegetables worth $$21\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year would be produced. Use a partial budget to decide whether the pump should be bought, and give the net change per year.
similar_questions.answer: Buy the pump: Added Returns + Reduced Costs = $$21\,000 + 7\,000 = 28\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ exceeds Added Costs = $$22\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, giving a net gain of $$5\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year.

solution_steps.title: Identify the tool and rule
solution_steps.detail: Buying one new tool for one hectare is a minor change, so use a partial budget: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add up the benefit side
solution_steps.detail: Added Returns are the extra vegetables, $$21\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$; Reduced Costs are the saved watering labour, $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Total $$= 28\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add up the cost side
solution_steps.detail: Added Costs are the pump price plus fuel and maintenance: $$18\,000 + 4\,500 = 22\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$. There are no reduced returns in this case.

solution_steps.title: Compare and conclude
solution_steps.detail: $$28\,000 > 22\,500$$, so the pump passes the test by $$28\,000 - 22\,500 = 5\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year and should be bought.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the partial-budget structure but changes the decision from a seed variety to buying a new tool, moves the setting to Massawa, and changes every figure so the test is passed rather than failed.

similar_questions.question: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands is considering joining a service cooperative instead of buying inputs alone. Membership costs $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year, and fertilizer bought through the cooperative is $$4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$ cheaper per year for the farm. However, seed must now be bought only from the cooperative, which is $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year more expensive, and cooperative members may not receive a $$500\text{ Nakfa}$$ a year input subsidy from a local buyer. Use a partial budget to decide whether to join.
similar_questions.answer: Join the cooperative: Added Returns + Reduced Costs = $$4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$ exceeds Added Costs + Reduced Returns = $$2\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, giving a net gain of $$1\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year.

solution_steps.title: Set up the partial budget
solution_steps.detail: Joining a cooperative changes only input purchase, a minor change, so apply: implement if $$\text{Added Returns} + \text{Reduced Costs} > \text{Added Costs} + \text{Reduced Returns}$$.

solution_steps.title: List the benefit side
solution_steps.detail: There is no extra output, so Added Returns $$= 0$$. Reduced Costs are the cheaper bulk fertilizer, $$4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$. Total benefit $$= 4\,300\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: List the cost side
solution_steps.detail: Added Costs are the membership fee of $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ plus the dearer seed of $$1\,200\text{ Nakfa}$$. Reduced Returns are the lost $$500\text{ Nakfa}$$ subsidy. Total $$= 700 + 1\,200 + 500 = 2\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare and conclude
solution_steps.detail: $$4\,300 > 2\,400$$, a net gain of $$1\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per year, so the farmer should join the cooperative.

similar_questions.variant_note: Applies the same partial-budget rule to a cooperative-membership decision instead of a variety change, adds a membership fee, and includes both a Reduced Cost and a Reduced Return so all four partial-budget categories are used.

questions.question: On 31 December a farm business near Asmara reports current assets of $$25\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and long-term assets of $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Its current liabilities are $$8\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and its long-term bank loan is $$12\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Calculate the farm's net worth (capital). (b) State whether the farm is solvent, and explain what the balance sheet would have to show for the farm to be insolvent.
questions.answer: (a) Net worth = $$100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (b) The farm is solvent because net worth is positive; it would be insolvent only if total liabilities exceeded total assets, giving a negative net worth.

solution_steps.title: State the balance-sheet equation
solution_steps.detail: A balance sheet reflects the financial position on a specific date and follows the accounting equation $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital (Net Worth)}$$.

solution_steps.title: Total the assets
solution_steps.detail: Current assets plus long-term assets: $$25\,000 + 75\,000 = 100\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Total the liabilities
solution_steps.detail: Current liabilities plus long-term liabilities: $$8\,000 + 12\,000 = 20\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Solve for net worth
solution_steps.detail: Rearranging the equation gives Net Worth $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities} = 100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Interpret solvency
solution_steps.detail: Net worth is positive ($$80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$), so assets exceed liabilities and the farm is solvent. It would be insolvent (bankrupt) only if liabilities exceeded assets, that is, if net worth were negative.

similar_questions.question: A farm business in Keren has cash of $$6\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, unsold crops valued at $$19\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, land and buildings valued at $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, a current debt of $$7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and a long-term loan of $$13\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Use the accounting equation to find the net worth, and identify which items are current assets.
similar_questions.answer: Net worth = $$100\,000 - 20\,000 = 80\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$; the current assets are the cash ($$6\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$) and the unsold crops ($$19\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$).

solution_steps.title: Write the accounting equation
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital (Net Worth)}$$, so Net Worth $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Liabilities}$$.

solution_steps.title: Separate current and long-term assets
solution_steps.detail: Cash and unsold crops are convertible to cash within $$12\text{ months}$$, so they are current assets: $$6\,000 + 19\,000 = 25\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Land and buildings are long-term assets of $$75\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the same accounting equation and totals but asks the student to classify assets by liquidity as well as compute net worth, and uses different component figures (cash, unsold crops, land instead of one lumped current-asset figure).

similar_questions.question: A farm business at Massawa lists total assets of $$65\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and a net worth of $$47\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Find its total liabilities. (b) If the long-term bank loan is $$11\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, what is the value of the current liabilities?
similar_questions.answer: (a) Total liabilities = $$18\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (b) Current liabilities = $$18\,000 - 11\,000 = 7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Start from the accounting equation
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Net Worth}$$, therefore Liabilities $$= \text{Assets} - \text{Net Worth}$$.

solution_steps.title: Split liabilities by maturity
solution_steps.detail: Long-term liabilities are debts such as long-term bank loans, and current liabilities are debts due within one year; together they make up total liabilities.

solution_steps.title: Find current liabilities
solution_steps.detail: Current liabilities $$= 18\,000 - 11\,000 = 7\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reverses the unknown: instead of finding net worth from assets and liabilities, the student must find total liabilities and then separate them into current and long-term components.

questions.question: A maize farmer near Barentu applies bags of nitrogen fertilizer to a fixed plot of land. The response of the crop is: with $$3$$ bags the total product is $$22\text{ quintals}$$, with $$4$$ bags it is $$28\text{ quintals}$$, with $$5$$ bags it is $$32\text{ quintals}$$ and with $$6$$ bags it is $$34\text{ quintals}$$. Maize sells at $$900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per quintal and each bag of fertilizer costs $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. (a) Compute the marginal product of the fourth, fifth and sixth bags. (b) Compute the Marginal Value Product for each of those bags. (c) State the profit-maximizing number of bags and explain why applying one more bag would reduce profit.
questions.answer: (a) MP: 4th bag $$= 6$$, 5th bag $$= 4$$, 6th bag $$= 2\text{ quintals}$$. (b) MVP: 4th $$= 5\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, 6th $$= 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$. (c) The profit-maximizing level is $$5$$ bags, because the 5th bag's MVP ($$3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$) still exceeds the input price ($$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$) while the 6th bag's MVP ($$1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$) is below it, so the 6th bag would cost more than it returns.

solution_steps.title: State the two formulas needed
solution_steps.detail: Marginal Product is $$\text{MP} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$ and Marginal Value Product is $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times P_y$$, where $$P_y$$ is the unit price of the output. Profit is maximized where $$\text{MVP} = P_x$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the marginal products
solution_steps.detail: Fourth bag: $$28 - 22 = 6\text{ quintals}$$. Fifth bag: $$32 - 28 = 4\text{ quintals}$$. Sixth bag: $$34 - 32 = 2\text{ quintals}$$. MP is falling, which is the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns in action.

solution_steps.title: Compute the marginal value products
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times 900\text{ Nakfa}$$. Fourth bag: $$6 \times 900 = 5\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$. Fifth bag: $$4 \times 900 = 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$. Sixth bag: $$2 \times 900 = 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare each MVP with the input price
solution_steps.detail: The price of the input is $$P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ per bag. The fourth bag adds $$5\,400\text{ Nakfa}$$ of value for $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, the fifth adds $$3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, and the sixth adds only $$1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify the profit-maximizing level
solution_steps.detail: The fifth bag still gives $$\text{MVP} = 3\,600\text{ Nakfa} > P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so it is worth applying. The sixth bag gives $$\text{MVP} = 1\,800\text{ Nakfa} < P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so it is not worth applying. The profit-maximizing level is therefore $$5$$ bags.

solution_steps.title: Explain the loss from over-application
solution_steps.detail: At the sixth bag the farmer pays $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ and receives output worth only $$1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, a net loss of $$200\text{ Nakfa}$$. All the levels examined still lie in Stage II, where MP is positive but falling; pushing inputs until MP becomes negative would enter Stage III, the irrational zone of waste.

similar_questions.question: A teff farmer in the Eritrean highlands applies units of fertilizer to a fixed plot. The total product is $$26\text{ quintals}$$ at $$2$$ units, $$30\text{ quintals}$$ at $$3$$ units, $$32\text{ quintals}$$ at $$4$$ units and $$33\text{ quintals}$$ at $$5$$ units. Teff sells at $$900\text{ Nakfa}$$ per quintal and each unit of fertilizer costs $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$. Find the marginal product and the Marginal Value Product of each additional unit and state the profit-maximizing number of units.
similar_questions.answer: MP: 3rd unit $$= 4$$, 4th $$= 2$$, 5th $$= 1\text{ quintal}$$. MVP: 3rd $$= 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, 4th $$= 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 900\text{ Nakfa}$$. The profit-maximizing level is $$2$$ units, because the 3rd unit's MVP is already below the $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ input price.

solution_steps.title: Recall the formulas
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{MP} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$, $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times P_y$$, and profits are maximized where $$\text{MVP} = P_x$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the marginal value products
solution_steps.detail: At $$P_y = 900\text{ Nakfa}$$: 3rd $$= 4 \times 900 = 3\,600\text{ Nakfa}$$, 4th $$= 2 \times 900 = 1\,800\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 1 \times 900 = 900\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the input price
solution_steps.detail: Every additional unit from the 3rd onward has $$\text{MVP} < P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so none of them pays for itself. The farmer should stop at $$2$$ units.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The profit-maximizing quantity is $$2$$ units of fertilizer, and each unit beyond that would reduce total profit.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the crop to teff, shifts the entire response table so that the optimum falls at a lower input level, and makes the answer a stop-at-the-start case rather than a mid-table optimum.

similar_questions.question: A sorghum farmer at Keren is offered subsidized fertilizer at $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ per bag, while sorghum sells at $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ per quintal. Total product is $$18\text{ quintals}$$ with $$3$$ bags, $$25$$ with $$4$$ bags, $$30$$ with $$5$$ bags and $$33$$ with $$6$$ bags. Compute the marginal product and the Marginal Value Product of the fourth, fifth and sixth bags and recommend the profit-maximizing number of bags.
similar_questions.answer: MP: 4th $$= 7$$, 5th $$= 5$$, 6th $$= 3\text{ quintals}$$. MVP: 4th $$= 4\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 3\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, 6th $$= 2\,100\text{ Nakfa}$$. The profit-maximizing level is $$6$$ bags, since even the 6th bag's MVP exceeds the $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ price.

solution_steps.title: State the decision rule
solution_steps.detail: Add input while $$\text{MVP} = \text{MP} \times P_y$$ exceeds the input price $$P_x$$, and stop at the level where the two are equal.

solution_steps.title: Compute marginal value products
solution_steps.detail: At $$P_y = 700\text{ Nakfa}$$: 4th $$= 7 \times 700 = 4\,900\text{ Nakfa}$$, 5th $$= 5 \times 700 = 3\,500\text{ Nakfa}$$, 6th $$= 3 \times 700 = 2\,100\text{ Nakfa}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the input price
solution_steps.detail: All three MVPs exceed $$P_x = 2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$, so the 4th, 5th and 6th bags all add more value than they cost.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Within the range given the farmer should apply all $$6$$ bags; the optimum would only be reached later, at the first bag whose MVP falls to $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the crop and location, lowers the output price to $$700\text{ Nakfa}$$ and the input price to $$2\,000\text{ Nakfa}$$ so that the optimum lies at or beyond the highest input level given instead of inside the table.

questions.question: Management (entrepreneurship) is described as the factor of production that combines land, labour and capital. Explain why management is regarded as the coordinating force among the other three factors of production, and contrast the main management objective of a commercial farm in Eritrea with that of a subsistence farm.
questions.answer: Management coordinates the other factors because it is the only human resource that combines land, labour and capital, makes the business decisions through planning, implementation and control, and bears all the risks of success or failure. A commercial farm aims at profit maximisation or cost minimisation, while a subsistence farm aims at household self-sufficiency rather than profit.

solution_steps.title: Identify what each factor can and cannot do alone
solution_steps.detail: Land (soil, water and climate) has a fixed supply and is immobile; labour is the physical and mental contribution of humans; capital is the human-made asset set, either fixed or working. None of these three can decide by itself how much of the others to use.

solution_steps.title: State the function of management
solution_steps.detail: Management is the human resource responsible for combining land, labour and capital, making the business decisions, and bearing all the risks of success or failure. It is therefore the decision-making and organisational factor.

solution_steps.title: Explain the coordinating role
solution_steps.detail: The farm manager performs the functions of planning, implementation and control. Planning decides the enterprise and input levels, implementation organises land, labour and capital into actual production, and control compares results with the plan, so the three physical factors are only brought together and adjusted through management.

solution_steps.title: State the commercial-farm objective
solution_steps.detail: On a commercial farm the main objective is the maximisation of profit or the minimisation of production costs, so decisions are driven by returns compared with costs.

solution_steps.title: State the subsistence-farm objective and conclude
solution_steps.detail: On a subsistence farm the main objective is not profit but achieving household self-sufficiency, so the same resources are organised to feed the household first. In both cases, however, it is management that decides, bears the risk, and coordinates land, labour and capital.

similar_questions.question: A farmer near Asmara has fertile land, six family workers and a tractor, yet the farm makes a loss. Using the factors of production, explain which factor is most likely to be the missing or weak element, and justify your answer with the functions of a farm manager.
similar_questions.answer: The weak factor is management (entrepreneurship): land, labour and capital are all present, but without effective planning, implementation and control the resources are not combined into a profitable plan.

solution_steps.title: List the four factors
solution_steps.detail: Production relies on land, labour, capital and management. The farm already has land (fertile soil), labour (six family workers) and capital (a tractor).

solution_steps.title: Recall the functions of a farm manager
solution_steps.detail: The functions of a farm manager are divided into planning, implementation and control.

solution_steps.title: Locate the gap
solution_steps.detail: Having resources is not the same as using them well: choosing what to produce, how much input to apply and how to check results are all planning, implementation and control decisions, which belong to management.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The missing element is management, because it is the factor responsible for combining land, labour and capital and for bearing the risk of the outcome.

similar_questions.variant_note: Turns the conceptual question into a diagnostic case: the student must first confirm that the other three factors are present and then argue that management is the weak factor, using the planning-implementation-control functions.

similar_questions.question: Two farms near Keren each hold the same area of land and hire the same number of workers. Farm X sells its whole harvest on the market; Farm Y keeps most of its harvest for its own household and sells only a small surplus. Using the factors of production, explain how the two farms differ in their management objective and in the risk each manager bears.
similar_questions.answer: Farm X is a commercial farm whose objective is maximisation of profit or minimisation of production costs, so its manager bears full market-price risk; Farm Y is a subsistence farm whose objective is household self-sufficiency, so its manager bears mainly production risk and takes little market risk.

solution_steps.title: Recognise that the resource base is identical
solution_steps.detail: Both farms use the same land and the same quantity of labour, so the difference must lie in the management factor rather than in the physical factors.

solution_steps.title: Classify Farm X
solution_steps.detail: Selling the whole harvest on the market is commercial farming, where the main objective is the maximisation of profit or the minimisation of production costs.

solution_steps.title: Classify Farm Y
solution_steps.detail: Consuming most of the harvest at home means the main objective is not profit but achieving household self-sufficiency.

solution_steps.title: Compare the risks borne
solution_steps.detail: Management is the factor that bears all risks of success or failure. Farm X's manager carries price and market risk on the whole output, whereas Farm Y's manager is largely shielded from price risk and mainly faces weather, pest and yield risk.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Identical land and labour produce different decisions because the management objective differs: profit maximisation on Farm X and household self-sufficiency on Farm Y.

similar_questions.variant_note: Moves from a definition-and-contrast answer to a comparative case study of two farms with identical land and labour, requiring the student to infer the objective and the type of risk borne by each manager.

questions.question: Which nutrient family supplies $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ of energy and has building blocks that combine one glycerol molecule with three fatty acids?
options: A. Carbohydrates
B. Proteins
C. Lipids
D. Water
questions.answer: C. Lipids ($$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, built from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids)

solution_steps.title: Identify the energy value
solution_steps.detail: Table 1.1 gives the energy yields per gram as carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and water $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$. Since lipids provide exactly double the energy of carbohydrates, the value $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ is the lipid value.

solution_steps.title: Identify the building blocks
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that lipids are made of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acids through condensation reactions, which matches the second clue in the question.

solution_steps.title: Check every distractor
solution_steps.detail: Carbohydrates yield $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and are built from monosaccharides such as glucose; proteins yield $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and are built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; water yields $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and is built from H and O atoms. None of these matches $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ together with glycerol and three fatty acids.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only lipids satisfy both clues, so option C is the single correct answer.

similar_questions.question: Which nutrient family yields $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and is built from single sugar units such as glucose?
similar_questions.answer: A. Carbohydrates ($$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, built from monosaccharides such as glucose)

solution_steps.title: Identify the energy value
solution_steps.detail: From Table 1.1, carbohydrates give $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and water $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$. The value in the question is therefore the carbohydrate value.

solution_steps.title: Match the building blocks
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that carbohydrates are classified into monosaccharides such as glucose, disaccharides such as sucrose, and polysaccharides such as starch, so single sugar units such as glucose are the building blocks of carbohydrates.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Proteins are built from amino acids, lipids from glycerol and three fatty acids, and water from H and O atoms. None of these consists of single sugar units, so none can be correct.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only carbohydrates match both the energy value $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and a monosaccharide building block, so the answer is A.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the nutrient from lipids to carbohydrates, replacing the energy value $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ with $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and the glycerol plus three fatty acids building blocks with monosaccharides such as glucose.

similar_questions.question: Which nutrient yields $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and is confirmed by blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink?
similar_questions.answer: D. Water ($$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, detected by cobalt chloride paper turning from blue to pink)

solution_steps.title: Identify the zero-energy nutrient
solution_steps.detail: Table 1.1 gives water an energy yield of $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, while carbohydrates, proteins and lipids yield $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ respectively. Water is therefore the only nutrient that releases no energy.

solution_steps.title: Match the laboratory test
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that water is tested with cobalt chloride paper, which turns from blue to pink in the presence of water.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Carbohydrates are tested with Benedict's solution (brick-red precipitate), proteins with the Biuret test (violet colour) and lipids with the ethanol emulsion test (cloudy white emulsion). None of these three uses cobalt chloride paper, and all three yield energy.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Water alone has an energy yield of $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and turns blue cobalt chloride paper pink, so the answer is D.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the nutrient to water and shifts the second clue from building blocks to a specific laboratory test (blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink), covering a nutrient family not tested in the main question.

questions.question: Complete the following passage with the correct terms. In the mouth, saliva contains the enzyme ______(i)______, which digests starch into ______(ii)______ at a neutral pH. In the stomach, gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid at about pH ______(iii)______, which kills bacteria and activates pepsinogen into ______(iv)______, the enzyme that breaks proteins down into polypeptides.
questions.answer: (i) salivary amylase (ptyalin); (ii) maltose; (iii) 1.5 (pH 1.5 to 2.0); (iv) pepsin

solution_steps.title: Recall the enzyme of saliva
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that saliva contains salivary amylase, also called ptyalin, so blank (i) is salivary amylase (ptyalin).

solution_steps.title: State the product of starch digestion in the mouth
solution_steps.detail: Salivary amylase digests starch into the disaccharide maltose at a neutral pH of about 7.0, so blank (ii) is maltose.

solution_steps.title: Recall the pH of gastric juice
solution_steps.detail: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 (given as approximately 1.5 to 2.0), so blank (iii) is 1.5.

solution_steps.title: Name the activated enzyme
solution_steps.detail: The acid activates the inactive pepsinogen into pepsin, which breaks proteins into polypeptides; mucus protects the stomach wall from this acid and enzyme. Blank (iv) is therefore pepsin.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following passage. The duodenum receives alkaline pancreatic juice containing pancreatic amylase, ______(i)______ and lipase. Bile from the liver contains no enzymes but performs ______(ii)______, breaking large fat droplets into tiny droplets, and because bile is ______(iii)______ it also neutralizes the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach.
similar_questions.answer: (i) trypsin; (ii) emulsification; (iii) alkaline

solution_steps.title: List the enzymes of pancreatic juice
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that pancreatic juice contains pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase, so blank (i) is trypsin, the enzyme that digests proteins.

solution_steps.title: Recall the action of bile
solution_steps.detail: Bile contains no enzymes but its bile salts perform emulsification, which physically breaks large fat droplets into many tiny droplets and increases the surface area for lipase. Blank (ii) is emulsification.

solution_steps.title: Recall the pH of bile
solution_steps.detail: Bile is alkaline, and this alkalinity neutralizes the acidic gastric chyme so that pancreatic lipase can work at its optimum pH. Blank (iii) is alkaline.

solution_steps.title: Check the completed passage
solution_steps.detail: The completed passage reads that pancreatic juice contains pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase, that bile performs emulsification, and that bile is alkaline, which is fully consistent with the chapter.

similar_questions.variant_note: Moves the completion exercise from the mouth and stomach to the duodenum, so the blanks test pancreatic juice enzymes, emulsification by bile and bile alkalinity instead of salivary amylase, maltose, gastric pH and pepsin.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following passage. The large intestine absorbs water, mineral salts and vitamins, and the symbiotic bacteria living in it synthesize vitamin ______(i)______ and vitamin ______(ii)______. Undigested material is stored in the ______(iii)______ and is removed through the anus in a process called ______(iv)______.
similar_questions.answer: (i) vitamin B12; (ii) vitamin K; (iii) rectum; (iv) egestion (defecation)

solution_steps.title: Recall the products of the symbiotic bacteria
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the large intestine harbours symbiotic bacteria that synthesize vitamin B12 and vitamin K, so blanks (i) and (ii) are B12 and K.

solution_steps.title: Recall storage of undigested matter
solution_steps.detail: Undigested matter is stored in the rectum, so blank (iii) is rectum.

solution_steps.title: Name the elimination process
solution_steps.detail: The removal of undigested matter as faeces through the anus is called egestion or defecation, so blank (iv) is egestion (defecation).

solution_steps.title: Check the completed passage
solution_steps.detail: The passage now correctly states that the large intestine absorbs water, mineral salts and vitamins, that its bacteria make vitamin B12 and vitamin K, and that undigested material is stored in the rectum and egested through the anus.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the completion format but changes the organ from the mouth and stomach to the large intestine, so the blanks test absorbed materials, bacterial vitamin synthesis, the rectum and egestion rather than enzymes and pH values.

questions.question: A student in Asmara eats a lunch of injera with shiro and boiled eggs containing $$80\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$25\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$12\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Using the energy values in Table 1.1 (carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$), calculate the total energy released when this meal is completely oxidized in the body. (b) State which nutrient supplies the greatest amount of energy and give that amount.
questions.answer: (a) The meal releases $$2374\text{ kJ}$$ of energy in total. (b) Carbohydrates supply the greatest amount of energy, $$1368\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working principle
solution_steps.detail: The energy released by a nutrient equals its mass in grams multiplied by its energy yield per gram from Table 1.1, so total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$).

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy from carbohydrates
solution_steps.detail: Energy from carbohydrates = $$80\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1368\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy from proteins
solution_steps.detail: Energy from proteins = $$25\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 550\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy from lipids
solution_steps.detail: Energy from lipids = $$12\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 456\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add the three values
solution_steps.detail: Total energy = $$1368\text{ kJ} + 550\text{ kJ} + 456\text{ kJ} = 2374\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the contributions
solution_steps.detail: The contributions are carbohydrates $$1368\text{ kJ}$$, proteins $$550\text{ kJ}$$ and lipids $$456\text{ kJ}$$. Since $$1368 > 550 > 456$$, carbohydrates supply the greatest amount of energy, even though lipids have the highest energy value per gram, because far more carbohydrate was eaten.

similar_questions.question: An evening meal in Keren contains $$45\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$30\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$10\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy this meal can release when completely oxidized. (b) Identify the nutrient that supplies the least energy and state its value.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The meal releases $$1809.5\text{ kJ}$$ in total. (b) Lipids supply the least energy, $$380\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working principle
solution_steps.detail: Total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$), using the energy yields from Table 1.1.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the carbohydrate and protein energy
solution_steps.detail: Carbohydrates: $$45\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 769.5\text{ kJ}$$. Proteins: $$30\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 660\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the lipid energy
solution_steps.detail: Lipids: $$10\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 380\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add the three values
solution_steps.detail: Total energy = $$769.5\text{ kJ} + 660\text{ kJ} + 380\text{ kJ} = 1809.5\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare and conclude
solution_steps.detail: The contributions are carbohydrates $$769.5\text{ kJ}$$, proteins $$660\text{ kJ}$$ and lipids $$380\text{ kJ}$$, so lipids contribute the least energy because only $$10\text{ g}$$ was eaten.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the same three-nutrient energy calculation but changes all three masses ($$45\text{ g}$$, $$30\text{ g}$$, $$10\text{ g}$$ instead of $$80\text{ g}$$, $$25\text{ g}$$, $$12\text{ g}$$), changes the setting to Keren, and asks for the nutrient with the least energy instead of the greatest.

similar_questions.question: A snack sold near a school in Massawa contains $$25\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$10\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$8\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy of the snack. (b) Which of these three nutrients has the highest energy value per gram, and what is that value?
similar_questions.answer: (a) The snack contains $$951.5\text{ kJ}$$ of energy. (b) Lipids have the highest energy value per gram, $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working principle
solution_steps.detail: Total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$).

solution_steps.title: Calculate the carbohydrate energy
solution_steps.detail: Carbohydrates: $$25\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 427.5\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the protein and lipid energy
solution_steps.detail: Proteins: $$10\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 220\text{ kJ}$$. Lipids: $$8\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 304\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add to find the total energy
solution_steps.detail: Total energy = $$427.5\text{ kJ} + 220\text{ kJ} + 304\text{ kJ} = 951.5\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the energy values per gram
solution_steps.detail: The values per gram are lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, so lipids have the highest energy value per gram, which is why only $$8\text{ g}$$ of lipid supplies more energy than $$10\text{ g}$$ of protein.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses smaller masses in a Massawa snack context and replaces the request for the greatest total contribution with a comparison of the energy values per gram, so the reasoning moves from total mass x value to the value per gram itself.

questions.question: Two students in Massawa compare their breakfasts before a long walk. Breakfast A contains $$60\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$15\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$5\text{ g}$$ of lipids. Breakfast B contains $$50\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$20\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$10\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy that each breakfast can release. (b) State which breakfast supplies more energy and by how many kJ.
questions.answer: (a) Breakfast A releases $$1546\text{ kJ}$$ and Breakfast B releases $$1675\text{ kJ}$$. (b) Breakfast B supplies more energy, by $$129\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working principle
solution_steps.detail: For each breakfast, total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$), using the energy yields of Table 1.1.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy of Breakfast A from carbohydrates
solution_steps.detail: Breakfast A carbohydrates: $$60\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1026\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the remaining energy of Breakfast A
solution_steps.detail: Breakfast A proteins: $$15\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 330\text{ kJ}$$. Breakfast A lipids: $$5\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 190\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the total energy of Breakfast A
solution_steps.detail: Total for A = $$1026\text{ kJ} + 330\text{ kJ} + 190\text{ kJ} = 1546\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the total energy of Breakfast B
solution_steps.detail: Breakfast B carbohydrates: $$50\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 855\text{ kJ}$$; proteins: $$20\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 440\text{ kJ}$$; lipids: $$10\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 380\text{ kJ}$$. Total for B = $$855\text{ kJ} + 440\text{ kJ} + 380\text{ kJ} = 1675\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two totals
solution_steps.detail: Breakfast B gives $$1675\text{ kJ}$$ and Breakfast A gives $$1546\text{ kJ}$$. Difference = $$1675\text{ kJ} - 1546\text{ kJ} = 129\text{ kJ}$$, so Breakfast B supplies more energy by $$129\text{ kJ}$$, because its extra protein and its double-sized lipid portion ($$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$) more than make up for the smaller amount of carbohydrate.

similar_questions.question: Two students compare their afternoon snacks. Snack A contains $$40\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$10\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$8\text{ g}$$ of lipids. Snack B contains $$30\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$15\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$12\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy of each snack. (b) Which snack gives more energy, and by how many kJ?
similar_questions.answer: (a) Snack A gives $$1208\text{ kJ}$$ and Snack B gives $$1299\text{ kJ}$$. (b) Snack B gives more energy, by $$91\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working principle
solution_steps.detail: For each snack, total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$) in kJ.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy of Snack A
solution_steps.detail: Carbohydrates: $$40\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 684\text{ kJ}$$; proteins: $$10\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 220\text{ kJ}$$; lipids: $$8\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 304\text{ kJ}$$. Total A = $$684 + 220 + 304 = 1208\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy of Snack B
solution_steps.detail: Carbohydrates: $$30\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 513\text{ kJ}$$; proteins: $$15\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 330\text{ kJ}$$; lipids: $$12\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 456\text{ kJ}$$. Total B = $$513 + 330 + 456 = 1299\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two totals
solution_steps.detail: Difference = $$1299\text{ kJ} - 1208\text{ kJ} = 91\text{ kJ}$$, so Snack B gives more energy by $$91\text{ kJ}$$, mainly because its lipid content is larger and lipids yield $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the two-meal comparison structure but changes every mass, shortens the context from breakfast to an afternoon snack, and reduces the difference between the meals so the comparison requires careful arithmetic.

similar_questions.question: A nurse in Asmara compares two energy sources for a patient: $$40\text{ g}$$ of lipids eaten as butter and $$80\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates eaten as bread. Calculate the energy supplied by each food and state which one supplies more energy, and by how many kJ.
similar_questions.answer: The butter supplies $$1520\text{ kJ}$$ and the bread supplies $$1368\text{ kJ}$$, so the butter (lipids) supplies more energy, by $$152\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working principle
solution_steps.detail: Energy supplied = mass in grams x energy yield per gram. From Table 1.1, lipids yield $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and carbohydrates yield $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, so lipids give double the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy from lipids
solution_steps.detail: Energy from butter = $$40\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 1520\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the energy from carbohydrates
solution_steps.detail: Energy from bread = $$80\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1368\text{ kJ}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two values
solution_steps.detail: Difference = $$1520\text{ kJ} - 1368\text{ kJ} = 152\text{ kJ}$$. Even though the mass of bread is twice the mass of butter, the lipids still supply more energy, which shows why lipids are described as the spare fuel tank of the body.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the comparison from two mixed meals to two single pure nutrients (butter lipids against bread carbohydrates) with unequal masses, so the double energy value of lipids is tested directly rather than through a three-nutrient total.

questions.question: A person eats a meal of fried fish. Describe the complete journey of the fish proteins from the mouth until their digestion products reach the liver. In your answer name each enzyme that acts on the proteins, the pH condition in each region, and the blood vessel that carries the products to the liver.
questions.answer: In the mouth the fish is only chewed and made into a bolus because saliva contains amylase, not a protein enzyme. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which breaks the proteins into polypeptides. In the alkaline duodenum (about pH 8.0) the pancreatic enzyme trypsin breaks them into peptides, and in the ileum peptidase releases amino acids. The amino acids are absorbed through the villi into blood capillaries and are carried by the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

solution_steps.title: Mouth and esophagus: mechanical preparation only
solution_steps.detail: The teeth chew the fish (mastication) and the tongue rolls it into a bolus, which is pushed into the pharynx and moves down the esophagus by peristalsis. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which acts on starch and not on protein, so no chemical digestion of protein occurs here.

solution_steps.title: Stomach: acid activation of pepsin
solution_steps.detail: Food enters the stomach through the cardiac sphincter. The gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 (about 1.5 to 2.0), mucus and pepsinogen. The acid kills bacteria and activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which hydrolyses the fish proteins into polypeptides, while mucus protects the stomach wall from being corroded or digested.

solution_steps.title: Duodenum: alkaline conditions and trypsin
solution_steps.detail: The partially digested food passes into the duodenum, where bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) neutralizes the acidic chyme and creates an alkaline environment of about pH 8.0. Pancreatic juice adds trypsin, which continues the hydrolysis of proteins into shorter peptides.

solution_steps.title: Ileum: peptidase and absorption through villi
solution_steps.detail: Intestinal juice in the ileum contains peptidase, which hydrolyses the peptides into amino acids. These amino acids are absorbed through the single layer of epithelial cells covering the villi into the network of blood capillaries inside each villus; the central lacteal of the villus absorbs fats instead, not amino acids.

solution_steps.title: Hepatic portal vein: delivery to the liver
solution_steps.detail: The capillaries of the villi join to form the hepatic portal vein, which carries the amino acids directly to the liver. The liver acts as a central checkpoint that sorts amino acids, regulates glucose levels and detoxifies harmful chemicals before the blood is distributed to the rest of the body.

similar_questions.question: Describe how the starch in a plate of injera is digested and absorbed from the mouth until the glucose reaches the liver, naming each enzyme involved and stating the pH conditions under which it works.
similar_questions.answer: In the mouth, salivary amylase (ptyalin) at neutral pH (about 7.0) digests starch into maltose. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 denatures salivary amylase so starch digestion stops. In the alkaline duodenum (about pH 8.0) pancreatic amylase digests starch into maltose, and in the ileum maltase digests maltose into glucose, which is absorbed through the villi into blood capillaries of the hepatic portal vein and carried to the liver.

solution_steps.title: Mouth: salivary amylase at neutral pH
solution_steps.detail: Chewing with the teeth increases the surface area of the injera, and saliva supplies salivary amylase (ptyalin), which hydrolyses starch into maltose at a neutral pH of about 7.0. The tongue forms a bolus that is swallowed and moved down the esophagus by peristalsis.

solution_steps.title: Stomach: the enzyme is denatured
solution_steps.detail: In the stomach the bolus mixes with gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 to 2.0. This extreme acidity denatures salivary amylase, so starch digestion stops completely, and gastric juice contains no enzyme that acts on starch.

solution_steps.title: Duodenum: pancreatic amylase in alkaline conditions
solution_steps.detail: Bile from the liver neutralizes the acidic chyme and makes the duodenum alkaline, about pH 8.0. Pancreatic juice supplies pancreatic amylase, which resumes the hydrolysis of starch into maltose at this optimum alkaline pH.

solution_steps.title: Ileum: maltase releases glucose
solution_steps.detail: Intestinal juice in the ileum contains maltase, which hydrolyses maltose into glucose. The glucose is absorbed through the epithelium of the villi into the blood capillaries inside them.

solution_steps.title: Transport to the liver
solution_steps.detail: The capillaries of the villi drain into the hepatic portal vein, which carries the absorbed glucose directly to the liver, where the glucose level of the blood is regulated before the blood passes to the rest of the body.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the macromolecule from fish protein to injera starch, so the enzyme sequence changes completely (salivary amylase, pancreatic amylase, maltase instead of pepsin, trypsin, peptidase) and the answer must add the important fact that stomach acid denatures amylase and stops starch digestion.

similar_questions.question: Explain how the lipids in a spoonful of butter are digested and absorbed, and name the vessel inside the villus that carries their digestion products away.
similar_questions.answer: No chemical digestion of the butter occurs in the mouth or stomach, only mechanical churning. In the duodenum, bile salts emulsify the large fat droplets into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area, and the alkaline bile also provides the optimum pH for pancreatic lipase, which hydrolyses the fats into fatty acids and glycerol. These products are absorbed into the central lacteal of the villus and are carried away in the lymphatic system.

solution_steps.title: Mouth and stomach: mechanical treatment only
solution_steps.detail: Saliva contains salivary amylase, which acts on starch, and gastric juice contains pepsin, which acts on proteins, so neither secretion can chemically digest the butter. The fat is only broken into smaller pieces mechanically by chewing and by churning in the stomach.

solution_steps.title: Duodenum: emulsification by bile
solution_steps.detail: Bile from the liver, stored in the gall bladder, contains no enzymes but contains bile salts. These perform emulsification, physically breaking the large fat droplets into millions of tiny droplets, which greatly increases the surface area available to the enzyme.

solution_steps.title: Optimum pH for lipase
solution_steps.detail: Bile is alkaline, so it neutralizes the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach and creates the alkaline conditions of about pH 8.0 in which pancreatic lipase works best.

solution_steps.title: Chemical digestion by pancreatic lipase
solution_steps.detail: Pancreatic juice supplies lipase, which hydrolyses the emulsified fat into fatty acids and glycerol. This is why bile is essential even though it contains no enzymes: without emulsification the lipase would have far too little surface area on which to act.

solution_steps.title: Absorption into the lacteal
solution_steps.detail: The fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the central lymphatic capillary of the villus called the lacteal, which carries them into the lymphatic system. This differs from the water-soluble products glucose and amino acids, which enter the blood capillaries of the villus and then the hepatic portal vein.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the macromolecule from fish protein to butter lipids, so the answer must show that no chemical lipid digestion occurs before the duodenum, explain emulsification by enzyme-free bile, and identify the lacteal and lymphatic system instead of the blood capillaries and hepatic portal vein.

questions.question: A Grade 10 student in Asmara observes a prepared slide of body tissue and sees very narrow vessels whose walls are only one cell thick. Which structural feature of these vessels allows them to carry out the exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes between the blood and the tissue fluid?
options: A. They are made of a single layer of simple endothelium, one cell thick
B. They are made of three thick, muscular and elastic layers that resist high pressure
C. They contain one-way valves along their whole length to prevent backflow
D. They have a wide lumen that carries blood away from the heart at high speed
questions.answer: A. A single layer of simple endothelium, one cell thick

solution_steps.title: Identify the vessel described
solution_steps.detail: The vessels described are microscopic and their walls are one cell thick, which is the defining structure of capillaries: microscopic vessels made of a single layer of simple endothelium.

solution_steps.title: Recall the function of capillaries
solution_steps.detail: Capillaries are the only vessels whose thin, semi-permeable walls allow nutrients, respiratory gases and wastes to diffuse between the blood and the surrounding tissue fluid.

solution_steps.title: Test each distractor
solution_steps.detail: Three thick muscular elastic layers describes arteries, not capillaries. One-way valves along the length describe veins, not capillaries. A wide lumen carrying blood away from the heart at high speed again describes an artery, and capillaries do not carry blood away from the heart.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only option A correctly states the one-cell-thick simple endothelium, which provides the short diffusion path required for exchange between blood and tissues.

similar_questions.question: Blood leaving the left ventricle is forced into the aorta at high pressure. Which structural feature of arteries is an adaptation to this high pressure?
similar_questions.answer: A. Walls made of thick, muscular and highly elastic tissue in three layers

solution_steps.title: Recall the function of arteries
solution_steps.detail: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so their walls must be able to stretch and recoil without bursting.

solution_steps.title: Match structure to function
solution_steps.detail: Arteries have thick, muscular and highly elastic walls composed of three layers, an adaptation that withstands and smooths the high-pressure surge of each ventricular contraction.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate wrong options
solution_steps.detail: A single layer of simple endothelium describes capillaries; valves at intervals describe veins; a narrow lumen that slows blood before it reaches the tissues contradicts the need for rapid one-way delivery.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The correct choice is A, the three-layered thick, elastic muscular wall.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed from capillaries and their exchange function to arteries and their high-pressure adaptation; the correct option now tests the thick three-layered elastic wall instead of the one-cell-thick wall, and the distractors are re-assigned so that the capillary and vein features become the wrong options.

similar_questions.question: Deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery on its way to the lungs. Which statement best explains why the pulmonary artery is an exception to the usual rule about arteries?
similar_questions.answer: A. It carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart

solution_steps.title: State the general rule
solution_steps.detail: Arteries always carry blood away from the heart and veins always carry blood back towards the heart.

solution_steps.title: Apply the rule to the pulmonary artery
solution_steps.detail: The pulmonary artery arises from the right ventricle and carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, so it follows the direction rule but breaks the common assumption that arterial blood is oxygenated.

solution_steps.title: Check the returning vessel
solution_steps.detail: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, which are veins carrying oxygenated blood.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Option A is correct: the vessel carries blood away from the heart, but that blood is deoxygenated.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the tested vessel from a capillary to the pulmonary artery and the tested idea from wall thickness to the direction and gas status of blood; the options now contrast the four possible direction-gas combinations instead of structural features.

questions.question:
A student in Keren cuts his hand while chopping firewood. The wound bleeds and then stops after a short time. Complete the statements below about the third stage of hemostasis (coagulation) by writing the missing terms.
Injured tissues and platelets release (i) ______. In the presence of calcium ions ($$Ca^{2+}$$) and Vitamin K, (ii) ______ is converted into the active enzyme thrombin. Thrombin then converts the soluble plasma protein (iii) ______ into insoluble (iv) ______ threads that trap blood cells to form a stable clot.
questions.answer: (i) thromboplastin, (ii) prothrombin, (iii) fibrinogen, (iv) fibrin

solution_steps.title: Name the substance released by injured tissue
solution_steps.detail: During coagulation, injured tissues and platelets release thromboplastin, which starts the clotting cascade, so (i) is thromboplastin.

solution_steps.title: Identify the protein activated to thrombin
solution_steps.detail: In the presence of calcium ions and Vitamin K, thromboplastin brings about the conversion of the inactive plasma protein prothrombin into active thrombin, so (ii) is prothrombin.

solution_steps.title: Identify the substrate of thrombin
solution_steps.detail: Thrombin acts as an enzyme on the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen, converting it into insoluble fibrin, so (iii) is fibrinogen and (iv) is fibrin.

solution_steps.title: Interpret the final clot
solution_steps.detail: The insoluble fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, producing the stable clot that seals the break in the vessel.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the statements below about the first two stages of hemostasis.
In the first stage, called vascular spasm, the smooth muscle in the wall of the damaged vessel ______ in order to reduce blood loss. In the second stage, called the platelet plug, platelets adhere to the exposed ______, change shape and stick to each other to seal the break.
similar_questions.answer: contracts; collagen

solution_steps.title: Recall stage 1
solution_steps.detail: Vascular spasm is the contraction of the smooth muscle in the vessel wall, which narrows the vessel and reduces blood loss, so the first blank is 'contracts'.

solution_steps.title: Recall stage 2
solution_steps.detail: In the platelet plug stage, platelets adhere to exposed collagen fibres of the damaged vessel, change shape and stick together, so the second blank is 'collagen'.

solution_steps.title: Check the sequence
solution_steps.detail: The order is correct: vascular spasm first, platelet plug second, and coagulation third.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the blanks from the third stage (coagulation, with thromboplastin, prothrombin, fibrinogen and fibrin) to the first two stages (vascular spasm and platelet plug), so the required terms are now 'contracts' and 'collagen' instead of the clotting proteins.

similar_questions.question:
A patient in Asmara has a blocked bile duct and bruises and bleeds very easily. Complete the explanation below.
Vitamin K is needed by the ______ to produce the clotting factor ______. Vitamin K is ______-soluble, so it can only be absorbed in the small intestine when bile salts are present; when the bile duct is blocked, the production of this clotting factor falls and severe bleeding can occur.
similar_questions.answer: liver; prothrombin; fat

solution_steps.title: Locate the site of clotting-factor production
solution_steps.detail: Vitamin K is a necessary cofactor for the liver to produce the clotting factor prothrombin, so the first blank is 'liver' and the second is 'prothrombin'.

solution_steps.title: Recall why bile is needed
solution_steps.detail: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and requires bile salts for absorption in the small intestine, so the third blank is 'fat'.

solution_steps.title: Link the blockage to the symptom
solution_steps.detail: A blocked bile duct prevents Vitamin K absorption, the liver therefore makes too little prothrombin, and the clotting cascade fails, producing the easy bruising and bleeding described.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed from filling in the clotting cascade itself to filling in the Vitamin K, liver and bile explanation behind a bleeding disorder; the missing terms are now 'liver', 'prothrombin' and 'fat' rather than thromboplastin and fibrin.

questions.question:
A blood bank in Asmara collects a $$200\text{ mL}$$ sample of whole blood from a donor. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume, and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the volume of plasma in the sample.
(b) Calculate the volume of water contained in that plasma.
(c) Calculate the volume of the sample occupied by the cellular components (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets).
questions.answer: (a) $$110\text{ mL}$$ of plasma; (b) $$101.2\text{ mL}$$ of water; (c) $$90\text{ mL}$$ of cellular components

solution_steps.title: List the given data
solution_steps.detail: Total blood volume = $$200\text{ mL}$$; plasma = $$55\%$$ of blood volume; water = $$92\%$$ of plasma volume; cellular components = $$45\%$$ of blood volume (since $$100\% - 55\% = 45\%$$).

solution_steps.title: Calculate the plasma volume
solution_steps.detail: Plasma volume = $$55\%$$ of $$200\text{ mL}$$ = $$0.55 \times 200 = 110\text{ mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the water in the plasma
solution_steps.detail: Water volume = $$92\%$$ of the plasma volume = $$0.92 \times 110 = 101.2\text{ mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the cellular volume
solution_steps.detail: Cellular volume = $$45\%$$ of $$200\text{ mL}$$ = $$0.45 \times 200 = 90\text{ mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check the result
solution_steps.detail: The two parts must rebuild the whole sample: $$110\text{ mL} + 90\text{ mL} = 200\text{ mL}$$, which agrees with the given sample volume.

similar_questions.question:
A clinic in Massawa sends a $$250\text{ mL}$$ sample of whole blood to the laboratory. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the plasma volume.
(b) Calculate the volume of water in the plasma.
(c) Calculate the volume of the cellular components.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$137.5\text{ mL}$$ of plasma; (b) $$126.5\text{ mL}$$ of water; (c) $$112.5\text{ mL}$$ of cellular components

solution_steps.title: Write the percentages
solution_steps.detail: Plasma = $$55\%$$, so cellular components = $$45\%$$, and water = $$92\%$$ of the plasma volume.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the plasma volume
solution_steps.detail: $$0.55 \times 250 = 137.5\text{ mL}$$ of plasma.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the water volume
solution_steps.detail: $$0.92 \times 137.5 = 126.5\text{ mL}$$ of water.

similar_questions.variant_note: Only the sample volume and the setting changed ($$200\text{ mL}$$ in Asmara to $$250\text{ mL}$$ in Massawa), so all three answers are re-scaled to $$137.5\text{ mL}$$, $$126.5\text{ mL}$$ and $$112.5\text{ mL}$$.

similar_questions.question: During a donation session in Nakfa, $$450\text{ mL}$$ of whole blood is collected. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the volume of water held in the plasma of this donation, and express that water volume as a percentage of the whole blood collected.
similar_questions.answer: $$227.7\text{ mL}$$ of water, which is $$50.6\%$$ of the whole blood volume

solution_steps.title: Calculate the plasma volume
solution_steps.detail: $$0.55 \times 450 = 247.5\text{ mL}$$ of plasma.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the water volume
solution_steps.detail: $$0.92 \times 247.5 = 227.7\text{ mL}$$ of water in the plasma.

solution_steps.title: Express the water as a percentage of whole blood
solution_steps.detail: $$\dfrac{227.7}{450} \times 100\% = 50.6\%$$, which is the same as $$0.55 \times 0.92 = 0.506$$ of the whole blood.

solution_steps.title: State the result clearly
solution_steps.detail: Just over half of the donated whole blood, $$227.7\text{ mL}$$, is water held in the plasma.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed both the volume (to $$450\text{ mL}$$) and the demand of the task: instead of three separate volumes, the student must combine the two percentages and report the plasma water as a percentage of whole blood ($$50.6\%$$).

questions.question: During a blood-typing practical at a secondary school in Asmara, the red blood cells of a student are found to carry antigen B and antigen D (Rh), while the plasma contains anti-A antibodies. What is the student's blood group?
options: A. A Rh-negative
B. A Rh-positive
C. B Rh-positive
D. AB Rh-positive
questions.answer: C. B Rh-positive

solution_steps.title: Use the antigens to fix the ABO group
solution_steps.detail: The red cells carry antigen B and the plasma contains anti-A antibodies, which is exactly the pattern of blood group B (B antigen with anti-A antibody).

solution_steps.title: Use antigen D to fix the Rh group
solution_steps.detail: The red cells also carry antigen D, and the presence of antigen D means the blood is Rh-positive; blood lacking antigen D is Rh-negative.

solution_steps.title: Test the other options
solution_steps.detail: Options A and B require antigen A on the red cells, which is absent. Option D requires both A and B antigens and no antibodies in the plasma, but this student has anti-A antibodies.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The only group matching antigen B, antigen D and anti-A antibodies is B Rh-positive.

similar_questions.question: A patient in Keren is typed before surgery. The red blood cells carry no A antigen and no B antigen and lack antigen D, while the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies. What is the patient's blood group?
similar_questions.answer: C. O Rh-negative

solution_steps.title: Interpret the absence of A and B antigens
solution_steps.detail: Red cells with neither A nor B antigen belong to group O, and such plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, exactly as described.

solution_steps.title: Interpret the absence of antigen D
solution_steps.detail: Red cells that lack antigen D are Rh-negative, so the group is O Rh-negative.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the other options
solution_steps.detail: A Rh-negative carries A antigen; AB Rh-negative carries both A and B antigens and has no antibodies; O Rh-positive would carry antigen D, which is absent here.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The patient is group O Rh-negative, the universal donor group.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the antigen-antibody pattern from B Rh-positive (antigen B, antigen D, anti-A) to the opposite extreme of O Rh-negative (no antigens, both antibodies, no antigen D), so the correct option changes from C to C but for a different underlying pattern, and the distractors test other groups.

similar_questions.question: An Rh-negative mother has already given birth to one Rh-positive child. During a second pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, the fetus may develop erythroblastosis fetalis because:
similar_questions.answer: A. The mother's anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the red blood cells of the fetus

solution_steps.title: Explain how the mother becomes sensitised
solution_steps.detail: During the first pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, fetal red blood cells enter the Rh-negative mother's blood and stimulate her immune system to produce anti-Rh antibodies.

solution_steps.title: Explain the effect in the second pregnancy
solution_steps.detail: In a later pregnancy with another Rh-positive fetus, these already formed anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and attack the fetal red blood cells.

solution_steps.title: Name the outcome
solution_steps.detail: The destruction of fetal red blood cells produces the condition called erythroblastosis fetalis.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Option B reverses the direction of the antibodies, option C describes clumping of maternal cells rather than destruction of fetal cells, and option D wrongly replaces anti-Rh with anti-A antibodies.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the task from identifying a blood group from antigens and antibodies to explaining the immunological mechanism of erythroblastosis fetalis, so the correct option is now a causal statement about anti-Rh antibodies rather than a blood-group label.

questions.question:
A laboratory technician in Asmara measures the volume of water contained in the plasma of a patient's blood sample and records $$2.53\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume, and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the volume of plasma in the sample.
(b) Calculate the patient's total blood volume.
(c) Calculate the volume occupied by the cellular components.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.75\text{ L}$$ of plasma; (b) $$5.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood; (c) $$2.25\text{ L}$$ of cellular components

solution_steps.title: Set up the relationships
solution_steps.detail: Water is $$92\%$$ of plasma, so water $$= 0.92 \times$$ plasma. Plasma is $$55\%$$ of blood, so plasma $$= 0.55 \times$$ blood. The cellular components are the remaining $$45\%$$ of blood.

solution_steps.title: Work backwards to the plasma volume
solution_steps.detail: Since $$0.92 \times \text{plasma} = 2.53\text{ L}$$, the plasma volume is $$\dfrac{2.53}{0.92} = 2.75\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Work backwards to the total blood volume
solution_steps.detail: Since $$0.55 \times \text{blood} = 2.75\text{ L}$$, the total blood volume is $$\dfrac{2.75}{0.55} = 5.0\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the cellular volume
solution_steps.detail: Cellular volume = total blood minus plasma = $$5.0\text{ L} - 2.75\text{ L} = 2.25\text{ L}$$, which also equals $$0.45 \times 5.0 = 2.25\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check the answer
solution_steps.detail: Plasma plus cells is $$2.75 + 2.25 = 5.0\text{ L}$$ of blood, and $$92\%$$ of the plasma is $$0.92 \times 2.75 = 2.53\text{ L}$$ of water, matching the measured value.

similar_questions.question: The plasma water in a blood sample taken at a health centre in Asmara is measured as $$2.024\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the plasma volume, the total blood volume and the volume of the cellular components.
similar_questions.answer: $$2.2\text{ L}$$ of plasma, $$4.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood and $$1.8\text{ L}$$ of cellular components

solution_steps.title: Find the plasma volume
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{plasma} = \dfrac{2.024}{0.92} = 2.2\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the total blood volume
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{blood} = \dfrac{2.2}{0.55} = 4.0\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the cellular volume
solution_steps.detail: Cellular volume = $$4.0 - 2.2 = 1.8\text{ L}$$, which agrees with $$0.45 \times 4.0 = 1.8\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check
solution_steps.detail: $$2.2 + 1.8 = 4.0\text{ L}$$, and $$0.92 \times 2.2 = 2.024\text{ L}$$ of water, as given.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the measured plasma-water volume from $$2.53\text{ L}$$ to $$2.024\text{ L}$$, which produces the round total blood volume of $$4.0\text{ L}$$ instead of $$5.0\text{ L}$$; the reasoning chain and the three requested quantities stay the same.

similar_questions.question: The cellular components (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets) of a patient's blood occupy $$3.6\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the patient's total blood volume, the plasma volume and the volume of water in that plasma.
similar_questions.answer: $$8.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood, $$4.4\text{ L}$$ of plasma and $$4.048\text{ L}$$ (about $$4.05\text{ L}$$) of water

solution_steps.title: Use the cellular percentage to find total blood
solution_steps.detail: Cellular components are $$45\%$$ of blood, so $$\text{blood} = \dfrac{3.6}{0.45} = 8.0\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the plasma volume
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{plasma} = 0.55 \times 8.0 = 4.4\text{ L}$$, which also follows from $$8.0 - 3.6 = 4.4\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the water in the plasma
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{water} = 0.92 \times 4.4 = 4.048\text{ L}$$, approximately $$4.05\text{ L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check
solution_steps.detail: $$4.4 + 3.6 = 8.0\text{ L}$$, so the plasma and cellular volumes rebuild the total blood volume correctly.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the starting measurement from the plasma water to the cellular component volume ($$3.6\text{ L}$$), so the student must first divide by $$45\%$$ and then work forwards through plasma to water, reversing the direction of the main question.

questions.question:
Complete the following paragraph using the terms that fit the chapter (write the two missing terms in order):

The walls of lymphatic capillaries are made of thin, ____________ endothelial cells that work like one-way swing doors [96, 97]. Because the lymphatic system has no pump of its own [95, 101, 103, 104], lymph is pushed slowly toward the heart by the squeezing action of nearby skeletal muscles, by breathing movements, and by ____________ along all lymphatic vessels that prevent backflow [88, 96, 103, 104].
questions.answer: overlapping ; valves

solution_steps.title: Recall the wall structure of lymphatic capillaries
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that lymphatic vessel walls are made of thin, overlapping endothelial cells that act like one-way swing doors: when tissue-fluid pressure outside is high they swing open, and when fluid tries to leave they swing shut, locking the fluid in as lymph [96, 97].

solution_steps.title: Recall how lymph is propelled without a pump
solution_steps.detail: The lymphatic system has no pump [95, 101, 103, 104]. Lymph moves through the massaging action of skeletal muscles, breathing movements, and one-way valves present along all lymphatic vessels, which close if fluid tries to flow backward [88, 96, 103, 104].

solution_steps.title: Fill the blanks in order
solution_steps.detail: First blank: the cells are described as overlapping (not ciliated, not muscular). Second blank: the anti-backflow structures mentioned in the chapter are valves. The paragraph therefore reads: overlapping endothelial cells ... and valves along all lymphatic vessels.

solution_steps.title: Check the completed sentence
solution_steps.detail: The completed paragraph now correctly links structure (overlapping endothelial cells producing one-way entry) with mechanism of flow (skeletal muscle squeeze, breathing, and one-way valves), matching the chapter exactly [88, 96, 103, 104].

similar_questions.question:
Complete the following paragraph (write the two missing terms in order):

Lymphatic capillaries are microscopic, ____________ capillaries that begin as dead-ends inside the tissues rather than forming a loop [87, 95, 97]. When the pressure of tissue fluid around them rises, fluid pushes the overlapping endothelial cells inward and enters; once inside it becomes ____________, a colourless watery fluid that lacks red blood cells and platelets [87, 95, 103].
similar_questions.answer: closed-ended ; lymph

solution_steps.title: Identify the capillary shape
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes lymphatic capillaries as microscopic, closed-ended capillaries that merge into larger vessels and start as dead-ends in the tissues, unlike the open loops of the circulatory system [87, 95, 97].

solution_steps.title: Identify the fluid formed inside
solution_steps.detail: Once interstitial (tissue) fluid has entered the lymphatic capillary and is locked in by the overlapping cells, it is called lymph: a colourless, watery fluid containing water, leaked proteins, cell products, digested lipids and white blood cells [87, 95].

solution_steps.title: Fill the blanks in order
solution_steps.detail: First blank: closed-ended. Second blank: lymph. The paragraph then reads correctly: lymphatic capillaries are closed-ended ... the fluid becomes lymph.

solution_steps.title: Verify against the chapter
solution_steps.detail: Both terms appear in the chapter's description of lymph and lymphatic vessels, and the completed sentence keeps the chapter's direction of flow (tissue fluid to lymph) intact [87, 95, 96, 97].

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question tested capillary wall structure and anti-backflow valves; this variant tests the closed-ended (dead-end) shape of lymphatic capillaries and the name of the fluid formed, with a different paragraph and different blanks.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the following paragraph (write the two missing terms in order):

Lymphatic capillaries that lie in the lining of the small intestine are called ____________, and the milky-white lymph they carry after absorbing digested fats is known as ____________ [86, 94, 97]. By contrast, the spleen is described as the largest lymphatic organ and acts mainly as a filter of ____________ [100, 102].
similar_questions.answer: lacteals ; chyle (and the spleen filters blood)

solution_steps.title: Identify the intestinal lymphatic capillaries
solution_steps.detail: The chapter names the specialized lymphatic capillaries in the lining of the small intestine lacteals; they absorb digested fats, which are too large to enter blood capillaries directly [86, 94, 97].

solution_steps.title: Identify the milky fluid
solution_steps.detail: Because of its high content of emulsified fat droplets, the lymph in lacteals looks milky-white and is called chyle [86, 94, 97].

solution_steps.title: Complete the third blank
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's pro-tip states that lymph nodes filter lymph while the spleen filters blood, so the spleen's role is blood filtration (removing old red blood cells, recycling iron, producing antibodies and storing blood) [100, 102].

solution_steps.title: Read the completed paragraph
solution_steps.detail: The paragraph now reads: intestinal lymphatic capillaries are lacteals, their fatty lymph is chyle, and the spleen filters blood - all directly supported by the chapter [86, 94, 97, 100, 102].

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant moves from vessel structure and flow mechanism to the chapter's named intestinal capillaries (lacteals), their fatty lymph (chyle), and the spleen's blood-filtering role, with three blanks instead of two.

questions.question: Large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen sometimes leak from blood capillaries into the tissue spaces. Which statement best explains why these large proteins can enter lymphatic capillaries but cannot re-enter blood capillaries?
options: A. Blood capillaries actively push large proteins back into the blood, but the proteins are too large to be pushed into lymphatic capillaries.
B. Blood capillaries have very tiny microscopic pores that block large proteins, while lymphatic capillaries have much larger openings formed by thin, overlapping endothelial cells.
C. Large proteins are digested into amino acids in the tissue fluid, absorbed by lymphatic capillaries, and rebuilt as proteins in the blood.
