D. Large proteins enter lymphatic capillaries only because lymph flows in one direction toward the heart, which pulls them away from blood capillaries.
questions.answer: B. Blood capillaries have very tiny microscopic pores that block large proteins, while lymphatic capillaries have much larger openings formed by thin, overlapping endothelial cells.

solution_steps.title: State what limits exchange at blood capillaries
solution_steps.detail: Blood capillaries have thin walls with very tiny microscopic pores. These pores allow water and small solutes to pass in two-way exchange but are too small for large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen, so once leaked these proteins cannot diffuse back into the blood [85, 93, 66, 74, 75].

solution_steps.title: State the structural feature of lymphatic capillaries
solution_steps.detail: Lymphatic capillaries are built from thin, overlapping endothelial cells that form large, flap-like openings. When tissue-fluid pressure rises these flaps swing inward and open, so even large proteins can enter the lymphatic capillary [95, 96, 97].

solution_steps.title: Link the two facts to the question
solution_steps.detail: The deciding factor is the size of the openings: tiny pores in blood capillaries exclude large proteins, whereas the large overlapping-cell openings of lymphatic capillaries admit them. This is why the lymphatic system is essential for returning leaked proteins to the blood and preventing loss of osmotic pressure and severe edema [85, 93, 95].

solution_steps.title: Test every option
solution_steps.detail: A is false: the chapter gives no active transport of proteins back into blood, and it states the opposite about lymphatic entry. C is false: lymph contains dissolved proteins that leaked from blood capillaries; there is no digestion-and-rebuilding step in the chapter. D is false: one-way lymph flow explains direction of movement, not why a large molecule is able to pass through a wall. Only B states the true structural reason.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Option B is the only statement supported by the chapter, because it correctly contrasts the tiny pores of blood capillaries with the large openings of lymphatic capillaries [85, 93, 95, 96].

similar_questions.question: A patient suffering from severe protein deficiency produces too few plasma proteins, so tissue fluid is not drawn back into the blood capillaries efficiently. Which statement best explains why the resulting accumulation of tissue fluid is called edema?
similar_questions.answer: D. Edema is the swelling caused by excess fluid accumulating in the interstitial spaces, and the lymphatic system normally drains this fluid back to the bloodstream.

solution_steps.title: Define the starting problem
solution_steps.detail: Some plasma proteins leak out of blood capillaries and are needed to maintain osmotic pressure; when proteins are lost or scarce, water is not reabsorbed well and collects in the interstitial spaces [75, 85, 93, 95].

solution_steps.title: Recall what edema is
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines edema (swelling) as the flooding that results when leaked tissue fluid is allowed to accumulate in the interstitial spaces instead of being drained away [95].

solution_steps.title: Recall the drainage route
solution_steps.detail: The lymphatic capillaries and vessels collect the excess fluid and large leaked proteins and return them to the venous bloodstream near the heart [85, 93, 95]. If this drainage fails or is overwhelmed, fluid stays in the tissues and swelling appears [95].

solution_steps.title: Test every option
solution_steps.detail: A is false: edema is not a shortage of red blood cells. B is false: edema is not caused by rapid movement of lymph into arteries; lymph enters veins near the heart. C is false: swelling is not the trapping of pathogens inside the blood only. D correctly defines edema as interstitial fluid accumulation normally drained by the lymphatic system.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Option D is the single defensible answer because it matches the chapter's cause (untrained tissue fluid) and the lymphatic system's drainage role [85, 93, 95].

similar_questions.variant_note: The main MC asked about the structural reason large plasma proteins enter lymphatic capillaries; this variant keeps the same protein-leak context but asks for the cause and definition of the resulting edema, with four different options and a different correct letter.

similar_questions.question: Blood is a red, viscous tissue that contains red blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins, whereas lymph is a clear or milky fluid. Which statement best describes the cellular content of healthy lymph?
similar_questions.answer: A. Lymph contains white blood cells (phagocytes and lymphocytes) but completely lacks red blood cells and platelets.

solution_steps.title: Recall the composition of lymph
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes lymph as a colourless, watery fluid containing water, dissolved leaked proteins, cell products such as hormones and enzymes, digested lipids, and white blood cells - especially lymphocytes and phagocytes [87, 95].

solution_steps.title: Recall the composition of blood
solution_steps.detail: Blood is a red, viscous tissue containing red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen [66, 74, 75].

solution_steps.title: Compare the two fluids
solution_steps.detail: Subtracting the blood list from the lymph list leaves white blood cells present in lymph but red blood cells and platelets completely absent. This is one of the chapter's listed differences in fluid composition [87, 95, 103].

solution_steps.title: Test every option
solution_steps.detail: B is false: red blood cells and platelets are absent, not abundant. C is false: platelets are absent from lymph. D is false: large plasma proteins are not the cellular component of lymph, and lymph does contain white blood cells.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Option A is the only statement consistent with the chapter: lymph carries white blood cells only, with no red blood cells and no platelets [87, 95, 103].

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant keeps an MC check on fluid composition but shifts the focus from protein entry through capillary walls to which blood components are completely absent from healthy lymph, with a different set of distractors.

questions.question: A patient recovering from a leg injury lies still for 3 hours. Because there is no walking movement to squeeze the lymphatic vessels, excess tissue fluid collects in the leg at a steady rate of $$180\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. A nurse then performs a 20-minute manual lymphatic drainage massage that removes $$75\%$$ of the fluid collected. Calculate the volume of lymph, in millilitres, still left in the tissue spaces after the massage.
questions.answer: $$135\ \text{mL}$$ of lymph remains in the tissue spaces.

solution_steps.title: Identify the principle
solution_steps.detail: When skeletal muscles do not contract, the massaging action that normally pushes lymph along is lost, so tissue fluid collects in the interstitial spaces [88, 96, 104]. The volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid collected in 3 hours
solution_steps.detail: Collected fluid $$= 180\ \text{mL/hour} \times 3\ \text{hours} = 540\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the volume removed by the massage
solution_steps.detail: Removed fluid $$= 75\%$$ of $$540\ \text{mL} = 0.75 \times 540 = 405\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid remaining
solution_steps.detail: Remaining fluid $$= 540\ \text{mL} - 405\ \text{mL} = 135\ \text{mL}$$, which is the same as $$25\%$$ of $$540\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the result
solution_steps.detail: After the massage, $$135\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid is still left in the leg tissues, so the drainage has only partly corrected the accumulation. This remaining fluid is what would be seen as pitting swelling (edema) until normal muscle movement resumes [88, 95, 96, 104].

similar_questions.question: During a long bus journey from Asmara to Massawa, a passenger sits without moving for 4 hours and interstitial fluid accumulates in the ankles at a steady rate of $$160\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. After the journey, 85% of this accumulated fluid is drained away as the passenger walks and the calf muscles squeeze the lymphatic vessels. Calculate the volume of fluid, in millilitres, remaining in the ankle tissues.
similar_questions.answer: $$96\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid remains in the ankle tissues.

solution_steps.title: Identify the principle
solution_steps.detail: Lymph has no pump, so prolonged sitting without skeletal muscle contraction allows tissue fluid to collect in the lower limbs, and only muscle movement restores drainage [88, 96, 104]. Volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid accumulated
solution_steps.detail: Accumulated fluid $$= 160\ \text{mL/hour} \times 4\ \text{hours} = 640\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid drained
solution_steps.detail: Drained fluid $$= 85\%$$ of $$640\ \text{mL} = 0.85 \times 640 = 544\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid remaining
solution_steps.detail: Remaining fluid $$= 640\ \text{mL} - 544\ \text{mL} = 96\ \text{mL}$$, which equals $$15\%$$ of $$640\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the result
solution_steps.detail: About $$96\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid is still trapped in the ankle tissues after walking, which is why ankles can stay puffy for a while after a long sedentary journey [71, 95, 96].

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question used a 3-hour collection at 180 mL/hour with 75% removed by a massage; this variant uses a 4-hour bus journey at 160 mL/hour with 85% drained by walking, an Eritrean travel setting, and a different remaining volume.

similar_questions.question: A nurse uses a compression bandage on a patient whose foot is swollen after an infection. Over 2.5 hours, tissue fluid collects in the foot at a steady rate of $$200\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. The bandage and gentle elevation then drain away $$72\%$$ of the collected fluid. Calculate the volume of lymph, in millilitres, still left in the tissue spaces.
similar_questions.answer: $$140\ \text{mL}$$ of lymph remains in the tissue spaces.

solution_steps.title: Identify the principle
solution_steps.detail: With impaired lymph movement, interstitial fluid accumulates and can be partly removed by external compression together with the muscle and breathing movements that normally drive lymph toward the heart [88, 96, 104]. Volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid collected
solution_steps.detail: Collected fluid $$= 200\ \text{mL/hour} \times 2.5\ \text{hours} = 500\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid drained
solution_steps.detail: Drained fluid $$= 72\%$$ of $$500\ \text{mL} = 0.72 \times 500 = 360\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the fluid remaining
solution_steps.detail: Remaining fluid $$= 500\ \text{mL} - 360\ \text{mL} = 140\ \text{mL}$$, which equals $$28\%$$ of $$500\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the result
solution_steps.detail: The bandage leaves $$140\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid in the foot tissues, so drainage is incomplete and the swelling only partly subsides [95, 96, 104].

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant changes the collection rate to 200 mL/hour, the time to 2.5 hours and the drained fraction to 72%, and replaces the manual massage with compression bandaging and elevation, giving a different remaining volume.

questions.question:
The heart of a healthy adult at rest pumps $$7500\ \text{mL}$$ of blood every minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$2.4\%$$ leaks out of the blood capillaries into the interstitial spaces as tissue fluid, and $$92\%$$ of that leaked fluid is eventually collected and returned to the bloodstream by the lymphatic system [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the total volume of lymph returned to the bloodstream in one day, giving your answer in litres.
(b) The same adult's spleen destroys old, damaged red blood cells at a rate that releases $$30\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day [77, 100], and this iron is sent to the red bone marrow for recycling. If each newly manufactured red blood cell needs $$2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77], calculate the number of new red blood cells that can be produced in 30 days from the recycled iron.
questions.answer: (a) $$238.464\ \text{L} \approx 238\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day (accept $$238.5\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 30 days.

solution_steps.title: Find the fluid leaking per minute
solution_steps.detail: Leaked tissue fluid $$= 2.4\%$$ of $$7500\ \text{mL/min} = 0.024 \times 7500 = 180\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].

solution_steps.title: Find the lymph returned per minute
solution_steps.detail: Lymph returned $$= 92\%$$ of $$180\ \text{mL/min} = 0.92 \times 180 = 165.6\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].

solution_steps.title: Convert the rate to litres per day
solution_steps.detail: In one day (24 hours $$= 1440$$ minutes) the volume is $$165.6\ \text{mL/min} \times 1440\ \text{min} = 238464\ \text{mL}$$. Since $$1\ \text{L} = 1000\ \text{mL}$$, this is $$238.464\ \text{L} \approx 238\ \text{L/day}$$ (about $$238.5\ \text{L}$$).

solution_steps.title: Find the iron salvaged in 30 days
solution_steps.detail: Iron per day $$= 30\ \text{mg} = 0.030\ \text{g}$$, so in 30 days the spleen releases $$30 \times 0.030\ \text{g} = 0.90\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

solution_steps.title: Find the number of new red blood cells
solution_steps.detail: Number of cells $$= \dfrac{0.90\ \text{g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ cells. This is the iron recycled to the red bone marrow to manufacture new haemoglobin for developing red blood cells [77].

solution_steps.title: Check the answers for sense
solution_steps.detail: Part (a): roughly 238 litres of lymph per day means the lymphatic system returns a volume comparable to the whole blood plasma volume many times over each day, consistent with continuous capillary leakage [85, 93, 95]. Part (b): $$4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ cells in 30 days (about $$1.5 \times 10^{10}$$ cells per day) is a large but plausible replacement rate for a marrow continuously recycling iron from destroyed red blood cells [77, 100].

similar_questions.question:
During hard farm work in the Keren area, a man's heart pumps $$9000\ \text{mL}$$ of blood per minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$3.0\%$$ leaks into the interstitial spaces, and the lymphatic system returns $$95\%$$ of the leaked fluid to the bloodstream [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the volume of lymph returned per day, in litres.
(b) His spleen releases $$25\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day from destroyed red blood cells [77, 100]. If each new red blood cell needs $$2.5 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77], how many new red blood cells can his marrow produce in 40 days from this recycled iron?
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$369.36\ \text{L} \approx 369\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day (accept $$369.4\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 40 days.

solution_steps.title: Find the fluid leaking per minute
solution_steps.detail: Leaked tissue fluid $$= 3.0\%$$ of $$9000\ \text{mL/min} = 0.030 \times 9000 = 270\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].

solution_steps.title: Find the lymph returned per minute
solution_steps.detail: Lymph returned $$= 95\%$$ of $$270\ \text{mL/min} = 0.95 \times 270 = 256.5\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].

solution_steps.title: Convert to litres per day
solution_steps.detail: In 1440 minutes the volume is $$256.5 \times 1440 = 369360\ \text{mL} = 369.36\ \text{L} \approx 369\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day.

solution_steps.title: Find the iron salvaged in 40 days
solution_steps.detail: Iron per day $$= 25\ \text{mg} = 0.025\ \text{g}$$; in 40 days the spleen releases $$40 \times 0.025\ \text{g} = 1.0\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

solution_steps.title: Find the number of red blood cells
solution_steps.detail: Number of cells $$= \dfrac{1.0\ \text{g}}{2.5 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells, all built from recycled iron sent to the red bone marrow [77].

solution_steps.title: Check the answers for sense
solution_steps.detail: Heavier exercise increases cardiac output and capillary leakage, so both the leak (270 mL/min) and the returned lymph (about 369 L/day) are larger than in the resting adult, as expected [61, 69, 85, 93]. Part (b) gives $$4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells over 40 days, a plausible marrow replacement rate [77, 100].

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question used a resting adult with a 7500 mL/min cardiac output, 2.4% leakage, 92% return and 30 mg iron per day for 30 days at 2.0 x 10^-12 g iron per cell; this variant uses an exercising Keren farmer at 9000 mL/min, 3.0% leakage, 95% return and 25 mg iron per day for 40 days at 2.5 x 10^-12 g iron per cell.

similar_questions.question:
A Massawa fish-processor works in hot conditions and his heart pumps $$8000\ \text{mL}$$ of blood per minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$3.5\%$$ becomes tissue fluid and the lymphatic system drains $$90\%$$ of it back into the blood [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the volume of lymph returned in one hour, in litres.
(b) His spleen releases $$40\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day [77, 100], and each new red blood cell needs $$2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77]. How many new red blood cells can be made from the iron salvaged in 15 days?
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$15.12\ \text{L} \approx 15\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per hour (accept $$15.1\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 15 days.

solution_steps.title: Find the fluid leaking per minute
solution_steps.detail: Leaked tissue fluid $$= 3.5\%$$ of $$8000\ \text{mL/min} = 0.035 \times 8000 = 280\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].

solution_steps.title: Find the lymph returned per minute
solution_steps.detail: Lymph returned $$= 90\%$$ of $$280\ \text{mL/min} = 0.90 \times 280 = 252\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].

solution_steps.title: Convert to litres per hour
solution_steps.detail: In 60 minutes the volume is $$252 \times 60 = 15120\ \text{mL} = 15.12\ \text{L} \approx 15\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per hour.

solution_steps.title: Find the iron salvaged in 15 days
solution_steps.detail: Iron per day $$= 40\ \text{mg} = 0.040\ \text{g}$$; in 15 days the spleen releases $$15 \times 0.040\ \text{g} = 0.60\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

solution_steps.title: Find the number of red blood cells
solution_steps.detail: Number of cells $$= \dfrac{0.60\ \text{g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells, produced in the red bone marrow from recycled iron [77].

solution_steps.title: Check the answers for sense
solution_steps.detail: The hourly figure $$15.12\ \text{L/hour}$$ equals about $$363\ \text{L/day}$$, in the same order of magnitude as the resting case after allowing for the larger leak and slightly lower drainage fraction; $$3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells over 15 days is consistent with the daily iron release [77, 85, 93, 100].

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant changes the requested time unit to one hour (instead of one day), uses a Massawa hot-climate worker at 8000 mL/min with 3.5% leakage and 90% return, and asks for the cells produced in 15 days from 40 mg of iron per day, giving different final values.

questions.question:
The thymus gland is a triangular, bilobed gland behind the sternum [100]. It is relatively large in infants but gradually shrinks after puberty [100].

(a) Explain the biological reason why the thymus is large and active in an infant and why it shrinks after puberty [100].
(b) In a particular Eritrean child, the thymus weighs $$44\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and then involutes at a steady rate of $$0.9\ \text{g}$$ per year [100]. Calculate its mass after 10 years of involution, and then calculate the percentage decrease from its puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop, so it is large and active early in life; once the immune system is fully developed and stocked with long-lived memory T-cells (around puberty) its active role declines and it involutes, shrinking as it is replaced by fat and connective tissue [100]. (b) Mass after 10 years $$= 35\ \text{g}$$, and the percentage decrease from the puberty mass is $$\dfrac{9}{44} \times 100 \approx 20.5\%$$.

solution_steps.title: State the role of the thymus early in life
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the thymus plays an essential role early in life as the site where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune responses [100]. It is therefore most active while the immune system is being built up in infancy and childhood.

solution_steps.title: Explain the shrinking after puberty
solution_steps.detail: Once the immune system is fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells, typically around puberty, the thymus's active role decreases and it undergoes involution, gradually shrinking and being replaced by fat and connective tissue [100].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass lost over 10 years
solution_steps.detail: Mass lost $$= 0.9\ \text{g/year} \times 10\ \text{years} = 9\ \text{g}$$ [100].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass after 10 years
solution_steps.detail: Mass after involution $$= 44\ \text{g} - 9\ \text{g} = 35\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the percentage decrease
solution_steps.detail: Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{\text{mass lost}}{\text{puberty mass}} \times 100 = \dfrac{9}{44} \times 100 = 20.45\% \approx 20.5\%$$.

solution_steps.title: State the final result
solution_steps.detail: After 10 years the thymus weighs $$35\ \text{g}$$, a decrease of about $$20.5\%$$ from its $$44\ \text{g}$$ mass at puberty, matching the chapter's statement that the gland shrinks after puberty as it is replaced by fat and connective tissue [100].

similar_questions.question:
(a) Explain why a person who had their thymus removed as a young adult might still fight infections reasonably well, even though the gland has a vital early role [100].
(b) In another child the thymus weighs $$40\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and involutes at a steady rate of $$0.8\ \text{g}$$ per year [100]. Calculate its mass after 20 years and the percentage decrease from its puberty mass.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The thymus's essential role is early in life, where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop; by adulthood the immune system is already fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells, so much of its protective capacity persists even after the gland involutes or is removed [100]. (b) Mass after 20 years $$= 24\ \text{g}$$; percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Recall the thymus's early role
solution_steps.detail: The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop, which is why it is essential early in life and relatively large in infants [100].

solution_steps.title: Explain why protection persists later
solution_steps.detail: Once the immune system is fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells (around puberty), the thymus's active role decreases and it undergoes involution [100]. The mature, long-lived lymphocytes already produced continue to provide immune protection, so infections can still be fought reasonably well after the gland is lost.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass lost over 20 years
solution_steps.detail: Mass lost $$= 0.8\ \text{g/year} \times 20\ \text{years} = 16\ \text{g}$$ [100].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass after 20 years
solution_steps.detail: Mass after involution $$= 40\ \text{g} - 16\ \text{g} = 24\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the percentage decrease
solution_steps.detail: Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40\%$$.

solution_steps.title: State the final result
solution_steps.detail: The thymus falls from $$40\ \text{g}$$ to $$24\ \text{g}$$, a $$40\%$$ decrease, illustrating the progressive involution described in the chapter [100].

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question asked for the reason the thymus is large in infancy and shrinks after puberty, with a 44 g gland involuting 0.9 g/year over 10 years; this variant asks instead why immune protection persists after the gland is lost, and uses a 40 g gland involuting 0.8 g/year over 20 years, giving a different mass and percentage.

similar_questions.question:
(a) Explain how the thymus differs in function from the spleen, even though both are lymphatic organs [100, 102].
(b) A patient's thymus weighs $$36\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and involutes steadily to $$21\ \text{g}$$ over 12 years [100]. Calculate the yearly rate of mass loss in grams per year and the percentage decrease from the puberty mass.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune responses early in life [100], whereas the spleen is a blood filter that removes old damaged red blood cells, recycles iron from haemoglobin, produces antibodies and stores extra blood [100, 102]. (b) Rate of loss $$= \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{12\ \text{years}} = 1.25\ \text{g/year}$$; percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{15}{36} \times 100 \approx 41.7\%$$.

solution_steps.title: State the thymus's function
solution_steps.detail: The thymus is a triangular, bilobed gland behind the sternum that serves as the maturation site for T-lymphocytes early in life and gradually shrinks after puberty [100].

solution_steps.title: State the spleen's function
solution_steps.detail: The spleen, the largest lymphatic organ in the upper left abdomen, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old damaged red blood cells, recycles iron from haemoglobin, produces antibodies and stores extra blood for release during heavy bleeding [100, 102].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass lost
solution_steps.detail: Mass lost $$= 36\ \text{g} - 21\ \text{g} = 15\ \text{g}$$ over 12 years [100].

solution_steps.title: Calculate the yearly rate of loss
solution_steps.detail: Rate $$= \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{12\ \text{years}} = 1.25\ \text{g/year}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the percentage decrease
solution_steps.detail: Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{15}{36} \times 100 = 41.67\% \approx 41.7\%$$.

solution_steps.title: State the final result
solution_steps.detail: The thymus loses $$1.25\ \text{g}$$ each year, a $$41.7\%$$ decrease from its $$36\ \text{g}$$ puberty mass, consistent with the chapter's account of involution [100].

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant replaces the infant-versus-puberty discussion with a comparison of thymus and spleen function, and reverses the calculation: it gives the starting and final masses and the time, and asks for the yearly rate of loss plus the percentage decrease.

questions.question: The trachea and bronchi are lined with a mucous membrane that contains sticky mucus and fine, beating cilia. Which statement correctly describes what happens to bacteria that become trapped in this mucus?
options: A. They are swept downwards by the cilia into the lungs, where they are engulfed by phagocytes in the alveoli.
B. They are swept upwards by the cilia to the pharynx, swallowed, and destroyed by the acidic gastric juice in the stomach.
C. They are killed exactly where they are trapped by keratin secreted by the ciliated epithelial cells.
D. They are dissolved by the fatty acids present in the mucus and then absorbed into the blood.
questions.answer: B. They are swept upwards by the beating cilia to the pharynx, swallowed, and destroyed by the acidic gastric juice in the stomach.

solution_steps.title: Identify the defence structure
solution_steps.detail: The trachea and bronchi are lined by the mucociliary escalator, which is part of the non-specific first line of defence and consists of sticky mucus plus fine, beating cilia.

solution_steps.title: Trapping of the microbes
solution_steps.detail: Inhaled bacteria, dust and spores stick to the mucus secreted by the mucous membrane of the air passages.

solution_steps.title: Direction of the ciliary beat
solution_steps.detail: The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the microbe-laden mucus upwards towards the pharynx; they do not beat downwards into the lungs.

solution_steps.title: Chemical destruction in the stomach
solution_steps.detail: The mucus is swallowed, and the trapped microbes are instantly digested by the highly acidic gastric juice ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH $$1.5$$).

solution_steps.title: Test the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Keratin is a protein of the cornified skin layer, not a secretion of ciliated cells, so C is wrong; fatty acids occur in sweat and sebum on the skin, not in airway mucus, so D is wrong; and because the cilia beat upwards, A is wrong. Only B matches the mucociliary escalator.

similar_questions.question: A child in Asmara inhales dust carrying bacteria. The bacteria are trapped in the sticky mucus of the air passages. In which organ are these trapped microorganisms finally destroyed by hydrochloric acid?
similar_questions.answer: B. The stomach

solution_steps.title: Trapping in the airways
solution_steps.detail: The nasal passages, trachea and bronchi are lined with sticky mucus that traps inhaled bacteria and dust.

solution_steps.title: Upward transport
solution_steps.detail: The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the dust-laden mucus upwards to the pharynx.

solution_steps.title: Swallowing and acid digestion
solution_steps.detail: The mucus is swallowed into the stomach, where gastric juice ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH $$1.5$$) instantly digests the microorganisms.

solution_steps.title: Reject the other options
solution_steps.detail: The alveoli are below the trachea and the cilia beat upwards, so A is wrong; the lymph nodes and bone marrow are sites where antibodies are manufactured, not sites of acid destruction, so C and D are wrong.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the mucociliary escalator idea but asks for the site of chemical destruction instead of the whole sequence, and uses different distractors (alveoli, lymph nodes, bone marrow).

similar_questions.question: Explain the role of the cilia that line the trachea, and state what would happen to the trapped dust and bacteria if these cilia stopped beating.
similar_questions.answer: The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the sticky mucus, together with the dust and bacteria trapped in it, upwards to the pharynx so that it can be swallowed and destroyed by gastric acid. If the cilia stopped beating, the mucus would no longer be swept upwards: it would accumulate in the air passages and the trapped microorganisms could remain in the respiratory tract and cause infection.

solution_steps.title: Describe the lining
solution_steps.detail: The trachea is lined with a mucous membrane that contains goblet cells secreting sticky mucus and ciliated epithelial cells.

solution_steps.title: State the normal role of cilia
solution_steps.detail: The cilia beat rhythmically and move the mucus with its trapped microbes upwards to the pharynx, where it is swallowed and destroyed by gastric acid.

solution_steps.title: Predict the consequence of ciliary failure
solution_steps.detail: Without the ciliary beat the mucus is not transported, so it accumulates and the trapped bacteria and dust stay in the respiratory tract, raising the risk of infection.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the task from selecting the correct mechanism to explaining the role of cilia and predicting the consequence of ciliary failure.

questions.question: Complete the following statement by writing the correct term in each blank: Antibodies, which are also called ______, are Y-shaped proteins manufactured by specialised white blood cells known as ______ in response to a specific antigen.
questions.answer: First blank: immunoglobulins. Second blank: plasma B-lymphocytes.

solution_steps.title: Recall the definition of an antibody
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines antibodies as Y-shaped proteins, also named immunoglobulins, that are manufactured in response to a specific antigen.

solution_steps.title: Identify the antibody-producing cell
solution_steps.detail: Antibodies are manufactured by specialised white blood cells called plasma B-lymphocytes.

solution_steps.title: Note where they are produced
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that antibodies are manufactured in the lymphatic system, bone marrow, spleen and intestines, which confirms the involvement of white blood cells of the lymphoid line.

solution_steps.title: Complete the sentence
solution_steps.detail: The two missing terms are therefore immunoglobulins (first blank) and plasma B-lymphocytes (second blank).

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statement by writing the correct term in each blank: The state of having sufficient biological defences to avoid infection, disease or other unwanted foreign invasion is called ______, while the immediate, general barriers that act irrespective of the nature of the pathogen are collectively called ______ immunity.
similar_questions.answer: First blank: immunity. Second blank: innate (inborn or natural) immunity.

solution_steps.title: Define the first term
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines immunity as the state of having sufficient biological defences to avoid infection, disease or other unwanted foreign invasion.

solution_steps.title: Identify the barrier type
solution_steps.detail: The non-specific, physical and chemical barriers that act immediately and generally, irrespective of the pathogen's nature, are collectively called innate (inborn or natural) immunity.

solution_steps.title: Complete the sentence
solution_steps.detail: The first blank is immunity and the second blank is innate (inborn or natural) immunity.

similar_questions.variant_note: Still a two-blank completion, but the target terms change from antibody terminology to the definition of immunity and of innate immunity.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statement: Antigens are macromolecules that are recognised as foreign by the body and trigger an immune response; on the surface of microbes they are usually ______ or ______.
similar_questions.answer: proteins and polysaccharides (large polysaccharides).

solution_steps.title: Recall what an antigen is
solution_steps.detail: An antigen is any macromolecule that is recognised as foreign by the body and triggers an immune response.

solution_steps.title: Recall the chemical nature of antigens
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that antigens are usually proteins or polysaccharides located on the surface of microbes.

solution_steps.title: Complete the statement
solution_steps.detail: The two missing words are proteins and polysaccharides.

questions.question:
A baby girl is born in a health centre in Asmara. Before birth she received maternal antibodies across the placenta, and after birth she received more through colostrum. This natural passive immunity protects her for the first $$6$$ months of life. Assume that $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days.
(a) For how many days does the maternal antibody protection last?
(b) At the age of $$5$$ months she is given the measles vaccine. Her own B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days to produce enough antibodies and memory cells. Is there any period during which she is completely unprotected? Show your reasoning.
(c) Name the type of acquired immunity she has once her own antibodies have been produced, and state whether memory cells are present.
questions.answer: (a) $$180$$ days. (b) No gap: her own antibodies appear on day $$160$$ while maternal protection lasts until day $$180$$, giving an overlap of $$20$$ days. (c) Artificial active immunity, with memory cells present.

solution_steps.title: Classify the immunity from the mother
solution_steps.detail: Antibodies crossing the placenta and passing in colostrum are ready-made antibodies produced by the mother, so the baby has natural passive immunity; her own cells made none of these antibodies.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the duration of maternal protection
solution_steps.detail: The protection lasts $$6$$ months, and $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days, so the duration is $$6 \times 30 = 180$$ days.

solution_steps.title: Find the day the vaccine is given
solution_steps.detail: At $$5$$ months of age she is $$5 \times 30 = 150$$ days old when the vaccine is given.

solution_steps.title: Find when her own antibodies appear
solution_steps.detail: Her B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days after vaccination, so her own protective antibodies appear on day $$150 + 10 = 160$$.

solution_steps.title: Check for a gap in protection
solution_steps.detail: Maternal antibodies protect her until day $$180$$, and her own antibodies begin on day $$160$$. Since $$160 < 180$$, there is no unprotected period; the two protections overlap for $$180 - 160 = 20$$ days.

solution_steps.title: Classify the vaccine-induced immunity
solution_steps.detail: The vaccine supplies antigens that stimulate the girl's own B-lymphocytes to make antibodies, so she develops artificial active immunity, and memory B-cells are formed.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusions
solution_steps.detail: (a) $$180$$ days of maternal protection; (b) no gap, with a $$20$$-day overlap; (c) artificial active immunity, and memory cells are present.

similar_questions.question:
A newborn boy in Keren receives maternal antibodies that give him natural passive immunity for the first $$6$$ months of life. Assume that $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days. He is given the BCG vaccine at the age of $$4$$ months, and his body needs $$14$$ days to build up protective antibody levels.
(a) How many days does the maternal protection last?
(b) Is there any period during which he is completely unprotected? Show your reasoning and state the number of overlapping days.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$180$$ days. (b) No gap: his own antibodies appear on day $$134$$ and maternal protection continues until day $$180$$, so there are $$46$$ days of overlap.

solution_steps.title: Duration of maternal protection
solution_steps.detail: $$6$$ months at $$30$$ days each gives $$6 \times 30 = 180$$ days of natural passive immunity.

solution_steps.title: Day of vaccination
solution_steps.detail: At $$4$$ months of age the boy is $$4 \times 30 = 120$$ days old.

solution_steps.title: Day his own antibodies appear
solution_steps.detail: His body needs $$14$$ days after vaccination, so his own antibodies appear on day $$120 + 14 = 134$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two dates
solution_steps.detail: Since day $$134$$ is earlier than day $$180$$, the boy is never unprotected; the protections overlap for $$180 - 134 = 46$$ days.

similar_questions.variant_note: Same timing logic, but the age of vaccination changes from $$5$$ to $$4$$ months and the time needed to make antibodies changes from $$10$$ to $$14$$ days, so the overlap becomes $$46$$ days instead of $$20$$.

similar_questions.question:
A man in Massawa is injected with anti-tetanus serum after a deep wound, and at the same time he begins a course of tetanus vaccine. The injected serum provides ready-made antibodies that protect him for $$21$$ days, while his own B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days to produce protective antibodies.
(a) Name the type of immunity given by the serum and the type that the vaccine will produce.
(b) Is there any period during which he is unprotected? Show your reasoning.
(c) For how many days do the injected antibodies and his own antibodies overlap?
similar_questions.answer: (a) The serum gives artificial passive immunity; the vaccine produces artificial active immunity. (b) No gap: his own antibodies appear on day $$10$$ while the injected antibodies last until day $$21$$. (c) $$21 - 10 = 11$$ days of overlap.

solution_steps.title: Classify the serum injection
solution_steps.detail: Ready-made antibodies produced by another human or animal and injected into the patient give artificial passive immunity, which acts immediately but forms no memory cells.

solution_steps.title: Classify the vaccination course
solution_steps.detail: The vaccine supplies antigens that stimulate the patient's own B-lymphocytes, so it produces artificial active immunity with memory cells.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two time courses
solution_steps.detail: The injected antibodies protect from day $$0$$ to day $$21$$, and his own antibodies begin on day $$10$$.

solution_steps.title: Decide whether a gap exists
solution_steps.detail: Because day $$10$$ comes before day $$21$$, protection is continuous; the overlap is $$21 - 10 = 11$$ days.

similar_questions.variant_note: Moves the same timing-of-protection reasoning from a mother-to-infant natural passive case to an adult receiving artificial passive serum plus a vaccine, and asks for both immunity types as well as the overlap.

questions.question:
A boy in Massawa is bitten by a stray dog suspected of carrying rabies. The doctor immediately injects him with anti-rabies serum and also begins a course of rabies vaccine. Using the types of acquired immunity:
(a) Name the type of acquired immunity provided by the serum injection.
(b) Name the type of acquired immunity that the vaccine course will produce.
(c) Explain why the serum is given immediately but the vaccine cannot protect the boy during the first few days.
(d) State which of the two provides immunological memory.
questions.answer: (a) Artificial passive immunity. (b) Artificial active immunity. (c) The serum already contains ready-made antibodies that bind and neutralise the rabies virus immediately, whereas active immunity takes several days because the boy's own B-lymphocytes must first produce the antibodies. (d) Only the vaccine course, that is artificial active immunity, provides memory cells.

solution_steps.title: Classify the serum injection
solution_steps.detail: The serum contains ready-made antibodies produced by another immune human or animal, so it gives artificial passive immunity.

solution_steps.title: Classify the vaccine course
solution_steps.detail: The vaccine contains dead, weakened or fragmented pathogens (antigens) that stimulate the boy's own B-lymphocytes, so it produces artificial active immunity.

solution_steps.title: Compare the speeds of protection
solution_steps.detail: Passive immunity is immediate because the injected antibodies can bind and neutralise the rabies virus at once; active immunity is slow because the body must first detect the antigen and its B-lymphocytes must divide, differentiate into plasma cells and synthesise new antibodies, which takes several days.

solution_steps.title: Apply this to the emergency
solution_steps.detail: Rabies is highly dangerous, so the boy cannot wait several days for his own active response; the ready-made serum neutralises the virus immediately while the vaccine builds long-term protection in the background.

solution_steps.title: Decide where memory comes from
solution_steps.detail: Only the vaccine (artificial active immunity) stimulates the boy's own cells, so only it forms memory B-cells; the injected serum provides no immunological memory and its antibodies are eventually broken down.

similar_questions.question:
A girl in Keren becomes ill with mumps, recovers fully, and is never infected again.
(a) Which type of acquired immunity does she now have?
(b) Would she still need a mumps vaccine later? Explain your answer using the idea of memory cells.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Natural active immunity. (b) No: she already has memory B-cells from the natural infection, and these recognise the mumps pathogen instantly on a second exposure and produce antibodies rapidly, so vaccination is unnecessary.

solution_steps.title: Identify how the immunity was acquired
solution_steps.detail: She caught mumps naturally and her own immune system fought the infection, so the immunity is natural active immunity.

solution_steps.title: Explain the lasting protection
solution_steps.detail: During the natural infection her B-lymphocytes produced antibodies and left long-lived memory cells, so protection is long-lasting.

solution_steps.title: Answer the vaccine question
solution_steps.detail: Because memory cells respond immediately if the same pathogen returns, re-infection is prevented and an additional vaccine is not needed.

similar_questions.variant_note: Replaces the emergency serum-plus-vaccine case with natural infection followed by recovery, and asks whether vaccination is still required.

similar_questions.question:
A newborn baby in Nakfa is fed colostrum, the first breast milk, which is rich in maternal antibodies.
(a) Which type of acquired immunity does the baby receive?
(b) Why does this protection last only about the first $$6$$ months and not a lifetime?
(c) Does the baby form memory cells against the pathogens covered by these antibodies? Explain.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Natural passive immunity. (b) The antibodies are ready-made and were not produced by the baby's own cells, so they are gradually broken down and the protection lasts only a few months (about $$6$$ months in this case). (c) No: because the baby's own B-lymphocytes were never stimulated, no memory cells are formed.

solution_steps.title: Classify the transferred antibodies
solution_steps.detail: Antibodies passed from mother to offspring through the placenta or through colostrum give natural passive immunity.

solution_steps.title: Explain the short duration
solution_steps.detail: The baby did not manufacture these antibodies, so they are eventually broken down and the protection lasts only a short time, protecting the infant for about the first $$6$$ months of life.

solution_steps.title: Explain the lack of memory
solution_steps.detail: Since the baby's own B-lymphocytes were not stimulated by the antigens, no memory cells are produced.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the route of antibody transfer to colostrum and focuses on the reasons for the short duration of protection and the absence of memory cells.

questions.question:
During a measles outbreak in a district near Nakfa, health workers study $$4000$$ children. $$3200$$ of the children had previously received the measles vaccine and $$800$$ had never been vaccinated. During the outbreak, $$8\%$$ of the unvaccinated children and $$0.25\%$$ of the vaccinated children contracted measles.
(a) Calculate the number of children who contracted measles in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of measles cases among the $$4000$$ children.
(c) What percentage of all the measles cases came from the unvaccinated group? Give your answer to one decimal place.
(d) State the type of acquired immunity that the vaccinated children were expected to have, and explain, in terms of memory cells, why so few of them became ill.
questions.answer: (a) $$64$$ unvaccinated children and $$8$$ vaccinated children. (b) $$72$$ measles cases in total. (c) $$88.9\%$$ of the cases came from the unvaccinated group. (d) The vaccinated children were expected to have artificial active immunity; the vaccine antigens made their B-lymphocytes form memory cells, which recognise the measles pathogen quickly on re-exposure and produce antibodies before the disease develops.

solution_steps.title: List the group sizes
solution_steps.detail: There are $$800$$ unvaccinated children and $$3200$$ vaccinated children, giving a total of $$4000$$ children studied.

solution_steps.title: Cases among the unvaccinated children
solution_steps.detail: $$8\%$$ of $$800$$ means $$800 \times \frac{8}{100} = 64$$ children contracted measles.

solution_steps.title: Cases among the vaccinated children
solution_steps.detail: $$0.25\%$$ of $$3200$$ means $$3200 \times \frac{0.25}{100} = 3200 \times 0.0025 = 8$$ children contracted measles.

solution_steps.title: Total cases in the district
solution_steps.detail: Adding the two groups gives $$64 + 8 = 72$$ measles cases in total.

solution_steps.title: Percentage of cases from the unvaccinated group
solution_steps.detail: The unvaccinated group contributed $$64$$ of the $$72$$ cases, so the percentage is $$\frac{64}{72} \times 100 = 88.888... \approx 88.9\%$$.

solution_steps.title: Explain the difference using immunity
solution_steps.detail: The vaccinated children were expected to have artificial active immunity: the vaccine antigens stimulated their B-lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells, so on re-exposure to measles the memory cells recognised the pathogen at once and produced antibodies rapidly, preventing the disease from developing.

solution_steps.title: State the final answers
solution_steps.detail: (a) $$64$$ unvaccinated and $$8$$ vaccinated children; (b) $$72$$ cases; (c) $$88.9\%$$; (d) artificial active immunity supported by memory cells.

solution_steps.title: Infections among the vaccinated children
solution_steps.detail: $$0.2\%$$ of $$4500$$ equals $$4500 \times \frac{0.2}{100} = 4500 \times 0.002 = 9$$ infected children.

solution_steps.title: Total infections
solution_steps.detail: $$30 + 9 = 39$$ infections in total.

solution_steps.title: Percentage from the vaccinated group
solution_steps.detail: The vaccinated group contributed $$9$$ of the $$39$$ infections, so the percentage is $$\frac{9}{39} \times 100 = 23.076... \approx 23.1\%$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the disease, the town and the group sizes, and asks for the share of cases coming from the vaccinated group rather than from the unvaccinated group.

similar_questions.question:
A health centre in Keren reports that of $$2500$$ children who received the measles vaccine, $$0.4\%$$ later contracted measles, while of the $$500$$ children who were not vaccinated, $$15\%$$ contracted measles.
(a) Calculate the number of cases in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of cases.
(c) How many times greater was the infection rate among the unvaccinated children than among the vaccinated children?
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$10$$ vaccinated children and $$75$$ unvaccinated children contracted measles. (b) $$85$$ cases in total. (c) The infection rate was $$\frac{15}{0.4} = 37.5$$ times greater among the unvaccinated children.

solution_steps.detail: $$15\%$$ of $$500$$ equals $$500 \times \frac{15}{100} = 75$$ children.

solution_steps.title: Total number of cases
solution_steps.detail: $$10 + 75 = 85$$ cases in total.

solution_steps.title: Compare the two infection rates
solution_steps.detail: The rate in the unvaccinated group was $$15\%$$ and in the vaccinated group $$0.4\%$$, so the ratio is $$\frac{15}{0.4} = 37.5$$ times greater.

solution_steps.title: Relate the rates to immunity
solution_steps.detail: The vaccinated children had artificial active immunity with memory B-cells, which explains the far lower infection rate; the unvaccinated children depended only on non-specific defences and, if infected, on slow natural active immunity.

questions.question: A biology class in Asmara is studying why oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged so rapidly inside the lungs. Which of the following combinations correctly states two structural adaptations of the alveoli that make this rapid diffusion possible?
options: A. A thick, multi-layered alveolar wall and a dry inner lining
B. A thin single-layer epithelial wall and a moist inner surface
C. Hard C-shaped cartilage rings around each alveolus and a moist inner surface
D. A dense network of capillaries and a thick, muscular alveolar wall
questions.answer: B. A thin single-layer epithelial wall and a moist inner surface

solution_steps.title: Recall where exchange happens
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the exchange of $$O_2$$ and $$CO_2$$ occurs entirely within the alveoli, and that it takes place by simple diffusion.

solution_steps.title: Check each stated adaptation
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists three adaptations of alveoli: extremely thin walls (a single layer of flat epithelial cells, giving a very short diffusion path), a moist inner surface (so gases dissolve in water first), and a massive surface area from about 600 to 700 million alveoli.

solution_steps.title: Test the options
solution_steps.detail: Option A is wrong because the alveolar wall is one cell thick, not thick and multi-layered, and the surface is moist, not dry. Option C is wrong because cartilage rings belong to the trachea, not to alveoli. Option D is wrong because a thick muscular wall would lengthen the diffusion path.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Option B alone names two genuine adaptations: the thin single-layer epithelial wall and the moist inner surface.

similar_questions.question: During a hospital visit in Keren, a student is told that a patient's lungs contain roughly 600 to 700 million tiny air sacs. Which of the following best explains why this huge number of alveoli is important for the patient?
similar_questions.answer: C. It creates a massive surface area for gas exchange by diffusion.

solution_steps.title: Recall the third adaptation
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the lungs contain approximately 600 to 700 million alveoli surrounded by a dense capillary network, providing a massive surface area for gas exchange.

solution_steps.title: Link structure to function
solution_steps.detail: Simple diffusion is faster when more surface is available, so a large total alveolar surface increases the rate of $$O_2$$ uptake and $$CO_2$$ removal.

solution_steps.title: Check the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Option A is wrong because surface area does not warm the air; warming and filtering happen in the nasal cavity. Option B is wrong because the total distance for diffusion is set by the thinness of the walls, not by the number of alveoli. Option D is wrong because the volume of each individual alveolus is microscopic, not large.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The large number of alveoli matters because it maximises the surface area available for diffusion.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the concept tested from the thin, moist alveolar wall to the massive surface area adaptation, and replaces the option set with size, warmth and distance misconceptions.

similar_questions.question: A student in Massawa draws a diagram of an alveolus and labels the surrounding capillary. Which of the following explains why both the alveolar wall and the capillary wall are only one cell thick?
similar_questions.answer: A. It keeps the diffusion path between air and blood very short.

solution_steps.title: Recall the first adaptation
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the walls of both the alveoli and the surrounding capillaries consist of a single layer of flat epithelial cells, creating an incredibly short diffusion path.

solution_steps.title: Relate thickness to diffusion
solution_steps.detail: The shorter the distance a gas must travel, the faster it diffuses across the membranes, so a one-cell-thick barrier speeds up $$O_2$$ and $$CO_2$$ movement.

solution_steps.title: Eliminate the distractors
solution_steps.detail: Option B is wrong because thin walls do not generate the pressure that drives ventilation; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles do. Option C is wrong because mucus and cilia for trapping dust are found in the nasal cavity and airways. Option D is wrong because the air inside the alveoli is warm because the nose warmed it before it arrived, not because the wall is thin.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The single-cell thickness exists to minimise the diffusion distance.

similar_questions.variant_note: Focuses on the thin-wall adaptation rather than the surface-area adaptation, uses a different Eritrean setting and a completely new set of distractors.

questions.question: In a school laboratory in Asmara, a group of Grade 10 students estimated that a small section of lung tissue they examined provided a total surface area for gaseous exchange of $$5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. The average surface area of a single alveolus is $$1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$. Calculate the number of alveoli present in that small section of lung tissue.
questions.answer: $$5.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli (50,000 alveoli)

solution_steps.title: Identify the given values
solution_steps.detail: Total surface area of the section $$= 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. Average surface area of one alveolus $$= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working formula
solution_steps.detail: Since the total surface area is supplied by many identical alveoli, the number of alveoli is found by dividing the total surface area by the surface area of one alveolus: $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{\text{Total surface area}}{\text{Surface area of one alveolus}}$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the values
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-7}}$$.

solution_steps.title: Carry out the arithmetic
solution_steps.detail: Dividing the coefficients gives $$5.0 \div 1.0 = 5.0$$, and dividing the powers of ten gives $$10^{-3} \div 10^{-7} = 10^{-3-(-7)} = 10^{4}$$. Therefore the number of alveoli $$= 5.0 \times 10^{4}$$.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The small section of lung tissue contains $$5.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli, that is 50,000 alveoli, which shows how densely packed the gas-exchange surface is.

similar_questions.question: A tissue sample taken from a healthy lung in Keren has a total surface area for gaseous exchange of $$8.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. If the average surface area of one alveolus is $$1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$, calculate the number of alveoli in the sample.
similar_questions.answer: $$8.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli (80,000 alveoli)

solution_steps.title: Identify the given values
solution_steps.detail: Total surface area $$= 8.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$ and surface area of one alveolus $$= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: State the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{\text{Total surface area}}{\text{Surface area of one alveolus}}$$.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The sample contains $$8.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli, that is 80,000 alveoli.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses a larger total surface area of $$8.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$ instead of $$5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$, giving a different final count, and shifts the setting to Keren.

similar_questions.question: During a practical lesson in Massawa, students measured the total surface area of a prepared lung-tissue slide as $$1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2$$. Given that one alveolus has an average surface area of $$1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$, determine the number of alveoli on the slide.
similar_questions.answer: $$1.2 \times 10^{5}$$ alveoli (120,000 alveoli)

solution_steps.title: Identify the given values
solution_steps.detail: Total surface area $$= 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2$$ and average surface area of one alveolus $$= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$.

solution_steps.title: State the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{\text{Total surface area}}{\text{Surface area of one alveolus}}$$.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The slide therefore contains $$1.2 \times 10^{5}$$ alveoli, that is 120,000 alveoli.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the surface area to $$1.2 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^2$$, which needs care with the decimal coefficient, and moves the context to Massawa.

questions.question: A student from Nakfa is resting before an examination in Asmara. Her breathing rate is measured as $$16\ \text{breaths per minute (bpm)}$$ and her tidal volume (the volume of air inhaled or exhaled per breath) is $$450\ \text{mL}$$. Calculate her total minute ventilation in litres of air per minute ($$\text{L/min}$$). Note: $$\text{Minute Ventilation (mL/min)} = \text{Breathing Rate (bpm)} \times \text{Tidal Volume (mL)}$$.
questions.answer: $$7.2\ \text{L/min}$$

solution_steps.title: Identify the given values
solution_steps.detail: Breathing rate $$= 16\ \text{bpm}$$ and tidal volume $$= 450\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the working formula
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives $$\text{Minute Ventilation (mL/min)} = \text{Breathing Rate (bpm)} \times \text{Tidal Volume (mL)}$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the values
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Minute Ventilation} = 16 \times 450\ \text{mL/min}$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert millilitres to litres
solution_steps.detail: Since $$1{,}000\ \text{mL} = 1\ \text{L}$$, we divide by 1,000: $$7{,}200\ \text{mL/min} = 7.2\ \text{L/min}$$.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Her minute ventilation is $$7.2\ \text{L/min}$$, meaning she moves 7.2 litres of air into and out of her lungs every minute while resting.

similar_questions.question: A farmer walking in the fields near Keren breathes at $$20\ \text{bpm}$$ with a tidal volume of $$300\ \text{mL}$$. Calculate the farmer's total minute ventilation in $$\text{L/min}$$.
similar_questions.answer: $$6.0\ \text{L/min}$$

solution_steps.title: Identify the given values
solution_steps.detail: Breathing rate $$= 20\ \text{bpm}$$ and tidal volume $$= 300\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Minute Ventilation} = \text{Breathing Rate} \times \text{Tidal Volume}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses a faster breathing rate of $$20\ \text{bpm}$$ with a smaller tidal volume of $$300\ \text{mL}$$, changing both numbers and the rural setting while testing the same ventilation formula.

similar_questions.question: During football practice in Massawa, an athlete breathes at $$40\ \text{bpm}$$ with a tidal volume of $$1{,}500\ \text{mL}$$. Calculate the athlete's minute ventilation in $$\text{L/min}$$.
similar_questions.answer: $$60\ \text{L/min}$$

solution_steps.title: Identify the given values
solution_steps.detail: Breathing rate $$= 40\ \text{bpm}$$ and tidal volume $$= 1{,}500\ \text{mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the formula
solution_steps.detail: $$\text{Minute Ventilation} = \text{Breathing Rate} \times \text{Tidal Volume}$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert and conclude
solution_steps.detail: $$60{,}000 \div 1{,}000 = 60\ \text{L/min}$$, showing how much ventilation rises during exercise.

similar_questions.variant_note: Sets the calculation in an exercise context with much larger values ($$40\ \text{bpm}$$ and $$1{,}500\ \text{mL}$$), so the product has more digits and needs careful conversion.

questions.question:
Complete the following statements about the mechanism of breathing.
(a) During inhalation the diaphragm ________ and moves downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract and pull the ribs ________ and outward.
(b) As a result the volume of the thoracic cavity ________, and the pressure inside the alveoli becomes ________ than atmospheric pressure, so air flows into the lungs.
(c) During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm relaxes and arches upward into a ________ shape.
questions.answer: (a) contracts; upward  (b) increases; lower  (c) dome

solution_steps.title: Recall the action of the muscles
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that during inhalation the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs upward and outward.

solution_steps.title: Recall the effect on volume and pressure
solution_steps.detail: This muscular action increases the volume of the thoracic cavity, which drops the pressure inside the alveoli below atmospheric pressure, so air flows down the pressure gradient into the lungs.

solution_steps.title: Recall exhalation at rest
solution_steps.detail: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, the diaphragm moves upward into a dome shape, the ribs lower, thoracic volume decreases and alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure.

solution_steps.title: Fill the blanks
solution_steps.detail: (a) contracts; upward. (b) increases; lower. (c) dome.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the following statement about the path of inhaled air.
Air enters the body through the nose and passes in order through the ________, the larynx, the ________, the bronchi and the bronchioles before reaching the alveoli.
similar_questions.answer: pharynx; trachea

solution_steps.title: Recall the route of air
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's pro-tip gives the path of inhaled air as: Nose, Pharynx, Larynx, Trachea, Bronchi, Bronchioles, Alveoli.

solution_steps.title: Match the missing terms
solution_steps.detail: The first blank comes after the nose and before the larynx, so it is the pharynx. The second blank comes after the larynx and before the bronchi, so it is the trachea.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The completed statement reads: nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.

similar_questions.variant_note: Switches the tested content from the breathing mechanism to the anatomical pathway of inhaled air, with two blanks instead of five.

similar_questions.question:
Complete the following statements about the protective and supporting structures of the respiratory tract.
(a) The trachea is supported by ________ cartilage rings that keep the airway open.
(b) The double membrane with fluid that lubricates the lung surface and reduces friction during breathing is called the ________ membrane.
similar_questions.answer: (a) C-shaped  (b) pleural

solution_steps.title: Recall the trachea's support
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the trachea has hard C-shaped cartilage rings that prevent it from collapsing when negative pressure pulls on it.

solution_steps.title: Recall the lubricating membrane
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's table lists the pleural membranes as a double membrane with fluid that lubricates the lung surface and reduces friction during breathing.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The blanks are filled with 'C-shaped' and 'pleural'.
