questions.question: A student in Asmara is revising quietly at her desk, while her brother is sprinting in a school athletics race. Explain which form of cellular respiration each of them mainly uses in their muscle cells, and compare the amount of ATP each pathway can release from one molecule of glucose.
questions.answer: The resting student's muscle cells mainly use aerobic respiration, which releases up to $$36\text{ to } 38\ \text{ATP}$$ per glucose molecule with oxygen, while the sprinting brother's muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), which releases only $$2\ \text{ATP}$$ per glucose molecule without oxygen, making aerobic respiration about 18 to 19 times more efficient.

solution_steps.title: Define cellular respiration
solution_steps.detail: Cellular respiration is the enzymatic oxidation of glucose inside cells to produce ATP. Both aerobic and anaerobic pathways begin with glycolysis, the splitting of a glucose molecule into two pyruvic acid molecules with a net gain of 2 ATP.

solution_steps.title: Identify the pathway used at rest
solution_steps.detail: While the student is resting quietly, oxygen is plentiful, so her muscle cells use aerobic respiration. Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondria and is completely broken down in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and up to 36 to 38 ATP per glucose molecule.

solution_steps.title: Identify the pathway used during sprinting
solution_steps.detail: During intense exercise the oxygen supplied by the lungs and blood is insufficient to meet the high ATP demand. Her brother's muscle cells therefore switch to anaerobic respiration in the cytoplasm, converting pyruvic acid into lactic acid and releasing only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

solution_steps.title: Compare the ATP yields
solution_steps.detail: Aerobic respiration yields about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose molecule, whereas anaerobic lactic acid fermentation yields only 2 ATP per glucose molecule, so aerobic respiration is roughly 18 to 19 times more efficient.

solution_steps.title: Relate to the observations
solution_steps.detail: This explains why the sprinter's muscles tire quickly: lactic acid accumulation makes muscles stiff and sore, while the resting student's cells obtain far more ATP from the same amount of glucose using oxygen.

similar_questions.question: A baker in Keren uses yeast to make bread dough rise, while a weightlifter in the same town performs a very heavy lift. State the type of respiration each process depends on and name the products formed from glucose in each case.
similar_questions.answer: The yeast carries out anaerobic respiration (alcohol fermentation), producing ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide with 2 ATP per glucose; the weightlifter's muscle cells carry out anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), producing lactic acid with 2 ATP per glucose.

solution_steps.title: Recall the two anaerobic pathways
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes alcohol fermentation in plants, yeast and some bacteria, and lactic acid fermentation in animal muscle cells during intense exercise.

solution_steps.title: Identify the yeast process
solution_steps.detail: In bread making, yeast converts glucose into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, and this carbon dioxide is what makes the dough rise. The energy released is only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

solution_steps.title: Identify the weightlifter's process
solution_steps.detail: During a very heavy lift the oxygen supply to the muscles is insufficient, so pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid, releasing 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

solution_steps.title: Conclude with products
solution_steps.detail: Yeast: ethyl alcohol, carbon dioxide and 2 ATP. Muscle: lactic acid and 2 ATP. Both occur in the absence of oxygen.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the comparison from aerobic versus anaerobic respiration in muscles to comparing the two anaerobic pathways (alcohol fermentation in yeast and lactic acid fermentation in muscle) and requires naming the products.

similar_questions.question: Explain why the lungs alone cannot move air in and out, and state which structures provide the force for breathing.
similar_questions.answer: Lungs are soft, elastic and non-muscular, so they cannot pump air by themselves; breathing is driven by pressure differences created by the contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.

solution_steps.title: Describe the lung tissue
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that lungs are soft, elastic and non-muscular, so they contain no skeletal muscle of their own and cannot actively expand or contract.

solution_steps.title: Explain the driving force
solution_steps.detail: Breathing is driven by pressure differences created by two sets of muscles: the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.

solution_steps.title: Link muscle action to air flow
solution_steps.detail: On inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles pull the ribs up and out, increasing thoracic volume and lowering alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure so air flows in; on exhalation these muscles relax, thoracic volume decreases and air is pushed out.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The lungs are passive; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change the volume of the thoracic cavity and create the pressure gradients that ventilate the lungs.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifts the focus from ATP yields of respiration pathways to the mechanical reason why lungs need the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to ventilate.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes excretion from egestion (defecation) in a mammal?
options: A. Excretion removes undigested food that has passed through the alimentary canal, while egestion removes urea made in the liver.
B. Excretion removes metabolic wastes produced by chemical reactions inside the body cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.
C. Excretion removes only sweat and bile pigments, while egestion removes carbon dioxide and urea.
D. Excretion and egestion both remove the chemical waste products formed by reactions inside the body cells.
questions.answer: B. Excretion removes metabolic wastes produced by chemical reactions inside the body cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.

solution_steps.title: Recall the definition of excretion
solution_steps.detail: Excretion is the biological process by which metabolic waste products, produced by chemical reactions inside the cells of the body, are removed. Typical examples are carbon dioxide, excess water and urea, and the process helps to maintain homeostasis.

solution_steps.title: Recall the definition of egestion
solution_steps.detail: Egestion (defecation) is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food material that has simply passed through the alimentary canal and leaves the body as faeces. Like the empty grocery boxes in the house-cleaning analogy, this material never became part of the cells' activities.

solution_steps.title: Test each option against the two definitions
solution_steps.detail: A reverses the two processes, so it is wrong. C is wrong because excretion also removes carbon dioxide and urea, not only sweat and bile pigments, and because egestion removes faeces, not carbon dioxide and urea. D is wrong because the materials removed by egestion were never products of reactions inside the cells.

solution_steps.title: Select the one correct statement
solution_steps.detail: Only B matches the definitions exactly: excretion removes metabolic wastes made inside the cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.

similar_questions.question: A student in Asmara claims that defecation is a form of excretion because both processes remove unwanted material from the body. Correct the student's statement using the biological definitions of excretion and egestion.
similar_questions.answer: Defecation (egestion) is not excretion. Egestion is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food material that passed through the alimentary canal and never entered the body cells, whereas excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes such as carbon dioxide, excess water and urea that were produced by chemical reactions inside the cells. Only the second process is excretion.

solution_steps.title: State what excretion removes
solution_steps.detail: Excretion removes metabolic waste products (for example carbon dioxide, excess water and urea) that are formed by chemical reactions inside the cells, and it maintains homeostasis.

solution_steps.title: State what egestion removes
solution_steps.detail: Egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal as faeces; this material passed through the gut without taking part in cell metabolism.

solution_steps.title: Correct the student
solution_steps.detail: Because faeces are not products of chemical reactions inside the cells, defecation cannot be called excretion. The two processes differ in the origin of the material removed, not merely in the route by which it leaves the body.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question is a multiple-choice identification; this variant turns the same distinction into a written correction of a stated misconception, with no options given.

similar_questions.question: Which one of the following materials is removed from the body by excretion and NOT by egestion?
similar_questions.answer: B. Urea carried in the blood plasma to the kidneys

solution_steps.title: Identify the origin of each material
solution_steps.detail: Excretion deals with wastes made by chemical reactions inside the cells; egestion deals with material that travelled through the alimentary canal without entering the cells.

solution_steps.title: Classify the options
solution_steps.detail: A, C and D are all unabsorbed materials that simply pass along the alimentary canal, so they are removed by egestion. Urea, however, is made in the liver by deamination and is a metabolic waste carried in the blood plasma.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Urea is the only listed material that is a product of cell metabolism, so B is the correct answer.

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant keeps the same concept but reverses the direction of the test: instead of defining the two processes, the student must classify specific materials as excretion or egestion in an MC format.

questions.question: Complete each of the following statements with the correct term. (a) Sweat, which consists of water, mineral salts and a small amount of urea, is produced by sweat glands located in the ______ layer of the skin. (b) The outer waterproof skin layer, which contains dead, keratinized cells, is the ______. (c) Urine passes from the pelvis of each kidney down to the urinary bladder through a tube called the ______.
questions.answer: (a) dermis; (b) epidermis; (c) ureter

solution_steps.title: Identify the layer that contains the sweat glands
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the thick inner dermis contains the sweat glands, blood vessels, hair roots and sensory nerve endings, so sweat is excreted through sweat glands in the dermis.

solution_steps.title: Identify the outer waterproof layer
solution_steps.detail: The outermost layer is the epidermis, which is waterproof and contains dead, keratinized cells.

solution_steps.title: Identify the tube that carries urine to the bladder
solution_steps.detail: Urine formed by the kidney collects in the pelvis and travels down a pair of ureters, one from each kidney, to the urinary bladder for temporary storage. The single tube that leaves the bladder is the urethra.

solution_steps.title: Give the completed statements
solution_steps.detail: (a) dermis; (b) epidermis; (c) ureter. Note that the ureter must not be confused with the urethra, which carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statements about a longitudinal section of a mammalian kidney. (a) The dark red outer region that contains the spherical filtering units called nephrons is the ______. (b) The middle region that contains funnel-shaped, hollow structures called pyramids is the ______. (c) The white inner chamber that stores urine temporarily before it passes into the ureter is the ______.
similar_questions.answer: (a) cortex; (b) medulla; (c) pelvis

solution_steps.title: Recall the three regions in order
solution_steps.detail: A longitudinal section of a kidney shows the cortex outside, the medulla in the middle and the pelvis inside.

solution_steps.title: Match each region to its description
solution_steps.detail: The cortex is the dark red outer region containing the nephrons; the medulla contains the pyramids; the pelvis is the white inner chamber that temporarily stores urine.

solution_steps.title: State the answers
solution_steps.detail: (a) cortex; (b) medulla; (c) pelvis.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question tests the layers of the skin and the ureter; this variant keeps the same FILL format but switches the content to the three anatomical regions of the kidney.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statements about the nephron. (a) The ball of blood capillaries enclosed by a double-walled cup is the ______. (b) The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the ______. (c) The single tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body is the ______.
similar_questions.answer: (a) glomerulus; (b) nephron; (c) urethra

solution_steps.title: Recall the structure of the nephron
solution_steps.detail: The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney and consists of the glomerulus enclosed in the Bowman's capsule, plus the renal tubule.

solution_steps.title: Recall the glomerulus
solution_steps.detail: The glomerulus is a ball of blood capillaries enclosed by a double-walled cup called the Bowman's capsule, where ultrafiltration occurs.

solution_steps.title: Recall the exit tube
solution_steps.detail: The urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside during urination; the ureters, by contrast, bring urine to the bladder.

solution_steps.title: State the answers
solution_steps.detail: (a) glomerulus; (b) nephron; (c) urethra.

similar_questions.variant_note: This variant keeps the same FILL format but replaces the skin and transit-tube items with nephron structures and the urethra, so the student must separate the ureter from the urethra.

questions.question: During a hot afternoon shift on the salt flats near Massawa, a labourer loses $$3.2\ \text{liters}$$ of sweat. In this sweat, mineral salts (NaCl) make up $$0.30\%$$ of the mass and urea makes up $$0.05\%$$ of the mass. Given that $$1\ \text{L} = 1000\ \text{mL}$$ and that $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate (a) the mass of mineral salts lost, (b) the mass of urea lost, and (c) the total mass of these two substances lost in the sweat.
questions.answer: (a) $$9.6\ \text{g}$$ of mineral salts; (b) $$1.6\ \text{g}$$ of urea; (c) $$11.2\ \text{g}$$ in total.

solution_steps.title: Convert the volume of sweat into a mass
solution_steps.detail: The volume is $$3.2\ \text{L} = 3.2 \times 1000 = 3200\ \text{mL}$$. Since $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, the total mass of sweat is $$3200\ \text{mL} \times 1\ \text{g/mL} = 3200\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of mineral salts
solution_steps.detail: Mineral salts are $$0.30\%$$ of the mass, so mass of salts $$= \frac{0.30}{100} \times 3200\ \text{g} = 0.0030 \times 3200 = 9.6\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of urea
solution_steps.detail: Urea is $$0.05\%$$ of the mass, so mass of urea $$= \frac{0.05}{100} \times 3200\ \text{g} = 0.0005 \times 3200 = 1.6\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add the two masses
solution_steps.detail: Total mass lost $$= 9.6\ \text{g} + 1.6\ \text{g} = 11.2\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Interpret the result biologically
solution_steps.detail: The sweat glands in the dermis have removed water, mineral salts and a small amount of urea from the blood. This shows the skin acting both as an organ of excretion (removing metabolic waste) and as a means of cooling the body by evaporation.

similar_questions.question: A student in Asmara walks home quickly on a warm afternoon and loses $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of sweat. The sweat contains $$0.25\%$$ mineral salts and $$0.04\%$$ urea by mass. Taking $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat as $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate (a) the mass of mineral salts lost and (b) the mass of urea lost.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$2.0\ \text{g}$$ of mineral salts; (b) $$0.32\ \text{g}$$ of urea.

solution_steps.title: Convert the volume of sweat to mass
solution_steps.detail: $$0.8\ \text{L} = 800\ \text{mL}$$, and since $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, the mass of sweat is $$800\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the mass of mineral salts
solution_steps.detail: Mass of salts $$= 0.25\% \times 800\ \text{g} = \frac{0.25}{100} \times 800 = 2.0\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Find the mass of urea
solution_steps.detail: Mass of urea $$= 0.04\% \times 800\ \text{g} = \frac{0.04}{100} \times 800 = 0.32\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The smaller sweat loss removes $$2.0\ \text{g}$$ of salts and $$0.32\ \text{g}$$ of urea, still showing that sweat carries away mineral salts and a trace of metabolic waste.

similar_questions.variant_note: The context, the volume of sweat and both percentage concentrations are changed ($$0.8\ \text{L}$$, $$0.25\%$$, $$0.04\%$$ instead of $$3.2\ \text{L}$$, $$0.30\%$$, $$0.05\%$$), and only two of the three parts are asked.

similar_questions.question: A healthy adult living in Keren excretes $$1.5\ \text{L}$$ of urine in one day. The urine contains $$2.0\%$$ urea and $$0.9\%$$ mineral salts by mass. Taking $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of urine as $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate the total mass of dissolved waste (urea plus mineral salts) excreted in the urine that day.
similar_questions.answer: $$43.5\ \text{g}$$ in total ($$30\ \text{g}$$ urea and $$13.5\ \text{g}$$ mineral salts).

solution_steps.title: Convert the urine volume into a mass
solution_steps.detail: $$1.5\ \text{L} = 1500\ \text{mL}$$, so the mass of urine is $$1500\ \text{mL} \times 1\ \text{g/mL} = 1500\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of urea
solution_steps.detail: Mass of urea $$= \frac{2.0}{100} \times 1500 = 30\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of mineral salts
solution_steps.detail: Mass of salts $$= \frac{0.9}{100} \times 1500 = 13.5\ \text{g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Add the two masses
solution_steps.detail: Total dissolved waste $$= 30\ \text{g} + 13.5\ \text{g} = 43.5\ \text{g}$$, all of it carried in the urine formed by the kidneys.

similar_questions.variant_note: The excretory fluid is changed from sweat to urine, the setting moves from Massawa to Keren, and the question asks for a single combined total rather than three separate answers.

questions.question: A camel kept near the hot coastal town of Massawa can go for many days with very little drinking water, while a dairy cow kept in the cool highlands of Asmara must drink frequently. Using the structure of the nephron and the process of osmoregulation, explain how the camel's extensive, extremely long loop of Henle allows it to survive on so little water.
questions.answer: The camel's very long loop of Henle extends deep into the medulla and maintains a steep concentration gradient there, so a large amount of water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct back into the blood. The camel therefore produces a small volume of highly concentrated urine and loses very little water. The cow's shorter loop of Henle produces only a small gradient, so less water is reabsorbed, more dilute urine is formed, and the cow must drink frequently.

solution_steps.title: Recall where water is reabsorbed in the nephron
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct, water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis, and that the loop of Henle is the region responsible for osmoregulation (water balance).

solution_steps.title: Relate loop length to the concentration gradient
solution_steps.detail: The camel's extremely long loop of Henle extends deep into the medulla of the kidney. Because the loop is so long, it builds and maintains a very steep concentration gradient in the medulla.

solution_steps.title: Explain the osmotic movement of water
solution_steps.detail: The steep gradient draws water out of the collecting duct and back into the surrounding blood capillaries by osmosis, so a very large proportion of the water in the filtrate is returned to the blood instead of being lost.

solution_steps.title: Link this to the volume and concentration of urine
solution_steps.detail: Because so much water is reabsorbed, the camel produces only a small volume of highly concentrated urine. Its water loss is therefore minimised, which is the advantage needed in a dry desert environment.

solution_steps.title: Contrast with the cow
solution_steps.detail: The cow has a much shorter loop of Henle, so only a small concentration gradient is maintained in the medulla. Less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, more dilute urine is produced in a larger volume, and the cow must therefore drink frequently to replace the water it loses.

similar_questions.question: On a hot afternoon in Massawa a worker sweats heavily and produces only a small volume of concentrated urine, but on a cool morning in Asmara the same worker produces a larger volume of dilute urine. Explain this difference in terms of osmoregulation in the nephron.
similar_questions.answer: Heavy sweating removes a large volume of water from the blood, so the blood becomes more concentrated. In the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, more water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis, leaving a small volume of highly concentrated urine. On the cool morning little water is lost by sweating, less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, and a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. In this way the nephron keeps the water content of the body constant.

solution_steps.title: State the effect of heavy sweating
solution_steps.detail: Sweat consists mainly of water, so heavy sweating on a hot day removes a large amount of water from the blood and body fluids.

solution_steps.title: Locate the site of water reabsorption
solution_steps.detail: Water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct, with the loop of Henle responsible for osmoregulation.

solution_steps.title: Explain the hot-day response
solution_steps.detail: Because the blood has lost water, more water is drawn back from the filtrate by osmosis, so a small volume of highly concentrated urine is formed and water is conserved.

solution_steps.title: Explain the cool-day response and conclude
solution_steps.detail: With little water lost by sweating, less reabsorption by osmosis is needed, so a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. The nephron therefore maintains a constant internal water balance (homeostasis).

similar_questions.variant_note: The desert-animal comparison is replaced by the same worker on a hot day in Massawa and a cool day in Asmara, and the explanation now moves from sweating to urine concentration instead of from loop length to urine concentration.

similar_questions.question: Describe the two main processes that take place in a nephron, ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption, stating clearly where each occurs and what each achieves.
similar_questions.answer: Ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, creating high blood pressure that forces water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts and urea out of the capillaries into the Bowman's capsule to form the glomerular filtrate, while red blood cells and large proteins remain in the blood. Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule: all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are actively transported back into the surrounding blood capillaries, so useful materials are not lost from the body.

solution_steps.title: Define ultrafiltration and give its site
solution_steps.detail: Ultrafiltration is high-pressure physical filtering that occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.

solution_steps.title: Explain how the pressure is produced
solution_steps.detail: The afferent arteriole entering the glomerulus is wider than the efferent arteriole leaving it, which creates high blood pressure inside the glomerular capillaries.

solution_steps.title: State what passes through and what is held back
solution_steps.detail: Water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts and urea are forced out to form the glomerular filtrate, while red blood cells and large proteins are too large to pass through the pores and stay in the blood.

solution_steps.title: Define selective reabsorption and give its site
solution_steps.detail: Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule, where all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are taken back into the blood capillaries by active transport.

solution_steps.title: State what is achieved
solution_steps.detail: Together the two processes remove nitrogenous waste and excess water and salts from the blood while returning useful materials such as glucose and amino acids to the body, which is why glucose is absent from the urine of a healthy person.

similar_questions.variant_note: Instead of focusing on one desert adaptation, this variant asks for a description of the two central nephron processes (ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption) with their sites and functions.

questions.question: Both kidneys of a healthy adult living in Asmara produce about $$180\ \text{liters}$$ of glomerular filtrate every day. During one particular day this adult excretes $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ of urine, loses $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ of sweat and about $$0.35\ \text{L}$$ of water vapour in expired air. (a) Calculate the total volume of fluid lost from the body on that day. (b) Express this total fluid loss as a percentage of the daily volume of glomerular filtrate. (c) Explain, using the events in the nephron, why the volume of fluid actually lost is so much smaller than the volume of filtrate produced.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.85\ \text{L}$$ of fluid is lost in total. (b) This is approximately $$1.58\%$$ of the daily glomerular filtrate. (c) Over $$99\%$$ of the filtrate is returned to the blood because glucose, amino acids and essential mineral salts are reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule, and water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct; only a small volume is finally excreted as urine, sweat and water vapour.

solution_steps.title: List the measured fluid losses
solution_steps.detail: Urine $$= 1.6\ \text{L}$$, sweat $$= 0.9\ \text{L}$$ and water vapour in expired air $$= 0.35\ \text{L}$$. All three are measured in the same unit, so they can be added directly.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the total volume lost (part a)
solution_steps.detail: Total volume lost $$= 1.6\ \text{L} + 0.9\ \text{L} + 0.35\ \text{L} = 2.85\ \text{L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Set up the percentage calculation (part b)
solution_steps.detail: Percentage lost $$= \frac{\text{total volume lost}}{\text{volume of glomerular filtrate}} \times 100 = \frac{2.85}{180} \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Complete the arithmetic
solution_steps.detail: $$\frac{2.85}{180} = 0.01583$$, and $$0.01583 \times 100 = 1.583\%$$, which rounds to approximately $$1.58\%$$. This means well over $$98\%$$ of the filtrate never leaves the body.

solution_steps.title: Explain the fate of the filtrate in the nephron (part c)
solution_steps.detail: As the filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are returned to the surrounding blood capillaries by active transport (selective reabsorption). In the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, water is reabsorbed by osmosis. More than $$99\%$$ of the filtered water is therefore returned to the blood.

solution_steps.title: Link the explanation to the numbers
solution_steps.detail: Of the $$180\ \text{L}$$ filtered, only $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ leaves as urine, so about $$178.4\ \text{L}$$ is reabsorbed. The remaining losses as sweat and water vapour are small additional losses from the body fluids. This high efficiency of reabsorption is what allows the body to lose only about $$2.85\ \text{L}$$ from a filtrate volume of $$180\ \text{L}$$.

similar_questions.question: Both kidneys of a labourer working in Massawa produce $$180\ \text{liters}$$ of glomerular filtrate in one day. On that day he excretes $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ of urine, loses $$2.4\ \text{L}$$ of sweat and about $$0.45\ \text{L}$$ of water vapour in expired air. (a) Calculate the total volume of fluid lost from his body. (b) Express this total as a percentage of the daily glomerular filtrate. (c) Explain why sweating heavily on a hot day leads to the production of a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$3.75\ \text{L}$$ of fluid is lost in total. (b) This is approximately $$2.08\%$$ of the glomerular filtrate. (c) Heavy sweating removes water from the blood; in response, more water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct back into the blood, so a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced and water is conserved.

solution_steps.title: Add the three fluid losses
solution_steps.detail: Total volume lost $$= 0.9\ \text{L} + 2.4\ \text{L} + 0.45\ \text{L} = 3.75\ \text{L}$$.

solution_steps.title: Set up the percentage
solution_steps.detail: Percentage lost $$= \frac{3.75}{180} \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Complete the arithmetic
solution_steps.detail: $$\frac{3.75}{180} = 0.02083$$, so the percentage is $$2.083\%$$, approximately $$2.08\%$$. Even with heavy sweating, more than $$97\%$$ of the filtrate is returned to the blood.

solution_steps.title: Explain the effect of sweating on urine
solution_steps.detail: Sweat consists mainly of water, so heavy sweating lowers the water content of the blood. More water is then reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, leaving a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

solution_steps.title: Conclude on osmoregulation
solution_steps.detail: The kidney adjusts the volume of water reabsorbed so that the water content of the body stays constant; this is osmoregulation, and it protects the body from dehydration on a hot day.

similar_questions.variant_note: The setting changes from Asmara to Massawa, the urine volume is reduced to $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ while sweat rises to $$2.4\ \text{L}$$, and part (c) asks about the link between heavy sweating and concentrated urine instead of a general explanation of reabsorption efficiency.

similar_questions.question: A nurse in Asmara records the fluid output of a patient over two days. On the cool day the patient forms $$180\ \text{L}$$ of glomerular filtrate and excretes $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ of urine; on the hot day the same volume of filtrate is formed, but only $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of urine is excreted. (a) Calculate the volume of filtrate returned to the blood on each day. (b) Explain, using the nephron, why less urine is formed on the hot day.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Cool day: $$180\ \text{L} - 1.6\ \text{L} = 178.4\ \text{L}$$ reabsorbed. Hot day: $$180\ \text{L} - 0.8\ \text{L} = 179.2\ \text{L}$$ reabsorbed. (b) On the hot day more water is lost from the body, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the collecting duct back into the blood, leaving less water in the filtrate and therefore a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

solution_steps.title: State the relationship between filtrate, urine and reabsorption
solution_steps.detail: Volume reabsorbed $$=$$ volume of glomerular filtrate $$-$$ volume of urine excreted.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the reabsorbed volume for the cool day
solution_steps.detail: $$180\ \text{L} - 1.6\ \text{L} = 178.4\ \text{L}$$, which is $$\frac{178.4}{180} \times 100 = 99.1\%$$ of the filtrate.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the reabsorbed volume for the hot day
solution_steps.detail: $$180\ \text{L} - 0.8\ \text{L} = 179.2\ \text{L}$$, which is $$\frac{179.2}{180} \times 100 = 99.6\%$$ of the filtrate.

solution_steps.title: Explain the difference using the nephron
solution_steps.detail: The loop of Henle maintains a concentration gradient in the medulla, and water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. On the hot day the body has lost more water, so a greater proportion is reabsorbed and only $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of concentrated urine remains to be excreted.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question computes one day's total fluid loss and its percentage; this variant compares two days, asks for the volume of filtrate returned to the blood each day, and shifts the explanation from overall reabsorption efficiency to the effect of heat on urine volume.

questions.question: A patient at an eye clinic in Asmara has a healthy retina whose rods and cones generate nerve impulses normally, but those impulses are not being interpreted as images. According to the table in the chapter, in which part of the brain are impulses from the eye normally interpreted?
options: A. Occipital lobe
B. Temporal lobe
C. Somatosensory cortex
D. Gustatory cortex
questions.answer: A. Occipital lobe

solution_steps.title: Identify the sense organ and its receptors
solution_steps.detail: The eye is the photoreceptive organ described in the chapter; its rods and cones convert light into nerve impulses that must be carried to the brain for interpretation.

solution_steps.title: Use the chapter's sense-organ table
solution_steps.detail: The table pairs each sense organ with its interpreting brain region: Skin - Somatosensory Cortex, Nose - Olfactory Bulb/Temporal Lobe, Tongue - Gustatory Cortex, Eye - Occipital Lobe, Ear - Temporal Lobe (Auditory)/Cerebellum.

solution_steps.title: Check every distractor
solution_steps.detail: The temporal lobe interprets auditory (and olfactory) input, the somatosensory cortex interprets touch, pressure, temperature and pain from the skin, and the gustatory cortex interprets impulses from the taste buds. None of these interprets visual impulses, so each is a pairing error for a different sense organ.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only the occipital lobe is given as the region for interpreting impulses from the eye, so option A is the single correct choice.

similar_questions.question: A student in Keren burns her tongue on hot tea and then tastes the sugar dissolved in it. According to the chapter's sense-organ table, in which brain region are impulses from the taste buds of the tongue interpreted? A) Gustatory cortex  B) Occipital lobe  C) Olfactory bulb  D) Somatosensory cortex
similar_questions.answer: A. Gustatory cortex

solution_steps.title: Identify the receptors firing
solution_steps.detail: The taste buds on the papillae of the tongue are chemoreceptors; they detect sweet, sour, salty and bitter chemicals dissolved in saliva.

solution_steps.title: Match the organ to the brain region
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's table pairs the Tongue (Chemoreceptors/Taste Buds) with the Gustatory Cortex.

solution_steps.title: Reject the distractors
solution_steps.detail: The occipital lobe serves the eye, the olfactory bulb serves the nose, and the somatosensory cortex serves the skin, so none of them interprets taste.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the sense organ from the eye to the tongue and the receptor from photoreceptors to taste-bud chemoreceptors, while testing the same table-matching skill.

similar_questions.question: A farmer near Nakfa picks up a smooth, cool stone. According to the chapter's sense-organ table, which brain region interprets the impulses coming from the mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors of his skin? A) Somatosensory cortex  B) Occipital lobe  C) Gustatory cortex  D) Olfactory bulb
similar_questions.answer: A. Somatosensory cortex

solution_steps.title: Identify the receptors involved
solution_steps.detail: The skin is the largest somatosensory organ and carries mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors that detect touch, pressure, heat and cold.

solution_steps.title: Match the organ to the brain region
solution_steps.detail: The table lists the Skin (Mechanoreceptors, Thermoreceptors) with the Somatosensory Cortex.

solution_steps.title: Reject the distractors
solution_steps.detail: The occipital lobe interprets light, the gustatory cortex interprets taste and the olfactory bulb interprets smell, so they cannot interpret skin sensations.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses the skin (mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors) instead of the eye, and the distractors are the brain regions of three other sense organs.

questions.question: The chapter states that one human retina contains about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells. During a laboratory lesson at a secondary school in Asmara, a student must compare the two populations. Calculate the ratio of rod cells to cone cells and express it in the form $$n : 1$$.
questions.answer: rod cells : cone cells = $$20 : 1$$ (there are 20 times as many rod cells as cone cells)

solution_steps.title: Identify the two quantities
solution_steps.detail: Number of rod cells = $$1.2 \times 10^8$$; number of cone cells = $$6.0 \times 10^6$$, both for a single retina.

solution_steps.title: Write the ratio
solution_steps.detail: rod cells : cone cells = $$1.2 \times 10^8 : 6.0 \times 10^6$$.

solution_steps.title: Make the powers of ten equal
solution_steps.detail: Convert the cone count to the same power of ten as the rod count: $$6.0 \times 10^6 = 0.060 \times 10^8$$, so the ratio becomes $$1.2 \times 10^8 : 0.060 \times 10^8$$.

solution_steps.title: Divide both parts by the cone value
solution_steps.detail: The common factor $$10^8$$ cancels, leaving $$1.2 : 0.060$$. Dividing both numbers by 0.060 gives $$1.2 \div 0.060 = 120 \div 6 = 20$$ and $$0.060 \div 0.060 = 1$$.

solution_steps.title: State the ratio
solution_steps.detail: rod cells : cone cells = $$20 : 1$$, meaning there are 20 times as many rod cells as cone cells in the retina.

similar_questions.question: The chapter gives about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells in one retina. A health club in Massawa wants the comparison written as the number of cone cells present for every 100 rod cells. Calculate this number.
similar_questions.answer: 5 cone cells for every 100 rod cells

solution_steps.title: Set up the comparison
solution_steps.detail: cones per 100 rods = $$\dfrac{6.0 \times 10^6}{1.2 \times 10^8} \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Scale to 100 rods
solution_steps.detail: $$0.05 \times 100 = 5$$, so there are 5 cone cells for every 100 rod cells.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reverses the ratio (cones relative to rods) and asks for a per-100 normalisation instead of the form $$n : 1$$.

similar_questions.question: The chapter gives about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells per retina. In a biology notebook kept at a school in Nakfa, a student wants the totals for both retinas of one person. Calculate the total number of rod cells and the total number of cone cells in both retinas.

solution_steps.title: Recognise that there are two retinas
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's figures are for one retina, so each population must be multiplied by 2 for a person with two eyes.

solution_steps.title: Double the rod cells
solution_steps.detail: $$2 \times 1.2 \times 10^8 = 2.4 \times 10^8$$ rod cells.

solution_steps.title: Double the cone cells
solution_steps.detail: $$2 \times 6.0 \times 10^6 = 12 \times 10^6 = 1.2 \times 10^7$$ cone cells.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the task from a ratio to doubling each population for both retinas, so the answer is two totals in scientific notation rather than $$n : 1$$.

questions.question: Complete each blank with the correct term from the chapter. (a) Baroreceptors located in the ______ and the ______ constantly measure the stretch of blood-vessel walls in order to monitor blood pressure. (b) Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect the partial pressures of ______ and ______ as well as the pH of arterial blood. (c) Proprioceptors are specialized mechanoreceptors found in muscles, ______ and ______ which give the brain continuous feedback about body position and muscle length.
questions.answer: (a) carotid sinuses and aortic arch; (b) oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$) and carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$); (c) tendons and joints

solution_steps.title: Recall the baroreceptor locations
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch, where they constantly measure the stretch of blood-vessel walls to monitor blood pressure.

solution_steps.title: Recall what peripheral chemoreceptors detect
solution_steps.detail: Carotid and aortic bodies contain peripheral chemoreceptors that detect the partial pressures of oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$) and carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$) as well as pH levels in arterial blood.

solution_steps.title: Recall the proprioceptor locations
solution_steps.detail: Proprioceptors are specialized mechanoreceptors located in muscles, tendons and joints, providing feedback about body position, muscle length and joint angles.

solution_steps.title: Assemble the completed statements
solution_steps.detail: (a) carotid sinuses and aortic arch; (b) oxygen and carbon dioxide; (c) tendons and joints.

similar_questions.question: Complete each blank with the correct term from the chapter. The internal thermoreceptors that act as the body's central thermostat are located in the ______ of the brain, and they directly monitor the temperature of the ______ flowing through the brain. When the core temperature rises, this centre triggers ______ of cutaneous blood vessels and ______ production.
similar_questions.answer: hypothalamus; blood; vasodilation; sweat

solution_steps.title: Locate the central thermostat
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that thermoreceptors within the hypothalamus of the brain act as the body's central thermostat, monitoring the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain.

solution_steps.title: Recall the response to a rise in core temperature
solution_steps.detail: A rise above the optimal $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ triggers vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels and sweat production.

solution_steps.title: Assemble the completed statement
solution_steps.detail: hypothalamus; blood; vasodilation; sweat.

similar_questions.variant_note: Switches from the mechano- and chemoreceptor groups to the thermoreceptor group and asks for the heat-loss responses rather than receptor locations.

similar_questions.question: Complete each blank with the correct term from the chapter. Stretch receptors in the ______ prevent over-inflation, while stretch receptors in the ______ signal the autonomic nervous system when a critical volume of fluid has been reached. Both belong to the internal receptor group called ______.
similar_questions.answer: lungs; bladder; mechanoreceptors

solution_steps.title: Recall the internal stretch receptors
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that stretch receptors in the lungs prevent over-inflation, while those in the bladder signal the autonomic nervous system when a critical volume of fluid is reached.

solution_steps.title: Classify the receptor group
solution_steps.detail: Stretch receptors respond to mechanical deformation, so they are mechanoreceptors - one of the three functional groups of internal receptors.

solution_steps.title: Assemble the completed statement
solution_steps.detail: lungs; bladder; mechanoreceptors.

questions.question: A Grade 10 class in Keren is preparing an eye-health leaflet using the chapter's figures for one retina: about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells. (a) Calculate the total number of photoreceptor cells in the two retinas of one person. (b) Calculate the percentage of this total that is made up of cone cells, giving your answer to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.52 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptor cells in both retinas; (b) cone cells make up about 4.8% of the total

solution_steps.title: Find the photoreceptors in one retina
solution_steps.detail: Total in one retina = rod cells + cone cells = $$1.2 \times 10^8 + 6.0 \times 10^6$$. Writing the cone count with the same power of ten, $$6.0 \times 10^6 = 0.060 \times 10^8$$, gives $$(1.2 + 0.060) \times 10^8 = 1.26 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptors.

solution_steps.title: Double it for two retinas
solution_steps.detail: $$2 \times 1.26 \times 10^8 = 2.52 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptor cells in both retinas (252,000,000 cells).

solution_steps.title: Find the cone cells in two retinas
solution_steps.detail: $$2 \times 6.0 \times 10^6 = 1.2 \times 10^7$$ cone cells.

solution_steps.title: Write the percentage relationship
solution_steps.detail: Percentage of cones = $$\dfrac{\text{cone cells}}{\text{total photoreceptors}} \times 100 = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^7}{2.52 \times 10^8} \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Convert to a percentage and round
solution_steps.detail: $$0.047619 \times 100 = 4.7619\%$$, which rounds to 4.8% to one decimal place.

similar_questions.question: A student in Asmara reads that one retina contains about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells. Calculate the total number of photoreceptor cells in one retina and the percentage of that total made up by rod cells, to one decimal place.
similar_questions.answer: total = $$1.26 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptors; rod cells make up about 95.2% of the total

solution_steps.title: Add the two populations
solution_steps.detail: $$1.2 \times 10^8 + 6.0 \times 10^6 = 1.2 \times 10^8 + 0.060 \times 10^8 = 1.26 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptors.

solution_steps.title: Form the rod percentage
solution_steps.detail: Percentage of rods = $$\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^8}{1.26 \times 10^8} \times 100 = \dfrac{1.2}{1.26} \times 100$$.

solution_steps.title: Divide and round
solution_steps.detail: $$\dfrac{1.2}{1.26} = 0.95238\ldots$$, so the percentage is $$95.238\% \approx 95.2\%$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses one retina instead of two and asks for the rod-cell percentage instead of the cone-cell percentage.

similar_questions.question: For a school eye-health campaign in Massawa, a nurse uses the chapter's figures for one retina: $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells. Calculate how many more rod cells than cone cells are present in one retina, and express that difference as a percentage of the total photoreceptors of that retina, to one decimal place.
similar_questions.answer: difference = $$1.14 \times 10^8$$ more rod cells, which is about 90.5% of the retina's photoreceptors

solution_steps.title: Find the total photoreceptors in one retina
solution_steps.detail: $$1.2 \times 10^8 + 6.0 \times 10^6 = 1.26 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptors.

solution_steps.title: Subtract to find the surplus of rods
solution_steps.detail: $$1.2 \times 10^8 - 0.060 \times 10^8 = 1.14 \times 10^8$$ more rod cells than cone cells.

solution_steps.title: Express the difference as a percentage
Divide and round
solution_steps.detail: $$\dfrac{1.14}{1.26} = 0.90476\ldots$$, so the difference is $$90.476\% \approx 90.5\%$$ of the total photoreceptors.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the operation from adding and doubling the populations to subtracting them, and asks for the surplus rods as a percentage of one retina's photoreceptors.

questions.question: A dockworker at the port of Massawa spends two hours working in very hot conditions and his core temperature rises above normal. Explain how the internal thermoreceptors of the hypothalamus detect this change and how the body brings the core temperature back towards $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$. Name the two corrective responses described in the chapter and state whether this control loop is negative feedback.
questions.answer: The hypothalamus thermoreceptors detect core blood temperature above $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ and trigger (i) vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels and (ii) sweat production; both responses remove heat and lower the core temperature back towards the optimum. A fall below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ would instead trigger vasoconstriction and shivering. The loop is negative feedback because the response reverses the initial change and restores homeostasis.

solution_steps.title: Identify the internal receptor and what it monitors
solution_steps.detail: Internal thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus act as the body's central thermostat. They do not monitor the outside air; they directly monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain.

solution_steps.title: Compare the detected value with the optimum
solution_steps.detail: The chapter gives the optimal core temperature as $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$. Working in the heat at Massawa pushes the core blood temperature above this set value, so the thermoreceptors increase their signalling to the hypothalamus.

solution_steps.title: Corrective response 1: vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels
solution_steps.detail: The hypothalamus triggers vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels, so a larger volume of warm blood flows close to the skin surface and heat is lost from the body to the surroundings.

solution_steps.title: Corrective response 2: sweat production
solution_steps.detail: The hypothalamus also triggers sweat production. Evaporation of sweat from the skin surface removes heat from the body and lowers the core temperature.

solution_steps.title: State the opposite arm of the same control system
solution_steps.detail: The same centre works in reverse: if the core temperature fell below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$, the hypothalamus would trigger vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels and shivering in order to conserve and generate heat.

solution_steps.title: Identify the type of feedback
solution_steps.detail: The responses reverse the original deviation - a rise in core temperature is answered by heat-losing mechanisms - so the loop is negative feedback, and it returns the internal state to the narrow survival range (homeostasis).

similar_questions.question: A student from Asmara goes camping in the highlands on a cold night and his core temperature begins to fall below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$. Explain how the internal thermoreceptors respond, name the two corrective responses described in the chapter, and state the type of feedback involved.
similar_questions.answer: The hypothalamic thermoreceptors detect core blood temperature below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ and the hypothalamus triggers (i) vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels to conserve heat and (ii) shivering to generate heat. This is negative feedback because the responses reverse the original fall in temperature and restore the optimum.

solution_steps.title: Detect the deviation
solution_steps.detail: The internal thermoreceptors of the hypothalamus continuously monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain; a value below the optimal $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ is the stimulus.

solution_steps.title: Response 1: conserve heat
solution_steps.detail: The hypothalamus triggers vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels, reducing blood flow near the skin surface so that less heat is lost to the cold surroundings.

solution_steps.title: Response 2: generate heat
solution_steps.detail: Shivering is triggered, and the muscular activity generates heat that raises the core temperature.

solution_steps.title: Classify the loop
solution_steps.detail: Both responses oppose the initial change, so the mechanism is negative feedback that brings the core temperature back towards $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reverses the direction of the temperature change (cold instead of heat), so the two corrective responses become vasoconstriction and shivering rather than vasodilation and sweating.

similar_questions.question: A runner at a stadium in Asmara sprints while holding his breath as long as he can, so carbon dioxide accumulates in his arterial blood. Using the chapter's description of internal receptors, explain how this change is detected and how the body responds, naming the receptor groups involved.
similar_questions.answer: Rising carbon dioxide makes the blood more acidic. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect the raised $$\text{CO}_2$$ partial pressure and lowered pH of arterial blood, while central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata monitor the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid. Together they trigger an immediate reflex to increase ventilation, expelling the excess carbon dioxide and restoring blood pH.

solution_steps.title: Identify the chemical change
solution_steps.detail: Holding the breath allows carbon dioxide to accumulate, and the chapter states that a rise in $$\text{CO}_2$$ leads to blood acidity (a fall in pH).

solution_steps.title: Peripheral detection
solution_steps.detail: The carotid and aortic bodies contain peripheral chemoreceptors that detect partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide as well as pH levels in arterial blood, so they detect the acidic blood.

solution_steps.title: Central detection
solution_steps.detail: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata monitor the pH of cerebrospinal fluid and serve as the primary controller of the respiratory drive.

solution_steps.title: The corrective response
solution_steps.detail: These chemoreceptors trigger an immediate reflex to increase ventilation, so excess carbon dioxide is expelled and blood pH is restored - another negative feedback loop that maintains homeostasis.

similar_questions.variant_note: Switches from thermoreceptors to chemoreceptors and from temperature regulation to the control of ventilation, while keeping the same detect-signal-respond-restore logic.

questions.question: A group of Grade 11 students in Asmara are classifying the glands of the human body according to how their secretions leave the gland. Which ONE of the following structures is classified as an endocrine gland?
options: A. Thyroid gland
B. Sweat gland
C. Salivary gland
D. Digestive gland opening into the small intestine
questions.answer: A. Thyroid gland

solution_steps.title: Recall the defining structural feature
solution_steps.detail: The chapter defines endocrine glands as entirely ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream or surrounding interstitial fluid, using a rich capillary network rather than a duct.

solution_steps.title: Recall the defining feature of exocrine glands
solution_steps.detail: Exocrine glands synthesize secretions that are channelled through anatomical ducts directly to an epithelial surface. Sweat glands, salivary glands and digestive organs are named in the chapter as exocrine examples.

solution_steps.title: Test each option in turn
solution_steps.detail: B (sweat gland) and C (salivary gland) deliver their secretions through ducts onto the skin and into the mouth respectively, and D (digestive gland) delivers digestive secretion through a duct into the intestinal lumen; all three are therefore exocrine. The thyroid gland has no duct and releases its hormones, such as thyroxine, into the blood.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only the thyroid gland is ductless and blood-borne in its secretion, so it is the only endocrine structure listed.

similar_questions.question: Which ONE of the following glands releases its secretion through an anatomical duct onto an epithelial surface?
similar_questions.answer: C. Salivary gland

solution_steps.title: State the criterion
solution_steps.detail: A gland whose product travels along an anatomical duct to an epithelial surface is by definition an exocrine gland.

solution_steps.title: Check the options
solution_steps.detail: The anterior pituitary (A), the parathyroid gland (B) and the adrenal cortex (D) are all ductless endocrine tissues that pour their hormones into the blood. The salivary gland pours saliva along a duct into the mouth.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Only the salivary gland uses a duct, so it is the exocrine gland required.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question asked the learner to pick the endocrine (ductless) member from a list dominated by exocrine glands; this variant reverses the direction and asks for the ducted, exocrine member from a list dominated by endocrine glands, with different distractors.

similar_questions.question: A gland in the neck of a patient in Keren is found to possess an extremely rich capillary network but no excretory duct of any kind. State, with a reason, whether this gland is endocrine or exocrine.
similar_questions.answer: The gland is endocrine, because it is ductless and its dense capillary network allows its hormonal product to diffuse directly into the bloodstream.

solution_steps.title: Use the two structural criteria given
solution_steps.detail: The chapter distinguishes the two gland types by the presence or absence of ducts and by the route the secretion takes: ducts to an epithelial surface for exocrine glands, capillaries and blood for endocrine glands.

solution_steps.title: Apply the criteria to the observation
solution_steps.detail: No duct is present, so the secretion cannot be channelled to an epithelial surface; a very rich capillary network is exactly the feature the chapter describes in endocrine glands.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The gland is endocrine and its secretion consists of hormones released into the blood for systemic transport.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the task from selecting a labelled option to reasoning from two observed anatomical features (rich capillary bed, absence of a duct) in a named Eritrean town, so no option list is used.

questions.question: Complete the following statement by writing the correct word or phrase in each numbered blank. The posterior lobe of the pituitary gland does not synthesize hormones of its own; instead it stores and releases (1) ______ and (2) ______, both of which are produced by neurosecretory cells of the (3) ______.
questions.answer: (1) Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH), (2) Oxytocin, (3) hypothalamus

solution_steps.title: Separate the two lobes of the pituitary
solution_steps.detail: The chapter divides the pituitary into the anterior lobe (adenohypophysis), which acts as a cellular factory and synthesizes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin, and the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis).

solution_steps.title: Identify what the posterior lobe handles
solution_steps.detail: The posterior lobe does not synthesize hormones; it stores and releases Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) and Oxytocin.

solution_steps.title: Trace the site of synthesis
solution_steps.detail: Both stored hormones are produced by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus and are transported to the posterior lobe for storage and release.

solution_steps.title: Complete the statement
solution_steps.detail: Blank (1) = Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH); blank (2) = Oxytocin; blank (3) = hypothalamus.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statement. The anterior lobe of the pituitary gland synthesizes and releases trophic hormones such as (1) ______, which acts on bones, skeletal muscles and the liver, and (2) ______, which stimulates the thyroid gland to synthesize and release thyroxine.
similar_questions.answer: (1) Growth Hormone (GH), (2) Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)

solution_steps.title: Read the target tissue clues
solution_steps.detail: The table of the chapter lists GH with bones, skeletal muscles and liver as its principal targets, where it promotes cellular division, protein synthesis and somatic growth.

solution_steps.title: Match the second clue
solution_steps.detail: The hormone whose principal target is the thyroid gland and whose action is to stimulate the synthesis and release of thyroxine is Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).

solution_steps.title: Confirm the gland
solution_steps.detail: Both GH and TSH are listed among the trophic hormones synthesized by the anterior lobe of the pituitary, so both blanks are consistent with the stated gland.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifted the focus from the posterior lobe and its hypothalamic origin to the anterior lobe and two of its trophic hormones, identified by their target tissues instead of by their storage site.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following statement. A patient who cannot reabsorb sufficient water in the renal distal tubules and collecting ducts is likely to be deficient in (1) ______, which is released by the (2) ______ lobe of the pituitary gland; the other hormone released from the same lobe is (3) ______, which is involved in childbirth.
similar_questions.answer: (1) Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH), (2) posterior, (3) Oxytocin

solution_steps.title: Use the target tissue clue
solution_steps.detail: The chapter table assigns ADH the renal distal tubules and collecting ducts as principal target tissue, with the action of increasing water reabsorption to regulate blood volume and pressure.

solution_steps.title: Locate the release site
solution_steps.detail: ADH is stored and released by the posterior lobe of the pituitary, although it is synthesized by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells.

solution_steps.title: Supply the second posterior-lobe hormone
solution_steps.detail: The only other hormone listed as stored and released by the posterior lobe is Oxytocin, so blank (3) is Oxytocin.

similar_questions.variant_note: Same posterior-lobe fact base, but the blanks are now reached through a clinical clue about a failure of water reabsorption, with ADH, the lobe name and oxytocin as the three answers instead of the original ordering.

questions.question: A patient in Asmara has a blood sample analysed after a meal and again after an overnight fast. Complete the following paragraph by supplying the missing terms. After a meal, the beta cells of the pancreatic islets release (1) ______, which facilitates glucose transport into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue and promotes the storage of glucose as glycogen, a process called (2) ______. During fasting, the alpha cells release (3) ______, which acts on liver tissue to raise blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and (4) ______, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.
questions.answer: (1) insulin, (2) glycogenesis, (3) glucagon, (4) gluconeogenesis

solution_steps.title: Identify the postprandial hormone and its source
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that beta cells of the islets of Langerhans produce insulin, which facilitates glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues during postprandial states and lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake and glycogenesis.

solution_steps.title: Name the storage process
solution_steps.detail: The conversion of absorbed glucose into stored glycogen is termed glycogenesis, so blank (2) is glycogenesis.

solution_steps.title: Identify the fasting hormone
solution_steps.detail: Alpha cells of the same islets synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, acting principally on liver tissue.

solution_steps.title: Name the second hepatic route to glucose
solution_steps.detail: Besides breaking glycogen down (glycogenolysis), glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, which fills blank (4).

solution_steps.title: State the completed paragraph
solution_steps.detail: (1) insulin, (2) glycogenesis, (3) glucagon, (4) gluconeogenesis.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following paragraph. The islets of Langerhans form the endocrine portion of the (1) ______, which is described as a dual exocrine-endocrine gland. Within the islets, the cells that secrete glucagon are the (2) ______ cells, while the cells that secrete insulin are the (3) ______ cells.
similar_questions.answer: (1) pancreas, (2) alpha, (3) beta

solution_steps.title: Name the gland holding the islets
solution_steps.detail: The chapter locates the islets of Langerhans inside the pancreas and describes the pancreas as operating as a dual exocrine-endocrine gland.

solution_steps.title: Assign the glucagon-secreting cell
solution_steps.detail: Within the islets, alpha cells synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting.

solution_steps.title: Assign the insulin-secreting cell
solution_steps.detail: Beta cells of the same islets produce insulin to facilitate glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues in postprandial states.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the pancreatic islet context but tests the identity of the gland and the names of the two cell types rather than the names and actions of the hormones themselves.

similar_questions.question: Complete the following paragraph describing emergency stress adaptation. The outer region of the adrenal gland, called the (1) ______, secretes steroid corticosteroids such as cortisol and aldosterone, whereas the inner region, called the (2) ______, produces the amine catecholamines (3) ______ and norepinephrine that orchestrate the fight-or-flight response.
similar_questions.answer: (1) cortex, (2) medulla, (3) epinephrine (adrenaline)

solution_steps.title: Recall the two zones of the adrenal gland
solution_steps.detail: The chapter describes the adrenal glands, situated atop each kidney, as consisting of an outer cortex and an inner medulla.

solution_steps.title: Match each zone to its secretion
solution_steps.detail: The outer cortex secretes steroid corticosteroids (glucocorticoids such as cortisol and mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone); the inner medulla produces the amine catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine.

solution_steps.title: Fill the third blank
solution_steps.detail: The catecholamine named together with norepinephrine is epinephrine (adrenaline), which stimulates rapid flight-or-fight sympathetic adaptations in the heart, blood vessels and liver.

concepts: antagonistic hormonal control of blood glucose
questions.question: A clinical laboratory in Asmara measures the effect of two pancreatic hormones on isolated liver hepatocytes. Explain how insulin and glucagon exert opposing effects on blood glucose concentration, and state the two processes by which glucagon raises blood glucose.
questions.answer: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake into muscle, adipose tissue and liver and by promoting glycogenesis; glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in liver tissue, making the two hormones antagonistic.

solution_steps.title: State the source and trigger of each hormone
solution_steps.detail: Within the islets of Langerhans, beta cells secrete insulin during postprandial (fed) states, while alpha cells secrete glucagon during fasting, so the two hormones are released under opposite physiological conditions.

solution_steps.title: Describe the action of insulin on hepatocytes
solution_steps.detail: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake of glucose and by promoting glycogenesis, that is, the conversion of glucose into stored glycogen in the liver; it also facilitates glucose transport into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

solution_steps.title: Describe the action of glucagon on hepatocytes
solution_steps.detail: Glucagon acts on liver tissue to raise blood glucose. It stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of stored glycogen back into glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.

solution_steps.title: Explain why the pair is described as antagonistic
solution_steps.detail: Because insulin drives glucose out of the blood into storage while glucagon mobilises glucose from storage into the blood, the two hormones produce opposite net movements of glucose and therefore hold blood glucose within its narrow physiological range.

solution_steps.title: Summarise the answer
solution_steps.detail: Insulin promotes cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis (lowering blood glucose); glucagon promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver (raising blood glucose). The two processes by which glucagon raises blood glucose are glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

similar_questions.question: A student in Keren writes that glucagon and insulin are secreted by the same cells of the pancreatic islets. Correct this statement and explain how the two hormones together maintain glucose homeostasis.
similar_questions.answer: The statement is wrong: glucagon is secreted by the alpha cells and insulin by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans. Together they maintain homeostasis because insulin lowers blood glucose during postprandial states (cellular uptake and glycogenesis), while glucagon raises it during fasting (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis).

solution_steps.title: Correct the cell assignment
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that alpha cells synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, while beta cells produce insulin to facilitate glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues during postprandial states, so two distinct cell populations are involved.

solution_steps.title: State the glucose-lowering arm
solution_steps.detail: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake of glucose and by promoting glycogenesis, the storage of glucose as glycogen.

solution_steps.title: State the glucose-raising arm
solution_steps.detail: Glucagon acts on liver tissue, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to release glucose into the blood during fasting.

solution_steps.title: Explain the homeostatic outcome
solution_steps.detail: Because the two hormones are released in opposite nutritional states and drive glucose in opposite directions, their balance keeps blood glucose within tight physiological bounds.

similar_questions.variant_note: Turns the explanation into an error-correction task: the learner must first reject the false claim that one cell type secretes both hormones and then justify the antagonistic pairing, instead of describing the two actions directly.

similar_questions.question: A student athlete in Asmara has not eaten for fourteen hours but continues to train. Identify the pancreatic hormone whose secretion predominates in this state, name its principal target tissue, and list the two metabolic processes it stimulates there.
similar_questions.answer: Glucagon predominates during fasting; its principal target tissue is the liver, where it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to raise blood glucose.

solution_steps.title: Identify the fasting hormone
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that alpha cells secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, whereas insulin acts in postprandial states.

solution_steps.title: Name the target tissue
solution_steps.detail: The summary table of the chapter lists glucagon with liver tissue as its principal target.

solution_steps.title: List the two processes
solution_steps.detail: In the liver glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, both of which raise blood glucose.

similar_questions.variant_note: Applies the same pancreatic hormones to a physical-activity and fasting scenario in Eritrea, and asks only about the dominant hormone, its target tissue and its processes rather than comparing insulin with glucagon.

questions.question:
A 50 kg woman in Asmara is diagnosed with myxoedema and is prescribed thyroxine replacement at a dose of 3.4 micrograms per kilogram of body mass, given once daily. Each 200-microgram tablet costs 0.40 Nakfa.
(a) Calculate her daily thyroxine dose in micrograms.
(b) Express this daily dose in milligrams.
(c) Calculate the total cost in Nakfa of her thyroxine supply for 30 days.
(d) State the endocrine reason why she must take thyroxine, and explain what will happen to her blood TSH level while the treatment is adequate.
questions.answer: (a) 170 micrograms per day; (b) 0.17 milligram per day; (c) 2.04 Nakfa for a 30-day supply; (d) the thyroxine must be supplied because of hyposecretion of thyroxine (myxoedema), and once the dose restores normal thyroxine the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary reduces the blood TSH level back towards normal.

solution_steps.title: Identify the given data and the relation needed
solution_steps.detail: Body mass = 50 kg; dose = 3.4 micrograms per kg per day; tablet content = 200 micrograms; tablet cost = 0.40 Nakfa; duration = 30 days. The daily dose equals the dose per kilogram multiplied by body mass. The chapter notes that hormones act in minute quantities measured in micrograms or picograms, so microgram units are appropriate here.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the daily dose in micrograms
solution_steps.detail: Daily dose = 3.4 micrograms per kg x 50 kg = 170 micrograms per day.

solution_steps.title: Convert micrograms to milligrams
solution_steps.detail: Since 1 milligram = 1000 micrograms, divide by 1000: 170 micrograms per day / 1000 = 0.17 milligram per day.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the 30-day supply and its cost
solution_steps.detail: Total mass required = 170 micrograms per day x 30 days = 5100 micrograms = 5.1 milligrams. Cost = 5.1 milligrams x 0.40 Nakfa per milligram = 2.04 Nakfa for the 30-day supply.

solution_steps.title: Give the endocrine explanation
solution_steps.detail: Myxoedema is caused by hyposecretion of thyroxine in an adult, and because thyroxine is the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, the missing hormone must be supplied from outside. Thyroxine normally exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary; when the replacement dose restores a normal circulating thyroxine concentration, that feedback is re-established and the pituitary stops over-secreting TSH, so blood TSH falls back towards normal.

solution_steps.title: State the final results
solution_steps.detail: (a) 170 micrograms per day; (b) 0.17 milligram per day; (c) 2.04 Nakfa for 30 days; (d) thyroxine replacement is required because the gland hyposecretes the hormone, and adequate treatment suppresses the previously elevated blood TSH back to normal through negative feedback.

similar_questions.question:

similar_questions.answer: (a) 150 micrograms per day; (b) 0.15 milligram per day; (c) 4.50 Nakfa for a 60-day supply.

solution_steps.title: Set up the dose relation
solution_steps.detail: Daily dose = dose per kilogram x body mass = 2.5 micrograms per kg x 60 kg.

solution_steps.title: Compute the daily dose
solution_steps.detail: 2.5 x 60 = 150, so the daily dose is 150 micrograms per day.

solution_steps.title: Convert to milligrams
solution_steps.detail: 150 micrograms / 1000 = 0.15 milligram per day.

solution_steps.title: Cost the 60-day supply
solution_steps.detail: Total mass = 150 micrograms per day x 60 days = 9000 micrograms = 9.0 milligrams. Cost = 9.0 milligrams x 0.50 Nakfa per milligram = 4.50 Nakfa.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the body mass from 50 kg to 60 kg, the dose from 3.4 to 2.5 micrograms per kg, the tablet strength from 200 to 250 micrograms, the tablet price from 0.40 to 0.50 Nakfa, the town from Asmara to Keren, and the supply period from 30 to 60 days; part (d) of the main question is dropped so that the variant is purely quantitative.

similar_questions.question:
A 40 kg woman with adult thyroxine hyposecretion receives a total daily thyroxine dose of 136 micrograms from 200-microgram tablets costing 0.40 Nakfa each.
(a) Calculate the dose per kilogram of body mass in micrograms per kg.
(b) Calculate how many whole tablets she must take each day to meet this dose without exceeding it.
(c) Calculate the cost of a 30-day supply based on the tablets actually taken.
similar_questions.answer: (a) 3.4 micrograms per kg; (b) she must take 1 whole tablet per day, providing 200 micrograms, since no whole number of tablets supplies 136 micrograms exactly; (c) 12.00 Nakfa for 30 days.

solution_steps.title: Find the dose per kilogram
solution_steps.detail: Dose per kg = total daily dose / body mass = 136 micrograms / 40 kg = 3.4 micrograms per kg.

solution_steps.title: Test whole-tablet amounts
solution_steps.detail: One tablet provides 200 micrograms, which exceeds 136 micrograms by 64 micrograms, so it is the smallest whole-tablet dose that covers the requirement and is the practical choice; any smaller whole number of tablets gives zero micrograms.

solution_steps.title: Cost the 30-day supply
solution_steps.detail: Cost = 1 tablet per day x 0.40 Nakfa per tablet x 30 days = 12.00 Nakfa.
