questions.question:
A 70 kg fisherman from Massawa is diagnosed with hyperthyroidism caused by Graves' disease, and his basal metabolic rate is measured at 168 percent of the value expected for a healthy man of his age and body mass. His expected normal basal metabolic rate is 6800 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy in kJ per day that his body expends above the normal value.
(c) Express this excess as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Explain the endocrine basis of this raised metabolic rate and name the gland and the hormone responsible.
questions.answer: (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day of excess expenditure; (c) 68 percent above the normal basal metabolic rate; (d) the thyroid gland is hypersecreting thyroxine, and because thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, energy expenditure rises far above normal.

solution_steps.title: Identify the given data and the principle
solution_steps.detail: Normal basal metabolic rate = 6800 kJ per day; measured rate = 168 percent of normal. Thyroxine is described in the chapter as the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, and hyperthyroidism accelerates metabolic rate to pathological levels.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the actual basal metabolic rate
solution_steps.detail: Actual rate = 1.68 x 6800 kJ per day = 11,424 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the excess expenditure
solution_steps.detail: Excess = 11,424 kJ per day - 6800 kJ per day = 4624 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Express the excess as a percentage
solution_steps.detail: Percentage excess = (4624 / 6800) x 100 percent = 0.68 x 100 percent = 68 percent, which agrees with the measured value being 68 percent above the normal 100 percent.

solution_steps.title: Explain the endocrine mechanism
solution_steps.detail: The gland responsible is the thyroid gland, which is hypersecreting thyroxine. Thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, so an excess of thyroxine raises oxygen and fuel consumption above normal. This explains the chapter's clinical picture of hyperthyroidism: rapid weight loss despite eating, heat intolerance, hyperactive reflexes and anxiety, together with chronic strain on the cardiovascular system from elevated heart rate and blood pressure.

solution_steps.title: State the final results
solution_steps.detail: (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day in excess; (c) 68 percent above normal; (d) hypersecretion of thyroxine by the thyroid gland elevates the basal metabolic rate of most somatic cells.

similar_questions.question:
A 55 kg woman in Asmara with adult thyroxine hyposecretion has a basal metabolic rate measured at 82 percent of the value expected for a healthy woman of her age and body mass. Her expected normal rate is 5400 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate her actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the energy deficit in kJ per day relative to the normal value.
(c) Express this deficit as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Name the hormone that is deficient and explain why this reduces her basal metabolic rate.
similar_questions.answer: (a) 4428 kJ per day; (b) 972 kJ per day below normal; (c) 18 percent below normal; (d) thyroxine is deficient, and since thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, its shortage lowers metabolism, matching the sluggish metabolism, weight gain and cold sensitivity of myxoedema.

solution_steps.title: Convert the percentage to a multiplier
solution_steps.detail: A rate at 82 percent of normal corresponds to a multiplying factor of 0.82 applied to the normal value of 5400 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the actual rate
solution_steps.detail: 0.82 x 5400 kJ per day = 4428 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the deficit
solution_steps.detail: Deficit = 5400 kJ per day - 4428 kJ per day = 972 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Express the deficit as a percentage
solution_steps.detail: (972 / 5400) x 100 percent = 18 percent, consistent with 100 percent - 82 percent = 18 percent.

solution_steps.title: Explain the endocrine cause
solution_steps.detail: The deficient hormone is thyroxine, the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate. With less thyroxine acting on most somatic cells, heat production and metabolic rate fall, producing the low metabolic rate, weight gain and cold sensitivity characteristic of myxoedema.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reversed the pathology from hyperthyroidism to hypothyroidism, changed the patient to a 55 kg woman, the setting from Massawa to Asmara, the normal rate from 6800 to 5400 kJ per day and the measured percentage from 168 percent to 82 percent, so the learner now computes a metabolic deficit rather than an excess.

similar_questions.question:
A 16-year-old boy in Keren with a pituitary tumour has a basal metabolic rate measured at 120 percent of the normal value for his age and body mass, his normal rate being 6000 kJ per day. The tumour is hypersecreting Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy expended per day.
(c) Express the excess as a percentage of the normal rate.
(d) Explain the full chain of events from the pituitary tumour to the raised metabolic rate.
similar_questions.answer: (a) 7200 kJ per day; (b) 1200 kJ per day in excess; (c) 20 percent above normal; (d) excess TSH from the tumour over-stimulates the thyroid gland, which synthesizes and releases excess thyroxine; thyroxine then acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, raising energy expenditure by 20 percent.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the actual rate
solution_steps.detail: 1.20 x 6000 kJ per day = 7200 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the excess
solution_steps.detail: Excess = 7200 kJ per day - 6000 kJ per day = 1200 kJ per day.

solution_steps.title: Express the excess as a percentage
solution_steps.detail: (1200 / 6000) x 100 percent = 20 percent, consistent with 120 percent - 100 percent = 20 percent.

solution_steps.title: Trace the hormonal chain
solution_steps.detail: TSH has the thyroid gland as its principal target tissue and stimulates the synthesis and release of thyroxine, so a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour drives thyroxine secretion upward.

solution_steps.title: Link thyroxine to metabolism
solution_steps.detail: Thyroxine's target is most somatic cells, where it elevates the basal metabolic rate and regulates heat production; the excess hormone therefore accounts for the measured 20 percent rise in energy expenditure.

similar_questions.variant_note: Introduces a secondary (pituitary-driven) cause of a raised metabolic rate in an adolescent boy, uses a different normal rate of 6000 kJ per day and a measured value of 120 percent, and requires an extra causal step linking a TSH-secreting tumour to thyroxine release.

questions.question: A health educator at the hospital in Keren traces the route followed by sperm from the site of their formation to the point where they leave the male body through the urethra. According to the chapter's SEVEN UP pathway, how many structures does a spermatozoon pass through during this journey, and what are they in order?
options: A. 4 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, urethra
B. 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, penis
C. 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, penis
D. 6 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis
questions.answer: D. 6 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis

solution_steps.title: Recall the SEVEN UP acronym
solution_steps.detail: The chapter's Pro-Tip gives SEVEN UP: S = Seminiferous tubules, E = Epididymis, V = Vas deferens, E = Ejaculatory duct, N = Nothing (a placeholder, not a structure), U = Urethra, P = Penis. Only the six lettered structures carry sperm; the N entry is a memory aid with no anatomical counterpart.

solution_steps.title: Check each structure against its stated role
solution_steps.detail: Seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis; the epididymis stores spermatozoa and allows them to acquire motility; the vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum and loops over the urinary bladder; the ejaculatory duct is where the vas deferens joins; the urethra is the final tube; and the penis delivers semen.

solution_steps.title: Reject the distractor pathways
solution_steps.detail: Options A and B place the vas deferens before the epididymis, but sperm enter the epididymis directly from the tubules and only later are propelled into the vas deferens. Options B and C omit the ejaculatory duct, which the chapter explicitly lists between the vas deferens and the urethra. Options A and C also stop at the urethra and drop the penis.

solution_steps.title: Count and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Six lettered structures remain once the placeholder N is excluded, giving the order seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis.

similar_questions.question: During a laboratory lesson in Asmara, a student models the pathway of seminal fluid by dropping coloured water at each named structure in turn. If she starts at the epididymis and ends at the ejaculatory duct, how many structures has she labelled along this stretch, and what are they in order?
similar_questions.answer: 3 structures: epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct

solution_steps.title: Locate the starting structure
solution_steps.detail: The SEVEN UP sequence places the epididymis immediately after the seminiferous tubules; within the epididymis sperm reside for several weeks and undergo biochemical maturation to acquire motility and fertilizing capability.

solution_steps.title: Move to the next structure
solution_steps.detail: During sexual arousal, mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens, the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum, traverses the inguinal canal into the abdominal cavity, and loops over the urinary bladder.

solution_steps.title: Identify the end point
solution_steps.detail: The vas deferens loops over the urinary bladder to join the ejaculatory duct, which is the stated end of this stretch.

solution_steps.title: Count and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Labelling the epididymis, the vas deferens and the ejaculatory duct gives three structures in that order.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question runs the whole SEVEN UP route and requires the placeholder N to be discarded; this variant asks only for a bounded stretch of the same route, so the count differs and the placeholder issue disappears.

similar_questions.question: A student in Massawa repeatedly writes the male pathway as seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis. How many structures are in the wrong order, and what is the correct arrangement of those structures?
similar_questions.answer: 2 structures are in the wrong order; the correct arrangement is seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis

solution_steps.title: Compare with SEVEN UP
solution_steps.detail: The correct SEVEN UP order is seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis. Comparing the student's list position by position: seminiferous tubules (correct), vas deferens (wrong for position 2), epididymis (wrong for position 3), ejaculatory duct (correct), urethra (correct), penis (correct).

solution_steps.title: Explain why the swap is an error
solution_steps.detail: Sperm reach the epididymis directly from the seminiferous tubules and mature there for several weeks before being propelled into the vas deferens. Writing the vas deferens first implies sperm bypass maturation, which contradicts the chapter.

solution_steps.title: Count the misplaced structures
solution_steps.detail: Only the vas deferens and the epididymis occupy wrong positions, so exactly two structures are out of order.

solution_steps.title: State the corrected order
solution_steps.detail: Swapping those two entries restores seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis.

similar_questions.variant_note: Instead of counting structures along a correct pathway, this variant supplies a faulty pathway and asks the student to detect and repair the error, exercising the same SEVEN UP ordering knowledge in reverse.

questions.question: A clinical technician in Asmara records a man's core body temperature as $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The chapter states that spermatogenesis cannot occur effectively at core body temperature, and that the scrotum maintains an optimal microenvironment approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core body temperature. Calculate the full optimal scrotal temperature range, then state which of the following scrotal measurements would fall inside that range: $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ or $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
questions.answer: Optimal scrotal range = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$; the only measurement inside this range is $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the governing principle
solution_steps.detail: The scrotum holds the testes outside the pelvic cavity so that sperm production occurs several degrees below core temperature, because high temperatures degrade the key germinal enzymes needed for spermatogenesis. The permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.

solution_steps.title: Compute the upper end of the range
solution_steps.detail: The upper end is only $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the lower end of the range
solution_steps.detail: The lower end is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The optimal range is therefore $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ inclusive.

solution_steps.title: Test each candidate measurement
solution_steps.detail: Compare each value with the interval $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C} \leq T \leq 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. For $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference from core is $$4.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which lies between $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ and $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it is inside. For $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference is only $$2.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; for $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$1.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; and for $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$0.8^{\circ}\text{C}$$. All three are less than $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature and therefore lie above $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, outside the range.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The optimal scrotal temperature range is $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and of the four measurements only $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ falls within it.

similar_questions.question: At a clinic in Massawa the ambient heat is high, and a technician notes that a man's testes are held at the extreme cool end of the permitted range while his core temperature reads $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. If the permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, calculate the temperature of the testes and state how many degrees cooler than core temperature this is.
similar_questions.answer: Testicular temperature = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature

solution_steps.title: Identify the relevant end of the range
solution_steps.detail: The extreme cool end corresponds to the largest permitted differential, which the chapter gives as $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature. Under warm conditions the dartos and cremaster muscles relax to promote heat loss, which drives the testes toward this cool end.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the core temperature
solution_steps.detail: Using core body temperature $$= 37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, the extreme cool testicular temperature is $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check against the full range
solution_steps.detail: The full range spans $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is indeed the lowest value in that interval.

solution_steps.title: State the cooling differential
solution_steps.detail: Subtracting the testicular temperature from the core temperature gives $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 32.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so the testes are held $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question computes the whole interval and screens four candidate values against it; this variant fixes the scenario at the extreme cool end and asks only for that single boundary value and its differential.

similar_questions.question: A man in Asmara takes a prolonged hot bath and his scrotal temperature rises to $$36.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ while his core temperature remains $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. Calculate how far this scrotal temperature lies below core temperature, and state whether it satisfies the $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential required for effective spermatogenesis.
similar_questions.answer: Only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, so it does not satisfy the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential and spermatogenesis is impaired

solution_steps.title: Calculate the actual differential
solution_steps.detail: The differential is core temperature minus scrotal temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 36.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the required differential
solution_steps.detail: Effective spermatogenesis requires the testes to be approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core temperature. The measured differential of $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is smaller than the minimum of $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it falls short of the requirement.

solution_steps.title: Relate the shortfall to enzyme function
solution_steps.detail: Spermatogenesis cannot proceed effectively at temperatures close to core body temperature because heat degrades key germinal enzymes. A differential of only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ leaves the testes far too warm for normal germ-cell development.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The hot bath leaves the testes only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, which fails the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential, so sperm production is impaired.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question works forward from core temperature to build the optimal range; this variant works backward from an elevated measured scrotal temperature to test whether the differential requirement is met, using a hot-bath context mentioned in the chapter.

questions.question: At a reproductive health session in Keren, a facilitator explains that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of the total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$, with the remainder coming from the bulbourethral glands and the spermatozoa themselves. If a single ejaculation has a total volume of $$3.0\text{ mL}$$, calculate the volume contributed by the seminal vesicles, the volume contributed by the prostate gland, and the combined volume contributed by all remaining sources.
questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.8\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.9\text{ mL}$$; all remaining sources $$= 0.3\text{ mL}$$ (together these sum to the $$3.0\text{ mL}$$ total).

solution_steps.title: Identify the known quantities
solution_steps.detail: Total semen volume $$= 3.0\text{ mL}$$. Seminal vesicle contribution $$= 60\%$$ of total. Prostate gland contribution $$= 30\%$$ of total. The bulbourethral glands and spermatozoa account for whatever remains.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the seminal vesicle volume
solution_steps.detail: Multiply the total volume by the seminal vesicle fraction: $$0.60 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 1.8\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid supplies fructose as metabolic fuel for sperm and prostaglandins that trigger contractions in the female reproductive tract, which is consistent with this gland providing the bulk of semen volume.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the prostate gland volume
solution_steps.detail: Multiply the total volume by the prostate fraction: $$0.30 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.9\text{ mL}$$. This thin, milky, slightly alkaline fluid contains citric acid and proteolytic enzymes that liquefy the semen coagulum after ejaculation.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the remaining volume
solution_steps.detail: First find the remaining percentage: $$100\% - 60\% - 30\% = 10\%$$. Then apply it: $$0.10 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.3\text{ mL}$$. This residue corresponds to the clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus of the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands together with the spermatozoa.

solution_steps.title: Check the total
solution_steps.detail: Add the parts: $$1.8\text{ mL} + 0.9\text{ mL} + 0.3\text{ mL} = 3.0\text{ mL}$$, which matches the stated total volume, so the calculation is consistent.

similar_questions.question: A laboratory in Asmara receives a semen sample of $$2.5\text{ mL}$$ for analysis. Using the chapter's values of $$60\%$$ for the seminal vesicles, $$30\%$$ for the prostate gland and the remaining percentage for the bulbourethral glands plus spermatozoa, calculate the volume contributed by each of the three components.
similar_questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.5\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.75\text{ mL}$$; bulbourethral glands plus spermatozoa $$= 0.25\text{ mL}$$

solution_steps.title: Set out the sample volume and fractions
solution_steps.detail: Total volume $$= 2.5\text{ mL}$$, seminal vesicle fraction $$= 0.60$$, prostate fraction $$= 0.30$$, and the remaining fraction is $$1 - 0.60 - 0.30 = 0.10$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the seminal vesicle share
solution_steps.detail: $$0.60 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 1.5\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fructose- and prostaglandin-rich fluid is the largest single contributor to semen volume.

solution_steps.title: Compute the prostate share
solution_steps.detail: $$0.30 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 0.75\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid with proteolytic enzymes neutralizes vaginal acidity and liquefies the semen coagulum after ejaculation.

solution_steps.title: Compute the remaining share
solution_steps.detail: $$0.10 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 0.25\text{ mL}$$, representing the clear lubricating mucus of the bulbourethral glands plus the spermatozoa.

solution_steps.title: Verify the total
solution_steps.detail: $$1.5\text{ mL} + 0.75\text{ mL} + 0.25\text{ mL} = 2.5\text{ mL}$$, matching the sample volume.

similar_questions.variant_note: The total ejaculate volume is changed from $$3.0\text{ mL}$$ to $$2.5\text{ mL}$$ and the answer is requested for all three components at once, so no volume value from the main question can be reused.

similar_questions.question: During a health talk in Barentu, a facilitator states that in one ejaculation the seminal vesicles contributed $$1.2\text{ mL}$$. Given that the seminal vesicles supply approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume, calculate the total volume of that ejaculate and the volume contributed by the prostate gland.
similar_questions.answer: Total ejaculate volume $$= 2.0\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland contribution $$= 0.6\text{ mL}$$

solution_steps.title: Set up the percentage relation
solution_steps.detail: The seminal vesicle volume equals $$60\%$$ of the total, so total volume $$= \dfrac{\text{seminal vesicle volume}}{0.60}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the total volume
solution_steps.detail: Substitute the known part: total $$= \dfrac{1.2\text{ mL}}{0.60} = 2.0\text{ mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compute the prostate volume
solution_steps.detail: The prostate contributes $$30\%$$ of the same total: $$0.30 \times 2.0\text{ mL} = 0.6\text{ mL}$$.

solution_steps.title: Check the remaining component
solution_steps.detail: The remaining $$10\%$$ is $$0.10 \times 2.0\text{ mL} = 0.2\text{ mL}$$, and $$1.2\text{ mL} + 0.6\text{ mL} + 0.2\text{ mL} = 2.0\text{ mL}$$, confirming the total.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question is a forward percentage calculation from a given total; this variant runs in the reverse direction, giving the seminal vesicle part and requiring the total to be recovered by division before the prostate volume can be found.

questions.question: A man in Massawa has been unable to conceive with his partner for two years. Semen analysis shows that sperm are being produced in normal numbers but almost all of them are immotile and none has acquired fertilizing capability, while the man's reproductive hormone levels are normal. Using only the structures and functions described in this chapter, identify the single structure whose function is most likely impaired, and justify your answer with two functions of that structure.
questions.answer: The epididymis. It normally stores spermatozoa and provides the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability; normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm point to failure of exactly these two functions.

solution_steps.title: Note that sperm production itself is intact
solution_steps.detail: The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis and the Sertoli cells provide nutrients and structural support to developing germ cells. Because sperm are produced in normal numbers, this function is clearly not the problem. The acrosome, which carries the hydrolytic enzymes needed to digest the egg's protective layers, is also formed during spermiogenesis in the testis, so the production line is working.

solution_steps.title: Identify which function is missing
solution_steps.detail: The two missing features are motility and fertilizing capability. The chapter states that sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability during their residence in the epididymis, where they undergo biochemical maturation over several weeks.

solution_steps.title: Match the missing functions to the correct structure
solution_steps.detail: The epididymis is the crescent-shaped tubule coiled on the superior-posterior margin of each testis in which spermatozoa reside for several weeks. Its two functions are (i) storing spermatozoa and (ii) facilitating the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability. An impairment of this structure explains normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm.

solution_steps.title: Confirm that the other ducts are not implicated
solution_steps.detail: The vas deferens is a thick-walled muscular duct that simply transports mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct; it does not mature sperm. The chapter also notes that mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens only during sexual arousal, whereas the immotility described here is a property of the sperm themselves, present regardless of arousal.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The impaired structure is the epididymis, because the sperm have normal production but lack precisely the two properties, motility and fertilizing capability, that the epididymis confers during maturation.

similar_questions.question: A 58-year-old man in Asmara undergoes a vasectomy in which the vas deferens is cut and sealed. His testes continue to produce sperm and his Leydig cells continue to secrete testosterone. Explain, using only the chapter's description of the male tract and of semen composition, what happens to the sperm produced after the operation and why the operation does not reduce his testosterone levels.
similar_questions.answer: Sperm are still produced in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis, but they can no longer pass beyond the sealed vas deferens, so they are not included in the ejaculate; testosterone is unaffected because it is secreted by the Leydig cells, which the chapter places under the control of LH from the anterior pituitary, not under the control of the vas deferens.

solution_steps.title: Locate the cut in the pathway
solution_steps.detail: The vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that carries mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis out of the scrotum, through the inguinal canal and over the urinary bladder to the ejaculatory duct. Sealing it blocks this single transport route.

solution_steps.title: Trace the fate of the sperm
solution_steps.detail: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules is unaffected, and sperm still pass into the epididymis to mature. However, they cannot be propelled beyond the blocked vas deferens, so no sperm reach the ejaculatory duct and urethra and none appear in the ejaculate, which is why vasectomy is a permanent surgical contraceptive method.

solution_steps.title: Locate the source of testosterone
solution_steps.detail: In the interstitial space between adjacent seminiferous tubules lie the Leydig cells, which synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone from the anterior pituitary. These cells are entirely separate from the vas deferens.

solution_steps.title: Explain why testosterone is unchanged
solution_steps.detail: Because the Leydig cells and the HPG axis that regulates them are untouched by the operation, testosterone secretion continues normally. Only the sperm delivery route, not the endocrine function of the testis, has been interrupted.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: After vasectomy, sperm are produced and matured but can no longer leave the tract, while testosterone levels remain normal because Leydig cells under LH control continue to secrete androgen independently of the vas deferens.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question diagnoses an impaired epididymis from semen-analysis evidence; this variant keeps the same structures and gland functions but poses a surgical-blockage scenario, asking the student to reason forward from a known interruption of the vas deferens instead of backward from symptoms.

similar_questions.question: A student in Keren claims that because the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands release a clear fluid before ejaculation, that fluid must be the main carrier of sperm. Explain, using the chapter's description of the male accessory glands, why this claim is incorrect, and state the two functions the bulbourethral glands actually perform.
similar_questions.answer: The claim is incorrect because the bulbourethral glands contribute only a small clear, viscous pre-ejaculatory mucus; the bulk of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles (about 60%) and the prostate gland (about 30%). Their two functions are lubricating the urethra and neutralizing residual acidic urine prior to ejaculation.

solution_steps.title: Establish the actual volume contributions
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$. Together these two glands account for about $$90\%$$ of semen, leaving only roughly $$10\%$$ for the bulbourethral gland secretion and the spermatozoa themselves.

solution_steps.title: Show why the student's claim fails
solution_steps.detail: A secretion that forms only a small fraction of the ejaculate cannot be its main carrier of sperm. The spermatozoa themselves are the cellular component, suspended in the fluid vehicle formed mainly by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.

solution_steps.title: State the real functions of the bulbourethral glands
solution_steps.detail: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete a clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus whose functions are to lubricate the urethra and to neutralize residual acidic urine before semen passes. These are preparatory and protective roles, not a sperm-carrying role.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The claim is incorrect: the bulbourethral secretion is a minor pre-ejaculatory lubricating and neutralizing fluid, while the seminal vesicles and prostate gland provide the bulk of the semen volume.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question concerns the epididymis and sperm maturation; this variant tests the same set of male reproductive structures from the gland-secretion side, using the chapter's percentage volumes to refute a misconception about the bulbourethral glands.

questions.question: A man's blood testosterone level rises well above its normal stable value. Applying the negative feedback loop described in this chapter, which of the following correctly states the resulting changes?
options: A. Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to increase GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so testosterone production rises further.
B. Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, so Leydig cell stimulation falls and testosterone production is reduced.
C. Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion but on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so the two effects cancel and testosterone production is unchanged.
D. Testosterone acts directly on the seminiferous tubules to decrease spermatogenesis, and the reduced sperm numbers feed back on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release.
questions.answer: B. Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, so Leydig cell stimulation falls and testosterone production is reduced.

solution_steps.title: Identify the axis being regulated
solution_steps.detail: Testosterone secretion is governed by the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis: the hypothalamus releases Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), which drives the anterior pituitary to release LH, and LH stimulates the Leydig cells of the testis to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

solution_steps.title: State the direction of a negative feedback loop
solution_steps.detail: In negative feedback, a rise in the level of the final hormone in the chain suppresses the earlier steps of the chain. The chapter states explicitly that as blood testosterone levels rise, testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, stabilizing hormone levels.

solution_steps.title: Evaluate each option
solution_steps.detail: Option A describes positive feedback, in which rising testosterone would further increase GnRH and LH, which contradicts the stabilizing negative feedback the chapter describes; it also misstates the effect on both organs. Option C is internally inconsistent, since the chapter gives decreases at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. Option D introduces a sperm-count feedback signal that the chapter never describes, and the chapter's loop is defined by blood testosterone acting on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, not on the seminiferous tubules.

solution_steps.title: Confirm the correct option and its consequence
solution_steps.detail: Option B matches the chapter exactly: decreased GnRH and decreased LH. With less LH reaching the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells are less stimulated, testosterone secretion falls, and the elevated blood level is brought back down toward its stable value.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Rising blood testosterone suppresses the HPG axis at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, so option B is the correct statement of the feedback response.

similar_questions.question: A laboratory report for a patient in Asmara shows a very low blood testosterone level together with an abnormally high LH level, and the hypothalamic GnRH secretion is found to be high. Which single structure does this pattern indicate is failing, and what is the normal response of that structure to LH?
similar_questions.answer: The Leydig cells (interstitial cells) of the testis are failing. Normally LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, so unrepaired Leydig cells should raise testosterone output when LH is high.

solution_steps.title: Read the pattern of hormones
solution_steps.detail: GnRH is high and LH is high, so the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary are both sending strong stimulatory signals down the HPG axis. The defect therefore lies below the pituitary.

solution_steps.title: Identify the target of LH
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells lying between adjacent seminiferous tubules, synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone secreted from the anterior pituitary.

solution_steps.title: Explain why high LH with low testosterone is diagnostic
solution_steps.detail: If the Leydig cells were responding normally, a high LH level would drive testosterone production upward. Instead testosterone remains very low, so the Leydig cells are not responding to LH stimulation and are the failing structure.

solution_steps.title: Account for the high upstream hormones
solution_steps.detail: Because testosterone is the signal that suppresses the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, low testosterone removes that inhibition. GnRH and LH therefore remain high, which is exactly what the report shows.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: The failing structure is the Leydig cell population of the testis, whose normal response to LH is to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question applies the negative feedback loop to a high-testosterone state and asks for the resulting hormonal changes; this variant presents laboratory data for a low-testosterone state and requires the student to localise the lesion by using the same HPG axis relationships in the opposite direction.

similar_questions.question: A man in Keren receives a treatment that keeps his blood testosterone concentration artificially high for several weeks. Predict the effect of this treatment on the secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone and Luteinizing Hormone, and explain how the treatment will affect the activity of his Leydig cells.
similar_questions.answer: GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus and LH release from the anterior pituitary will both decrease through negative feedback; with less LH stimulation the Leydig cells will become less active and their own testosterone secretion will fall.

solution_steps.title: Recognise the feedback signal
solution_steps.detail: Blood testosterone is the final hormone of the HPG axis and acts as the inhibitory signal on the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. An artificially raised level therefore acts as a strong inhibitory signal.

solution_steps.title: Predict the hypothalamic response
solution_steps.detail: The hypothalamus responds by decreasing its secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone, the hormone that normally drives the anterior pituitary.

solution_steps.title: Predict the pituitary response
solution_steps.detail: The anterior pituitary responds to the raised testosterone directly, as well as to the reduced GnRH, by decreasing its release of Luteinizing Hormone.

solution_steps.title: Trace the effect on Leydig cells
solution_steps.detail: Leydig cells synthesize and secrete testosterone when stimulated by LH. With LH release suppressed, the Leydig cells receive less stimulation and become less active, so the testis's own contribution to blood testosterone declines even while the external treatment maintains a high total level.

solution_steps.title: Conclude
solution_steps.detail: Sustained high blood testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH through negative feedback, and the reduced LH stimulation in turn lowers the secretory activity of the Leydig cells.

similar_questions.variant_note: The main question is a structured multiple-choice identification of the feedback changes; this variant removes the answer options and requires a written prediction of the same cascade one step further, down to the altered activity of the Leydig cells.

questions.question: The adult human vertebral column (spine) is made up of 33 vertebrae. Which of the following correctly matches each region of the spine with its number of vertebrae?
options: A. 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 caudal
B. 12 cervical, 7 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 caudal
C. 7 cervical, 5 thoracic, 12 lumbar, 4 sacral, 5 caudal
D. 5 cervical, 12 thoracic, 7 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 caudal
questions.answer: A. 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 caudal vertebrae

solution_steps.title: Recall the total number of vertebrae
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the vertebral column (spine) consists of 33 vertebrae separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, and that it is divided into five regions.

solution_steps.title: Assign the cervical and thoracic counts
solution_steps.detail: The cervical region contains 7 vertebrae, which include the atlas and axis that permit head rotation. The thoracic region contains 12 vertebrae.

solution_steps.title: Assign the lumbar, sacral and caudal counts
solution_steps.detail: The lumbar region contains 5 vertebrae. The sacral region contains 5 fused vertebrae that form the sacrum, and the caudal (coccygeal) region contains 4 fused vertebrae that form the coccyx.

solution_steps.title: Check the sum and select the matching option
solution_steps.detail: Adding the regions: 7 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 33, which agrees with the stated total. Option B wrongly gives 12 cervical and 7 thoracic vertebrae; option C wrongly gives 5 thoracic, 12 lumbar, 4 sacral and 5 caudal vertebrae; option D wrongly gives only 5 cervical and 7 lumbar vertebrae. Only option A is fully consistent with the chapter.

similar_questions.question: An anatomy chart in a school laboratory in Asmara lists 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones. Calculate the total number of bones in the skull, and state the type of joint that fuses the cranial bones together.
similar_questions.answer: The skull contains 22 bones (8 cranial + 14 facial), and the cranial bones are fused at immovable (fibrous) joints called sutures.

solution_steps.title: Identify the two groups of skull bones
solution_steps.detail: The chapter divides the skull into 8 cranial bones, which are fused together to protect the brain, and 14 facial bones, which form the architecture of the face and support the teeth.

solution_steps.title: Add the two groups
solution_steps.detail: Total skull bones = 8 cranial + 14 facial = 22 bones.

solution_steps.title: Name the joint type
solution_steps.detail: The cranial bones are joined at immovable fibrous joints called sutures, which allow zero movement in order to protect the delicate brain tissue.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed from the regional counts of the vertebral column to the cranial and facial bone counts of the skull, and asked for the joint type instead of matching a list of options.

similar_questions.question: A vertebral column model in a biology laboratory in Keren has lost 3 of its thoracic vertebrae. How many vertebrae remain in the model, and how many of the remaining vertebrae are fused?
similar_questions.answer: 30 vertebrae remain in the model, of which 9 are fused (5 sacral and 4 caudal).

solution_steps.title: State the complete column
solution_steps.detail: A complete vertebral column contains 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused caudal vertebrae.

solution_steps.title: Subtract the lost thoracic vertebrae
solution_steps.detail: The model has lost 3 thoracic vertebrae, so the thoracic region now has 12 - 3 = 9 vertebrae and the whole column has 33 - 3 = 30 vertebrae.

solution_steps.title: Count the fused vertebrae
solution_steps.detail: Only the sacral and caudal regions are fused: 5 sacral + 4 caudal = 9 fused vertebrae. These are unaffected by the loss of thoracic vertebrae, so 9 of the remaining 30 vertebrae are fused.

similar_questions.variant_note: Kept the same regional counts but applied them to a subtraction problem about a damaged laboratory model, requiring the sum of the fused sacral and caudal regions as an extra answer.

questions.question: A fresh long bone sample taken from a slaughtered ox at the abattoir in Asmara has a total mass of 480 g. In bone, the organic matrix makes up approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of the total bone mass and the inorganic mineral salts make up the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$. (a) Calculate the mass of the organic matrix and the mass of the inorganic mineral salts in this sample. (b) The sample is then soaked in a weak acid (vinegar) for several days. State the mass of the sample that remains and describe its physical properties, giving the chemical reason for the change.
questions.answer: (a) Organic matrix = 160 g and inorganic mineral salts = 320 g. (b) 160 g of the sample remains; the bone becomes soft, flexible and rubbery because the acid dissolves the calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) mineral matrix, leaving only the organic collagen matrix.

solution_steps.title: Identify the composition fractions from the chapter
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the organic portion is approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of total bone mass (collagen fibres, ground substance and bone cells) and that the inorganic mineral salts are the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$ (mainly calcium phosphate crystals in the form of hydroxyapatite).

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of the organic matrix
solution_steps.detail: Organic mass = $$\frac{1}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 160\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of the inorganic mineral salts
solution_steps.detail: Inorganic mass = $$\frac{2}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 320\text{ g}$$. Check: 160 g + 320 g = 480 g, which equals the total mass of the sample.

solution_steps.title: Work out the mass remaining after the acid soak
solution_steps.detail: The weak acid dissolves the inorganic mineral matrix (the calcium phosphate salts). Only the organic collagen matrix is left intact, so the remaining mass equals the organic mass, 160 g.

solution_steps.title: Describe the physical change and conclude
solution_steps.detail: Because the hard, rigid mineral component that gives bone its compressional strength has been removed, the bone loses its hardness and rigidity and becomes highly flexible and rubbery, so it can be bent or twisted without breaking.

similar_questions.question: A bone sample of 300 g is baked in an oven at a high temperature for several hours. Using the composition $$\frac{1}{3}$$ organic and $$\frac{2}{3}$$ inorganic, calculate the mass of the sample that remains and describe its physical properties, explaining the chemical basis for the change.
similar_questions.answer: 200 g of the sample remains; the bone becomes extremely brittle and chalky because the heat destroys (denatures) the organic collagen matrix, leaving only the inorganic mineral salts.

solution_steps.title: State the composition of the sample
solution_steps.detail: The organic matrix is $$\frac{1}{3}$$ and the inorganic mineral salts are $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of bone mass, as given in the chapter.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass of organic matrix destroyed
solution_steps.detail: Organic mass = $$\frac{1}{3} \times 300\text{ g} = 100\text{ g}$$. High temperature denatures the collagen fibres and proteins, so this 100 g is destroyed.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the mass remaining
solution_steps.detail: Remaining mass = 300 g - 100 g = 200 g, which is exactly the inorganic fraction $$\frac{2}{3} \times 300\text{ g} = 200\text{ g}$$ of mineral salts.

solution_steps.title: Describe the physical result and conclude
solution_steps.detail: With the organic matrix gone, the bone loses its flexibility and tensile strength; only the hard mineral salts remain, so the bone becomes extremely brittle, chalky and easy to shatter under minimal pressure.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the treatment from soaking in weak acid (which removes the inorganic matrix) to baking at high temperature (which removes the organic matrix), and changed the sample mass from 480 g to 300 g.

similar_questions.question: A dried bone sample from a butcher's shop in Keren is found to contain 210 g of inorganic mineral salts. If the inorganic salts make up $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of bone mass, calculate the total mass of the sample and the mass of its organic matrix.
similar_questions.answer: The total mass of the sample is 315 g and its organic matrix is 105 g.

solution_steps.title: Set up the fraction relationship
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that inorganic mineral salts form $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of total bone mass. Let the total mass be $$M$$, so $$\frac{2}{3}M = 210\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Solve for the total mass
solution_steps.detail: Multiply both sides by $$\frac{3}{2}$$: $$M = 210 \times \frac{3}{2} = 315\text{ g}$$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the organic mass
solution_steps.detail: Organic mass = total mass - inorganic mass = 315 g - 210 g = 105 g. Check: $$\frac{1}{3} \times 315\text{ g} = 105\text{ g}$$, which agrees.

similar_questions.variant_note: Reversed the calculation: the inorganic mass is given and the total mass and organic mass must be derived, using a different sample mass and context.

questions.question: In a Grade 11 biology laboratory in Nakfa, students assemble a model of the adult axial skeleton, which consists of the skull, the vertebral column and the thoracic cage. Using the numbers given in the chapter, (a) calculate the total number of bones in the axial skeleton by adding the skull bones (8 cranial + 14 facial), the 33 vertebrae and the thoracic cage (1 sternum + 12 pairs of ribs); and (b) express this axial total as a percentage of the 206 bones of the adult skeleton, correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) The axial skeleton contains 80 bones. (b) This is $$\frac{80}{206} \times 100\% \approx 38.8\%$$ of the 206 bones of the adult skeleton.

solution_steps.title: Count the skull bones
solution_steps.detail: The skull = 8 cranial bones + 14 facial bones = 22 bones.

solution_steps.title: State the number of vertebrae
solution_steps.detail: The vertebral column contains 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused caudal).

solution_steps.title: Count the bones of the thoracic cage
solution_steps.detail: The thoracic cage = 1 sternum + 12 pairs of ribs = 1 + (12 $$\times$$ 2) = 1 + 24 = 25 bones.

solution_steps.title: Add the three parts to obtain the axial total
solution_steps.detail: Axial skeleton = 22 + 33 + 25 = 80 bones. This agrees with the chapter value of 80 bones for the axial skeleton.

solution_steps.title: Express the axial total as a percentage of the whole skeleton
solution_steps.detail: Percentage = $$\frac{80}{206} \times 100\% = 38.8349\ldots\% \approx 38.8\%$$. Check: the appendicular skeleton is 206 - 80 = 126 bones, and $$\frac{126}{206} \times 100\% \approx 61.2\%$$, and 38.8% + 61.2% = 100%.

similar_questions.question: The bones of one lower limb, as listed in the chapter, are the femur, the patella, the tibia, the fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges. (a) Calculate the number of bones in one lower limb and in both lower limbs. (b) Express the bones of both lower limbs as a percentage of the 126 bones of the appendicular skeleton, correct to one decimal place.
similar_questions.answer: (a) One lower limb has 30 bones, so both lower limbs have 60 bones. (b) $$\frac{60}{126} \times 100\% \approx 47.6\%$$ of the appendicular skeleton.

solution_steps.title: List the single bones of one lower limb
solution_steps.detail: The chapter lists the femur (thigh bone), the patella (kneecap), and the tibia and fibula (shin bones), which are 4 individual bones.

solution_steps.title: Add the numbered groups of one lower limb
solution_steps.detail: One lower limb = 4 + 7 tarsals + 5 metatarsals + 14 phalanges = 4 + 7 + 5 + 14 = 30 bones.

solution_steps.title: Calculate both lower limbs
solution_steps.detail: Both lower limbs = 2 $$\times$$ 30 = 60 bones.

solution_steps.title: Express as a percentage of the appendicular skeleton
solution_steps.detail: Percentage = $$\frac{60}{126} \times 100\% = 47.6190\ldots\% \approx 47.6\%$$.

similar_questions.variant_note: Moved the calculation from the axial skeleton (skull + vertebrae + thoracic cage) to the appendicular lower limb, using per-limb bone counts and a different percentage denominator.

similar_questions.question: The thoracic cage contains 12 pairs of ribs. The top 7 pairs are true ribs, the next 3 pairs are false ribs and the bottom 2 pairs are floating ribs. (a) Calculate the total number of individual ribs. (b) Calculate the percentage of the total ribs that are true ribs and the percentage that are floating ribs, each correct to one decimal place.
similar_questions.answer: (a) There are 24 individual ribs. (b) True ribs = $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% \approx 58.3\%$$ and floating ribs = $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% \approx 16.7\%$$ of all ribs.

solution_steps.title: Convert pairs of ribs into individual ribs
solution_steps.detail: 12 pairs of ribs = 12 $$\times$$ 2 = 24 individual ribs.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the number of true ribs
solution_steps.detail: True ribs are the top 7 pairs, which connect directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilages: 7 $$\times$$ 2 = 14 ribs.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the number of floating ribs
solution_steps.detail: Floating ribs are the bottom 2 pairs, which do not connect to the sternum at all: 2 $$\times$$ 2 = 4 ribs.

solution_steps.title: Express each group as a percentage of 24 ribs
solution_steps.detail: True ribs: $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% = 58.333\ldots\% \approx 58.3\%$$. Floating ribs: $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% = 16.666\ldots\% \approx 16.7\%$$. The remaining 6 false ribs give $$\frac{6}{24} \times 100\% = 25.0\%$$, and 58.3% + 25.0% + 16.7% = 100%.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the calculation to the rib groups of the thoracic cage, converting pairs into individual bones and computing two different percentages instead of one.

questions.question: A cyclist riding from Asmara down to Massawa falls from her bicycle and injures her knee. At the hospital the doctor explains that the knee is a freely movable joint. (a) Describe the structural features of a freely movable (synovial) joint and explain how these features prevent wear and tear on the articulating bone ends during high-impact movement. (b) Classify the elbow joint, the shoulder joint and the atlas-axis joint by their mechanical shape, and state the movement that each one permits.
questions.answer: (a) In a synovial joint the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid and enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane. Articular (hyaline) cartilage cushions the bone ends and absorbs compressional shock, while the synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, so wear and tear are prevented. (b) The elbow is a hinge joint (flexion and extension in a single plane), the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint (multidirectional rotation), and the atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint (rotation around a central axis).

solution_steps.title: Define the freely movable joint
solution_steps.detail: A freely movable (synovial) joint is one in which the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, and the whole joint is enclosed by a tough articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

solution_steps.title: Explain the role of articular cartilage
solution_steps.detail: The bone ends are covered by a layer of articular (hyaline) cartilage. This cartilage cushions the bone ends, absorbs compressional shock and minimises friction between the moving surfaces.

solution_steps.title: Explain the role of synovial fluid and the capsule
solution_steps.detail: The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity; this slippery fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, while the articular capsule holds the fluid in place and keeps the joint stable.

solution_steps.title: Classify the elbow joint
solution_steps.detail: The elbow is a hinge joint, in which a convex surface fits into a concave depression, permitting flexion and extension in a single plane.

solution_steps.title: Classify the shoulder and the atlas-axis joints
solution_steps.detail: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, in which a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes. The atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint, in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation of the head around a central axis.

similar_questions.question: A metalworker in Asmara can swing his arm freely in all directions, yet the bones of his skull cannot move at all. Compare the skull sutures and the shoulder joint in terms of the connective tissue that binds the bones, the range of movement allowed, and the protective or mechanical advantage each arrangement provides.
similar_questions.answer: The skull sutures are immovable (fibrous) joints, bound tightly by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue, allowing zero movement so that the delicate brain is protected. The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) ball-and-socket joint with a joint cavity, synovial fluid, an articular capsule and a synovial membrane, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes so that the arm can be used for mechanical work.

solution_steps.title: Describe the immovable joint
solution_steps.detail: Immovable (fibrous) joints, such as the sutures of the skull, are bound together by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue and allow zero movement.

solution_steps.title: State the advantage of the immovable joint
solution_steps.detail: Because no movement is possible, the fused skull bones form a rigid protective case for the delicate tissues of the brain.

solution_steps.title: Describe the freely movable joint
solution_steps.detail: The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) joint: the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

solution_steps.title: State the mechanical advantage and conclude
solution_steps.detail: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, so a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket and rotational movement in multiple planes is possible. This gives the arm a wide range of movement for lifting and manipulating objects, whereas the skull sutures give protection instead of mobility.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the task from describing one injured knee joint to an explicit comparison between an immovable fibrous joint (skull sutures) and a freely movable ball-and-socket joint (shoulder), adding the protective versus mobility trade-off.

similar_questions.question: A long-distance bus driver in Keren complains of stiffness and pain in his back. Explain how the type of joint between the vertebrae allows the spine to be both flexible and shock-absorbing, and contrast this with the joint that allows the head to turn from side to side.
similar_questions.answer: The vertebrae are joined by slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, which permit limited, restricted movement so the spine is flexible and the discs absorb shock. The side-to-side turning of the head is produced by the pivot joint between the atlas and the axis, which allows rotation around a central axis.

solution_steps.title: Identify the joint between the vertebrae
solution_steps.detail: The 33 vertebrae are separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, making these slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints that are connected by resilient pads of cartilage.

solution_steps.title: Explain the movement and shock absorption
solution_steps.detail: Slightly movable joints permit only limited, restricted movement; this gives the spine flexibility while the discs absorb shock and provide stability.

solution_steps.title: Identify the joint used for turning the head
solution_steps.detail: The first two cervical vertebrae form the atlas-axis joint, which is a pivot joint in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation around a central axis.

solution_steps.title: Contrast the two joint types and conclude
solution_steps.detail: The vertebral joints are cartilaginous and allow only slight movement distributed along the column, whereas the atlas-axis pivot joint allows full rotation of the head. Neither joint is a freely movable synovial joint of the ball-and-socket kind.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the context from a knee injury to back stiffness, and shifted the comparison from hinge/ball-and-socket/pivot classification to slightly movable cartilaginous joints versus a pivot joint.

questions.question: A 13-year-old student in Keren is told by a doctor that the long bones of her arms and legs are still elongating. (a) Explain how endochondral ossification at the epiphyseal plates allows a long bone to increase in length, naming the cells and processes involved. (b) Explain why elongation stops at skeletal maturity. (c) The chapter states that approximately 10% of the entire adult skeleton is completely replaced every year by bone remodeling. Deduce the number of years required for a complete turnover of the skeleton, and name the two cell types responsible for remodeling and state the role of each.
questions.answer: (a) The embryonic cartilage model is invaded by blood vessels that deliver osteoblasts, which replace cartilage with mineralised bone, while at the epiphyseal plate chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side and osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates. (b) Elongation stops because the epiphyseal plates completely ossify at skeletal maturity, leaving no cartilage to be converted into bone. (c) A complete turnover of the skeleton takes $$\frac{100\%}{10\%} = 10\text{ years}$$; the two cell types are osteoblasts (which build and mineralise bone matrix) and osteoclasts (which dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium).

solution_steps.title: State the starting material of the embryonic skeleton
solution_steps.detail: During early fetal development the skeleton is composed almost entirely of flexible hyaline cartilage, and ossification is the process by which this embryonic cartilage is transformed into solid bone.

solution_steps.title: Describe endochondral ossification
solution_steps.detail: In endochondral ossification, blood vessels invade the cartilage models and deliver osteoblasts, which gradually replace the cartilage with a hard mineralised matrix.

solution_steps.title: Explain growth at the epiphyseal plate
solution_steps.detail: In children the epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones. Chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate, while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates.

solution_steps.title: Explain why growth stops at skeletal maturity
solution_steps.detail: The plates continue to allow elongation only until they completely ossify at skeletal maturity. Once the plate has ossified there is no cartilage left for the chondrocytes to divide and for the osteoblasts to replace, so the bone can no longer increase in length.

solution_steps.title: Calculate the time for complete skeletal turnover
solution_steps.detail: If 10% of the skeleton is replaced each year, then the time for a complete turnover is $$\frac{100\%}{10\%\text{ per year}} = 10\text{ years}$$.

solution_steps.title: Name the remodeling cells and their roles
solution_steps.detail: Osteoblasts are bone-building cells that synthesise and deposit the organic osteoid matrix and facilitate its mineralisation. Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated bone-resorbing cells that secrete acids and enzymes to dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium into the blood.

similar_questions.question: A 15-year-old boy in Massawa fractures the shaft of his femur while playing football, and the doctor says the bone will heal rapidly. Explain why bone heals much faster than cartilage following physical trauma, referring to the blood supply and cells of each tissue.
similar_questions.answer: Bone heals rapidly because it is highly vascular: the periosteum is rich in blood vessels and contains bone-forming osteoblasts, and the central canals and perforating canals deliver nutrients and cells directly to the injury site. Cartilage is entirely avascular and must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding perichondrium, so it heals much more slowly.

solution_steps.title: Describe the blood supply and cells of bone
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the outer surface of a bone is covered by the periosteum, a fibrous membrane rich in blood vessels, nerves and bone-forming stem cells called osteoblasts, and that central canals and perforating canals carry vessels into the bone.

solution_steps.title: Link this to rapid repair
solution_steps.detail: Because nutrients and osteoblasts are delivered directly to the fracture site by the rich blood supply, the bone matrix can be rebuilt quickly, which is why a fractured femur shaft heals rapidly.

solution_steps.title: Describe the blood supply of cartilage
solution_steps.detail: Cartilage is entirely avascular (lacking blood vessels), so it must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding tissues (perichondrium) to repair itself.

solution_steps.title: Conclude the comparison
solution_steps.detail: The absence of a direct blood supply makes cartilage repair slow, whereas the highly vascular periosteum, central canals and perforating canals of bone make bone repair comparatively rapid.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed the focus from growth at the epiphyseal plate and remodeling to the comparative healing of a fractured femur versus cartilage, using the vascular supply of bone and the avascular nature of cartilage.

similar_questions.question: A child in Asmara suffers a disorder in which the epiphyseal plates of the long bones ossify completely at the age of 8 years instead of at skeletal maturity. Predict the effect on the length of the child's arms and legs, and explain the role of the growth plate in normal bone elongation, naming the cells involved.
similar_questions.answer: The arms and legs will stop elongating at 8 years and the child will remain unusually short, because the epiphyseal plates have ossified and no cartilage remains. Normally chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone keeps elongating until the plate ossifies at skeletal maturity.

solution_steps.title: Recall the normal role of the epiphyseal plate
solution_steps.detail: The epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones; chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side.

solution_steps.title: Relate the plate to elongation
solution_steps.detail: This continuous division and replacement is what allows bones to elongate during childhood, so the arms and legs grow longer year by year.

solution_steps.title: Apply the premature ossification
solution_steps.detail: If the plates ossify completely at 8 years, there is no cartilage left for chondrocytes to divide and no cartilage for osteoblasts to replace, so elongation of the long bones ceases permanently.

solution_steps.title: State the predicted outcome
solution_steps.detail: The child's arms and legs will stop growing at 8 years and remain short, so the child will be unusually short, whereas normally elongation continues until the plates ossify at skeletal maturity.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changed from a normal 13-year-old with active growth and remodeling to a disorder causing premature ossification of the epiphyseal plates, requiring a prediction of the effect on limb length.
